API reference

Look a name up

Every variable, function, event and option of oav-p5, and every export of every package. Names, signatures and source links are read from the code on each build; what is written about them is checked against the code in CI, so a name cannot be added, renamed or removed without this page noticing.

489 names · 489 described · oav-p5 0.8.3 · framework 0.1.0

One-page cheat sheet → · The same data for tools: reference.json · Adding a name? How to document it

/

Every sketch starts with one line

js
document.head.prepend(Object.assign(document.createElement('script'), { src: 'https://openaudiovisual.com/p5/oav-p5.js' }));

The examples below leave it out to stay short. Copy puts it at the top for you, so what you paste into OpenProcessing (or the p5 editor) runs as it is.

MIDI: knobs, faders, pads, keys#

Read a controller like the mouse (knob1, notePressed), and the raw MIDI messages behind it. 39

oav-p5

controlChange()#

eventoav-p5
function controlChange(cc, value, channel) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI control change (a knob, a fader, the mod wheel, the sustain pedal), whether or not the controller is known.

Declare it the way you declare keyPressed():

js
function controlChange(cc, value, channel) {
  // a control moved
}

It hears every control, including the ones that are not a knob or a fader, such as the mod wheel and the pedals, which knobMoved() never reports. The latest value of every controller number is also in OAVp5.cc, so a sketch that only wants to look can read OAVp5.cc[1] in draw().

For one incoming message the order is: midiMessage(), then the specific one (noteOn(), controlChange(), pitchBend()), then the friendly one (padPressed(), knobMoved(), notePressed() and their partners).

Before it has a value

Defining the function is enough. oav-p5 asks the browser for Web MIDI when it loads (the default, ?oav_hardware=auto), and a sketch that defines it also gets a card if Web MIDI is missing or blocked. Keys from 🎹, a phone, OAVp5.input() and other programs reach it too. OAVp5.on('controlChange', fn) does the same without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops it.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
ccNumberThe controller number, 0 to 127 (1 is the mod wheel, 64 the sustain pedal, 74 the first knob on a MiniLab 3).
valueNumberWhere the control is now, 0 to 1 (MIDI's 0 to 127 divided by 127).
channelNumberThe MIDI channel, 1 to 16.

Notes

  • An error inside it does not stop the music: the next message is still handled, and the message shows in the console and on a card beside the 🎹, with the file and line.

Examples

Related

  • knobMoved() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it whenever a knob moves.
  • faderMoved() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it whenever a fader moves.
  • OAVp5.cc An array of 128 numbers, one per MIDI controller number: where each control last was, 0 to 1. OAVp5.cc[1] is the mod wheel, OAVp5.cc[64] the sustain pedal.
  • midiMessage() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI message it receives, with the raw bytes and where they came from.
  • OAVp5.on() Listens to a MIDI event by name without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops listening.
  • OAVp5.input() Sends one MIDI message into oav-p5 by hand, as bytes: the whole sketch reacts as if a controller had sent it.

fader1#

variableoav-p5
fader1

Also: fader2 fader3 fader4 fader5 fader6 fader7 fader8

The position of a controller fader (slider), from 0 to 1: fader1 is the first fader, up to fader8.

Works exactly like knob1, for the controller's faders, numbered in the order the controller's profile lists them (as printed on the device). A controller with only four faders, like the MiniLab 3, has fader1 to fader4.

Type
Number
Range
0..1

Changes when the fader moves; 0 until it has moved.

Before it has a value

Nothing to call. Web MIDI is asked for at load, exactly as for a knob (knob1); reading a fader also makes a missing or refused Web MIDI show as a card.

Examples

Related

  • fader() Returns the position of fader number n, from 0 to 1: the same as fader1 to fader8, for any n.
  • knob1 The position of a controller knob, from 0 to 1: knob1 is the first knob, knob2 the second, up to knob8.
  • faderMoved() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it whenever a fader moves.

knob()#

functionoav-p5
knob(n)

Returns the position of knob number n, from 0 to 1: the same as knob1 to knob8, for any n.

Use it when the number of the knob is a variable: for (let i = 1; i <= 16; i++) bar(i, knob(i));. It also works in a sketch that has its own knob1, which oav-p5 then leaves alone.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
nNumberWhich knob, counting from 1 (as printed on the controller).

Returns

Number The knob's position, 0..1; 0 until it has been turned.

  • pad() Returns how hard pad number n is pressed, 0 to 1: the same as pad1 to pad16, for any n.

knob1#

variableoav-p5
knob1

Also: knob2 knob3 knob4 knob5 knob6 knob7 knob8

The position of a controller knob, from 0 to 1: knob1 is the first knob, knob2 the second, up to knob8.

Read it in draw() the way you read mouseX: background(knob1 * 255). Knobs are numbered the way they are printed on the controller, so knob 1 is knob 1 on any controller OAV has a profile for: the MiniLab 3's first knob is CC 74, the LPD8's is CC 70. The sketch never needs to know a CC number.

On a controller OAV has no profile for, the first knob you turn becomes knob1, the next one knob2, and so on, in the order you turn them. Past eight, use knob(n).

Type
Number
Range
0..1

Changes when the knob moves, not once per frame; the sketch just reads the latest value. 0 until the knob has been turned.

Before it has a value

Nothing to call. With the default hardware=auto, oav-p5 asks the browser for Web MIDI as soon as it loads, whatever the sketch reads (Chrome, Edge and Firefox have it; Safari and iPad do not: use 🎹 or a phone there). Reading a knob also tells oav-p5 the sketch plays from MIDI, so when Web MIDI is missing or refused a card beside the 🎹 says so; a sketch that uses none of this never sees that card. ?oav_hardware=click waits for the 🎹 panel instead.

Notes

  • A sketch that already has its own knob1 (a let, a function) keeps it, and a card beside the 🎹 says what to read instead (knob(1)).
  • With OP Configurator, knobs also drive the OPC sliders in the order they are declared. A knob the sketch reads itself stays the sketch's: that slider no longer follows it.

Examples

Related

  • knob() Returns the position of knob number n, from 0 to 1: the same as knob1 to knob8, for any n.
  • fader1 The position of a controller fader (slider), from 0 to 1: fader1 is the first fader, up to fader8.
  • pad1 How hard a drum pad is pressed, from 0 to 1: pad1 is the first pad, up to pad16; 0 when it is let go.
  • knobMoved() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it whenever a knob moves.
  • noteIsDown() True while the key n (a MIDI number or a name like 'C4') is held down.

knobMoved()#

eventoav-p5
function knobMoved(n, value) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it whenever a knob moves.

Like mouseMoved() for knobs:

js
function knobMoved(n, value) {

It is called for every step the knob sends, so many times per second while it turns. To read a knob once a frame, use knob1 instead.

midiMessage()#

eventoav-p5
function midiMessage(bytes, source) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI message it receives, with the raw bytes and where they came from.

Declare it the way you declare keyPressed():

js
function midiMessage(bytes, source) {
  // anything that came in
}

It is the widest net: it is called first for every note, control change and pitch bend, and it is the only function that hears the messages oav-p5 has no friendlier name for, such as channel pressure (0xD0), polyphonic aftertouch (0xA0) and program change (0xC0). The OAVp5.last object keeps the latest note, control change or pitch bend, but not those.

It does not hear system messages: the MIDI clock, start, stop and song position go to OAVp5.clock, and system-exclusive messages are dropped. A note-on with velocity 0 arrives here as it was sent (a note-on with 0), while noteOff() is the one that treats it as a release.

For one incoming message the order is: midiMessage(), then the specific one (noteOn(), controlChange(), pitchBend()), then the friendly one (padPressed(), knobMoved(), notePressed() and their partners).

Before it has a value

Defining the function is enough. oav-p5 asks the browser for Web MIDI when it loads (the default, ?oav_hardware=auto), and a sketch that defines it also gets a card if Web MIDI is missing or blocked. Keys from 🎹, a phone, OAVp5.input() and other programs reach it too. OAVp5.on('midiMessage', fn) does the same without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops it.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
bytesArray<Number>The message as three numbers [status, data1, data2]. The status byte holds the kind in its top half and the channel in its bottom half (0x90 is a note-on on channel 1, 0x93 on channel 4). The data bytes are 0 to 127, and a byte the message does not have is 0.
sourceStringWhere it came from: 'hardware' (a real controller), 'screen' (the 🎹), 'phone', 'virtual-out' (a program playing into OAV Virtual MIDI), 'link' (another page in the same room), or whatever label you gave OAVp5.input().

Notes

  • An error inside it does not stop the music: the next message is still handled, and the message shows in the console and on a card beside the 🎹, with the file and line.

Examples

Related

  • noteOn() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI note-on, with the key, how hard and the channel.
  • controlChange() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI control change (a knob, a fader, the mod wheel, the sustain pedal), whether or not the controller is known.
  • pitchBend() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it whenever the pitch wheel moves, with its position from −1 to 1.
  • OAVp5.last The latest note, control change or pitch bend that arrived: its type, number, value, channel, where it came from and which control it is. null before any.
  • OAVp5.on() Listens to a MIDI event by name without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops listening.
  • OAVp5.input() Sends one MIDI message into oav-p5 by hand, as bytes: the whole sketch reacts as if a controller had sent it.

note#

variableoav-p5
note

The MIDI number (0 to 127) of the last key pressed.

Middle C is 60, A4 is 69. noteName(note) writes the number as a name (60 → 'C4') and noteFreq(note) as a frequency in Hz. velocity says how hard it was pressed. For every key, not just the last, define notePressed().

Type
Number
Range
0..127

Set when a key goes down and kept after it is released; 0 before any key has been pressed.

Before it has a value

Nothing to call. Web MIDI is asked for at load (see knob1). Unlike a knob, merely reading note does not tell oav-p5 the sketch plays from MIDI: defining notePressed() or reading a knob or pad does, which is what makes a missing or refused Web MIDI show as a card. 🎹 and a phone always work.

Notes

  • A sketch with its own note (a let note, a function) keeps it; read midi.last.note instead. oav-p5 says so in a card the first time.

Examples

Related

  • velocity How hard the last key was pressed, from 0 to 1.
  • noteIsPressed True while at least one key is held down.
  • notePressed() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it each time a key (or a pad) goes down.
  • noteName() Turns a MIDI number into a note name: noteName(61) is 'C#4'.

noteOff()#

eventoav-p5
function noteOff(note, channel) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI note-off, with the key and the channel.

The partner of noteOn():

js
function noteOff(note, channel) {
  // a key or pad came up
}

It is called for a note-off message and also for a note-on with velocity 0, which many keyboards send instead. There is no velocity: oav-p5 does not pass the release velocity.

For one incoming message the order is: midiMessage(), then the specific one (noteOn(), controlChange(), pitchBend()), then the friendly one (padPressed(), knobMoved(), notePressed() and their partners).

Before it has a value

Defining the function is enough. oav-p5 asks the browser for Web MIDI when it loads (the default, ?oav_hardware=auto), and a sketch that defines it also gets a card if Web MIDI is missing or blocked. Keys from 🎹, a phone, OAVp5.input() and other programs reach it too. OAVp5.on('noteOff', fn) does the same without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops it.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
noteNumberThe MIDI number of the key that came up, 0 to 127.
channelNumberThe MIDI channel, 1 to 16.

Notes

  • An error inside it does not stop the music: the next message is still handled, and the message shows in the console and on a card beside the 🎹, with the file and line.

Examples

Related

  • noteOn() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI note-on, with the key, how hard and the channel.
  • noteReleased() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it each time a key (or a pad) is let go.

noteOn()#

eventoav-p5
function noteOn(note, velocity, channel) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI note-on, with the key, how hard and the channel.

Declare it the way you declare keyPressed():

js
function noteOn(note, velocity, channel) {
  // a key or pad went down
}

It is called once per note-on message, as it came in. It is the level below notePressed(): the same moment, but with the channel, and for pads too, even when the sketch defines padPressed(). A note-on with velocity 0, which some keyboards send instead of a note-off, is not a note-on here: it calls noteOff().

For one incoming message the order is: midiMessage(), then the specific one (noteOn(), controlChange(), pitchBend()), then the friendly one (padPressed(), knobMoved(), notePressed() and their partners).

Before it has a value

Defining the function is enough. oav-p5 asks the browser for Web MIDI when it loads (the default, ?oav_hardware=auto), and a sketch that defines it also gets a card if Web MIDI is missing or blocked. Keys from 🎹, a phone, OAVp5.input() and other programs reach it too. OAVp5.on('noteOn', fn) does the same without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops it.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
noteNumberThe MIDI number of the key, 0 to 127 (60 is middle C). noteName(note) turns it into a name.
velocityNumberHow hard, above 0 and up to 1 (MIDI's 1 to 127 divided by 127).
channelNumberThe MIDI channel, 1 to 16. Pads on the MiniLab 3 and the LPD8 send on channel 10.

Notes

  • An error inside it does not stop the music: the next message is still handled, and the message shows in the console and on a card beside the 🎹, with the file and line.

Examples

Related

  • noteOff() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI note-off, with the key and the channel.
  • notePressed() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it each time a key (or a pad) goes down.
  • padPressed() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it each time a drum pad is hit.
  • midiMessage() You define this function; oav-p5 calls it for every MIDI message it receives, with the raw bytes and where they came from.

  • OAVp5.input() Sends one MIDI message into oav-p5 by hand, as bytes: the whole sketch reacts as if a controller had sent it.

notePressed()#

eventoav-p5
function notePressed(note, velocity) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it each time a key (or a pad) goes down.

Declare it the way you declare keyPressed():

js
function notePressed(note, velocity) {
  // a key went down
}

It is called once per key, with the key and how hard. A pad also calls it, unless the sketch defines padPressed().

Before it has a value

Defining it is enough: oav-p5 calls it from every source, and if Web MIDI is missing or refused it says so in a card beside the 🎹 (Web MIDI itself is asked for at load, see knob1). Keys from 🎹 and from a phone call it too.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
noteNumberThe MIDI number of the key (60 is middle C). noteName(note) turns it into a name.
velocityNumberHow hard, 0..1.

Notes

  • An error inside it does not stop the music: the next key still plays, and the message shows in the console and on a card beside the 🎹, with the file and line.

pad1#

variableoav-p5
pad1

Also: pad2 pad3 pad4 pad5 pad6 pad7 pad8 pad9 pad10 pad11 pad12 pad13 pad14 pad15 pad16

How hard a drum pad is pressed, from 0 to 1: pad1 is the first pad, up to pad16; 0 when it is let go.

Read it like a held mouse button that also knows how hard: if (pad1 > 0) fill(255, 90, 31). Pads are numbered in the order the controller's profile lists them. To react once per hit rather than ask every frame, define padPressed().

Type
Number
Range
0..1

The velocity of the hit while the pad is held (1 is as hard as the controller sends), and 0 as soon as it is released.

Before it has a value

Nothing to call. Web MIDI is asked for at load, exactly as for a knob (knob1); reading a pad also makes a missing or refused Web MIDI show as a card.

Examples

Related

pitchBend()#

eventoav-p5
function pitchBend(value, channel) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it whenever the pitch wheel moves, with its position from −1 to 1.

Declare it the way you declare keyPressed():

js
function pitchBend(value, channel) {
  // the wheel moved
}

A pitch wheel usually springs back to the middle when you let go, so you will hear a stream of values ending at 0. MIDI sends the position as 14 bits (0 to 16383, with 8192 in the middle). oav-p5 hands it to you as −1 to 1. The latest position is also in OAVp5.bend.

For one incoming message the order is: midiMessage(), then the specific one (noteOn(), controlChange(), pitchBend()), then the friendly one (padPressed(), knobMoved(), notePressed() and their partners).

Before it has a value

Defining the function is enough. oav-p5 asks the browser for Web MIDI when it loads (the default, ?oav_hardware=auto), and a sketch that defines it also gets a card if Web MIDI is missing or blocked. Keys from 🎹, a phone, OAVp5.input() and other programs reach it too. OAVp5.on('pitchBend', fn) does the same without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops it.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
valueNumberThe wheel's position: −1 all the way down, 0 in the middle, 1 all the way up.
channelNumberThe MIDI channel, 1 to 16.

Notes

  • Pitch bend is not mapped to anything else: there is no bend variable, only this function and OAVp5.bend.
  • An error inside it does not stop the music: the next message is still handled, and the message shows in the console and on a card beside the 🎹, with the file and line.

Examples

OAVp5.bend

Where the pitch wheel is, from −1 (all the way down) through 0 (middle) to 1 (all the way up).

Read it in draw() like a knob that goes both ways: x = width / 2 + OAVp5.bend * 150. MIDI sends the position as 14 bits (0 to 16383, with 8192 in the middle). oav-p5 maps the two halves to −1..0 and 0..1, so full travel reaches exactly −1 and 1. To be told on every movement, define pitchBend().

OAVp5.connectHardware()#

functionoav-p5
OAVp5.connectHardware()

Asks the browser for Web MIDI now, and returns a promise that says whether a real controller can be heard.

It does what ?oav_hardware=auto does at load, at a moment you pick: from a button, after an intro, or when hardware is click or off. It works whatever the option says. After a refusal you can call it again to retry, but browsers usually remember a refusal and answer at once, so the way out is the lock icon left of the address.

Before you call it

A browser with Web MIDI (Chrome, Edge, Firefox), on https or localhost. Some browsers want a click first: call it from mousePressed() or a button handler if setup() is too early. Safari and iPad have none: the promise resolves false and OAVp5.hardware is 'unavailable'.

Returns

Promise<Boolean> Resolves to true once the browser has allowed Web MIDI (with or without a device plugged in), and to false if it refused or there is no Web MIDI in this browser. Calling it again while it is asking, or after it said yes, gives the same answer.

Examples

Related

  • OAVp5.devices The names of the MIDI controllers plugged in, as the browser reports them: an array of text, empty when there is none.
  • hardware When oav-p5 asks the browser for Web MIDI, which a real controller needs: auto at load, click when the 🎹 panel opens, or off.

OAVp5.hardware#

OAVp5.hardware

Where Web MIDI stands: 'off', 'asking', 'connected', 'waiting', 'denied' or 'unavailable'.

'off': Web MIDI has not been asked for yet (see hardware). 'asking': waiting for the browser's permission answer. 'connected': allowed, and at least one device is plugged in (OAVp5.devices lists them). 'waiting': allowed, but no device yet: plug one in and it becomes 'connected' by itself. 'denied': the permission was refused. 'unavailable': the browser has no Web MIDI (Safari, iPad) or could not open it.

It is only about real hardware. The on-screen controller and a phone work in every state.

OAVp5.input()#

functionoav-p5
OAVp5.input(bytes, [source], [device])

Sends one MIDI message into oav-p5 by hand, as bytes: the whole sketch reacts as if a controller had sent it.

It is the door every input goes through, and you can knock on it yourself: a sketch can test itself without a controller, drive itself from a timer, or take messages from a WebSocket or another library. The sketch cannot tell the difference: knob1, notePressed(), OAVp5.note, the sound if startSound() is on and the drum cues all react. OAVp5.play() is the friendlier way to send a note.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
bytesArray<Number>One message, [status, data1, data2]: [0x90, 60, 100] is a note-on for key 60 with velocity 100 on channel 1, [0xB0, 74, 127] a control change, [0xE0, 0, 64] a pitch bend in the middle. The status byte sets the kind (top half) and the channel (bottom half). Only the first three numbers are read, and the data bytes are held to 0 to 127. System messages are not for this: the clock bytes (0xF8, 0xFA, 0xFB, 0xFC, 0xF2) go to OAVp5.clock, and anything else from 0xF0 up is ignored.
sourceStringA label for where it came from, which shows up as OAVp5.last.source and as the second argument of midiMessage(). Any text. 'hardware' and 'virtual-out' are taken as those real sources and are not repeated to a sketch's own Web MIDI code. optional default 'screen'
deviceStringA profile id such as 'akai-lpd8': the numbering of knob1, pad1 … follows that controller for this message. Left out, it is the controller on the on-screen panel. optional

Notes

  • midi.input(…) is the same function. It returns nothing. A message with a source other than 'screen' also lights the keys of the on-screen controller if it is open.

Examples

OAVp5.last

A single object that is replaced on every message, so read it, do not keep it. It is how a sketch finds out where a message came from (OAVp5.last.source) or which knob moved (OAVp5.last.control), and what to read when the sketch has its own note or velocity that keeps the plain names: OAVp5.last.note and OAVp5.last.value.

OAVp5.on()#

functionoav-p5
OAVp5.on(name, fn)

Listens to a MIDI event by name without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops listening.

The event functions (notePressed(), knobMoved(), noteOn() …) are defined once, by name. OAVp5.on('notePressed', fn) is the other way: any number of listeners, added and removed while the sketch runs, with no global names taken. It is how a library, a class or a Hydra sketch listens, and the way to listen for a while and stop.

A listener counts as a defined function for the pad rule: once anything listens to 'padPressed', a pad stops calling notePressed(). An error inside fn shows in the console and on a card, and the other listeners still run. For the microphone's events use OAVp5.mic.on().

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
nameStringThe event: 'notePressed', 'noteReleased', 'knobMoved', 'faderMoved', 'padPressed', 'padReleased', 'noteOn', 'noteOff', 'controlChange', 'pitchBend' or 'midiMessage'. 'noteon' and 'noteoff' work in any case. Anything else throws an error that lists the names.
fnFunctionCalled with the same arguments the function of that name would get (notePressed(note, velocity), knobMoved(n, value) …).

Returns

Function A function that takes fn off again: const off = OAVp5.on(…); off();.

Notes

  • midi.on(…) is the same function.

Plays a key as if a controller did: midi.play(60, 0.8) presses middle C, midi.play(60, 0) lets it go.

Lists which controller knob, fader or pad drives which OpenProcessing OPC variable right now: [{ control: 'knob1', name: 'radius' }, …].

With OP Configurator, OPC.slider('radius', 10) declares a variable and oav-p5 wires the controller to the OPC variables in order: knob 1 to the first slider, knob 2 to the second, the faders after the knobs, pad 1 to the first toggle or button. Microphone and audio analysis#

How loud (micLevel), bass / mid / treble, beats; @openav/audio underneath. 26

bass#

variableoav-p5
bass

Also: mid treble

How much of the microphone's sound is low (bass), middle (mid) or high (treble), each from 0 to 1.

Use them like micLevel, one number per band: fill(200 + bass * 160, 70, 100) pushes the colour with the low end. The three share one entry because they behave the same; only the frequency range differs.

Unlike micLevel they are not measured in decibels: each is the average strength of the frequencies in its band, scaled by micSensitivity() and held to 1. A band that is faint in your room can stay close to 0; raise the sensitivity rather than multiplying by a large number.

Type
Number
Range
0..1

The energy in 20–250 Hz (bass), 250–2000 Hz (mid) and 2000–8000 Hz (treble). Updated once per display frame while the microphone is on; 0 otherwise.

Before it has a value

Reading any of them asks for the microphone the first time, exactly like micLevel; until you allow it they are 0.

Notes

  • A sketch that already has its own variable, function or library called bass, mid or treble keeps it: oav-p5 leaves that name alone and never starts the microphone for it. Assigning one later turns the name back into a plain variable.

beat#

variableoav-p5
beat

True for one frame each time the microphone (or the drum machine) hears a beat.

It behaves like mouseIsPressed while a button is down, except the "press" lasts one frame: if (beat) flash = 1; is all it takes to react to the music. A beat is a jump in loudness over what the room has been doing, with at least 100 ms between two beats; two beats between two frames count as one.

When the drum machine is playing, beat is also true for a frame on every kick and snare, so a sketch written for the microphone moves over to the machine unchanged.

Type
Boolean

True in the first draw() after a beat, and false until the next one. Reading it twice in the same frame gives the same answer.

Before it has a value

Reading beat asks for the microphone the first time, like micLevel. If you would rather be called, define beatDetected().

Examples

beatDetected()#

eventoav-p5
function beatDetected(level) {}

You define this function; oav-p5 calls it each time the microphone (or the drum machine) hears a beat.

Declare it the way you declare keyPressed():

js
function beatDetected(level) {
  // flash, spawn, jump to the next scene
}

It is called once per beat, right when the beat lands, not once per frame. Use beat instead if you would rather ask each frame.

Before it has a value

A sketch that defines beatDetected() and reads no microphone value starts the microphone on the first click or key. When the drum machine is on, the same function is called for its kicks and snares and the microphone is not opened for it. OAVp5.mic.on('beat', fn) hears the same beats without defining a global and returns a function that stops listening, but a listener alone never starts the microphone: read micLevel or call startMic() as well.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
levelNumberHow loud it was at that moment, 0..1 (the value of micLevel).

Notes

  • If your function throws, the sketch keeps running: the error appears in the console and as a card beside the 🎹 with the file and line.

Examples

kickDetected()#

eventoav-p5
function kickDetected(level) {}

Also: snareDetected hatDetected

You define these; oav-p5 calls them when the microphone (or the drum machine) hears a kick, a snare or a hat.

The microphone splits what it hears into three drum-like bands and calls the matching function when each band jumps: 20–120 Hz for the kick, 150–800 Hz for the snare, 6–14 kHz for the hat. There is no machine learning in it, just a transient in a frequency band, so a bass voice can trigger a kick.

When the drum machine plays, each of its hits calls the same functions: kick for the kick, snare for a snare, clap or rim, hat for a closed, open or pedal hat. A sketch written for the microphone therefore works with startDrums() unchanged.

While the drum machine plays, only its hits call these functions (from oav-p5 0.8.1). A microphone that is on at the same time mostly hears the drums coming out of the speakers, so its hits would call the same function twice and hear a kick as a snare. micLevel, bass, mid and treble still follow the microphone; the microphone's hits come back when the drums stop.

Before it has a value

Defining one of them is not enough to open the microphone once the drum machine has started; reading micLevel (or calling startMic()) is. Without the drum machine, a sketch that defines any of them and reads nothing starts the microphone on the first click or key.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
levelNumberHow strong the hit was, 0..1 (for the drum machine, its velocity).

Examples

kickIsDetected#

kickIsDetected

True in the one frame after a kick (snare, hat) is heard, from the drum machine or the microphone, like mouseIsPressed for a hit.

The same hits that call kickDetected(), snareDetected() and hatDetected(), as a value you read in draw() instead of a function you write. Hand it to lag() and it becomes a number that jumps to 1 on the hit and fades: lag(kickIsDetected, 0, 0.3) is 1 on a kick and back near 0 about 0.3 s later, ready for an alpha or a size. lag() takes true as 1.

While the drum machine plays, only its hits count. Reading these does not ask for the microphone by itself: with no drums, it counts as wanting the microphone's hits, the way defining kickDetected() does, so the first click on the page opens it.

lastKickTs#

variableoav-p5
lastKickTs

Also: lastSnareTs lastHatTs lastBeatTs

When the last kick (snare, hat, beat) came, on the millis() clock: millis() - lastKickTs is how many ms ago.

micLevel#

variableoav-p5
micLevel

How loud the microphone hears things, from 0 (a quiet room) to 1 (shouting).

Read it in draw() the way you read mouseX: circle(width / 2, height / 2, 50 + micLevel * 300) grows when someone talks. It is a loudness in decibels, which is how an ear hears it, measured from the room itself: the bottom of the scale follows the room's own noise (it settles within a second or two and rises at most 1.5 dB a second, so a voice never becomes the new silence), and −10 dBFS, shouting into a laptop, is 1.

In practice a quiet room reads 0, a quiet voice about 0.4 to 0.6, shouting close to 1. If the microphone is quiet or far away, raise it with micSensitivity().

It follows the browser's animation frames rather than draw(), so a sketch running at frameRate(10) still reads the latest value, and the number stops changing while the tab is hidden (browsers pause animation frames there).

Type
Number
Range
0..1

Updated once per display frame while the microphone is on. It is 0 while the microphone is off, still asking, blocked or missing.

Before it has a value

Nothing to call. The first time a sketch reads micLevel (or bass, mid, treble, beat), oav-p5 asks the browser for the microphone, and every value stays 0 until you allow it. The page needs https or localhost. If the browser kept audio quiet until a click, the first click or key starts it. ?oav_mic=click makes only the 🎤 button and startMic() turn it on; ?oav_mic=off means nothing can.

Notes

  • In the 🎹 panel the 🎤 button turns the microphone on and off by hand and shows the level. When the browser blocked it, a card beside the 🎹 says why and what to press: click the lock left of the address, set Microphone to Allow, then click the canvas.
  • On openprocessing.org the sketch frame allows the microphone and MIDI (checked 2026-10-19: its allow list contains microphone and midi), and the first read of micLevel there asks for the microphone. An embed code copied from OpenProcessing does not carry that: add allow="microphone" to that <iframe>.
  • The raw numbers behind it are OAVp5.mic.rms (0..1), OAVp5.mic.db and OAVp5.mic.floor (the room's own noise, in dBFS).

Examples

On openprocessing.org the pasted sketch runs, loads oav-p5 and asks for the microphone, but the sound itself was not tried there: the browser used for the check blocks the microphone, so the allow-and-listen step is still unconfirmed on that site.

micSensitivity()#

functionoav-p5
micSensitivity([v])

Makes the microphone more or less sensitive: micSensitivity(2) is twice as sensitive, micSensitivity() says what it is now.

The number multiplies what the microphone hears. On micLevel, 2 adds 6 dB; on bass, mid and treble it multiplies by 2 (they stay held to 1). Use it for a quiet microphone or a far-away voice: micSensitivity(3) in setup() adds about 9.5 dB.

startMic()#

functionoav-p5
startMic()

Turns the microphone on and returns a promise that says whether it worked.

You rarely need it: reading micLevel and its friends already starts the microphone. Call it when you want to choose the moment (a button, the end of an intro) or know the answer: startMic().then((ok) => { … }). Calling it again while it is on, or while the browser is still asking, returns the same result.

Before you call it

Browsers want a click before audio plays: call it from mousePressed() or a button handler if setup() is too early. It works whatever the mic option is, except ?oav_mic=off, where nothing can start the microphone.

Returns

Promise<Boolean> Resolves to true once the microphone is on, false if it was blocked, is missing, or the mic option is off.

Notes

  • After stopMic(), only startMic() (or 🎤) turns it back on; reading micLevel does not.

Examples

Related

OAVp5.mic#

objectoav-p5
OAVp5.mic

The microphone under the plain names: its state, the numbers of micLevel and bass that never turn it on when read, the raw loudness, start, stop and events.

Everything the microphone names (micLevel, bass, micIsOn, startMic() …) read from here. The difference is that reading OAVp5.mic.level never asks for the microphone: the plain micLevel does, the first time. So OAVp5.mic is for code that must look without waking anything: a status line, a library, a sketch with ?oav_mic=click.

The members: state, error, sensitivity (also gain), level, bass (also mid, treble), rms, db, floor, analyzer, start(), stop() and on().

Notes

  • This is advanced. For most sketches the plain names are all you need.

Examples

OAVp5.mic.analyzer

The AudioAnalyzer from @openav/audio that listens to the microphone, while the microphone is on; null otherwise.

A way into the audio itself when the 0 to 1 numbers are not enough: read the spectrum of the microphone with the browser's own OAVp5.mic.analyzer.analyser.getByteFrequencyData(array), or connect your own Web Audio nodes to it. oav-p5 updates the analyzer once per frame, so do not call its update() yourself.

Type
AudioAnalyzer | null

Made when the microphone starts and dropped when it stops. It has its own AudioContext (OAVp5.mic.analyzer.ctx) and the Web Audio AnalyserNode it reads from (OAVp5.mic.analyzer.analyser).

OAVp5.mic.floor#

variableoav-p5
OAVp5.mic.floor

The room's own noise as oav-p5 has measured it, in dBFS: the level that micLevel treats as silence (plus 6 dB).

A humming classroom should not read as loud, so micLevel is measured from the room itself: this floor follows the quietest recent readings. It drops within a second when the room gets quieter and rises at most 1.5 dB a second when it gets noisier, so a voice never becomes the new silence. 6 dB above the floor reads 0 on micLevel.

Type
Number
Range
-70..-45

Starts at −60 and is always held between −70 and −45. Updated once per display frame while the microphone is on.

Notes

  • Stopping the microphone does not reset it: the next start continues from the last floor.

Listens to a microphone event ('beat', 'kick', 'snare' or 'hat') without defining a global function, and returns a function that stops listening.

@openav/audio

AudioAnalyzer#

class@openav/audio
new AudioAnalyzer({ signals = null, fftSize = 2048, smooth = 0.7 } = {})

Listens to the microphone, an audio element or any Web Audio node, and turns it into loudness, three bands, onsets and kick, snare and hat hits.

An AudioAnalyzer wraps one Web Audio AnalyserNode. You give it a sound (enableMic(), enableElement(el), or connect your own node into input()), call update() once per frame, and it returns a plain object of numbers, which it also publishes as audio/* signals if you gave it a signals bus. This is the analysis under the microphone of a p5 sketch: micLevel is its rms turned into decibels, bass, mid and treble are its low, mid and high, and beat and kickDetected() come from its onset and kick.

update() returns null until a source is enabled. After that it returns { rms, peak, low, mid, high, centroid, onset, kick, snare, hat }. rms is the smoothed loudness and peak the loudest sample of the moment, both 0..1 of full scale (from float samples where the browser has them, so a quiet room is measured, not rounded to one 8-bit step). A voice is a small rms: scale it, or map it through a window. low, mid and high are the average strength of the spectrum in 20–250 Hz, 250–2000 Hz and 2000–8000 Hz, 0..1, taken from the analyser's byte spectrum, so they are not decibels and a faint band stays near 0. centroid is the spectrum's centre of mass, 0..1 of the way from 0 Hz to half the sample rate (the brightness). onset is true for the one update() in which the loudness jumped over its adaptive floor, with at least 100 ms between two onsets.

kick, snare and hat are { hit, level, env }, found by looking for a sudden rise in one band of the spectrum, with no machine learning: kick 20–120 Hz, snare 150–800 Hz, hat 6000–14000 Hz. hit is true on the update that found one (at least 90, 90 and 60 ms apart), level is the band's strength now, and env is 0..1: it jumps to min(1, level × 2) on a hit and then shrinks by 12% every update(), about 120 ms at 60 frames a second. Because it decays per update, it falls faster if you call update() less often.

With a signals bus, these are published: audio/rms, audio/peak, audio/band/low, audio/band/mid, audio/band/high, audio/centroid, audio/kick/env, audio/snare/env and audio/hat/env (continuous, 0..1), and the pulses audio/onset { rms }, audio/kick { level }, audio/snare { level } and audio/hat { level }. Pulses fire only when something was found.

Before you call it

Browsers start audio only after a user gesture. enableMic() asks for the microphone, and the analyser's AudioContext stays suspended until the page has had a click or a key: update() calls resume() on every frame, so the numbers start by themselves after the first click. Until then they are all 0. The page needs https or localhost for the microphone.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsA Signals bus to publish into. With one, the audio/* signals are defined when you construct the analyzer and set on every update(). Without one, update() only returns the numbers. optional default null
fftSizeNumberThe size of the analyser's FFT, a power of two from 32 to 32768. The spectrum has half as many bins. optional default 2048
smoothNumberHow much of the previous rms is kept each update, 0..1. Higher is smoother and slower: rms = rms × smooth + now × (1 − smooth). optional default 0.7

Members

NameDescription
enableMic()methodAsks the browser for the microphone, with echo cancellation, noise suppression and auto gain off, and connects it. Returns a promise that resolves to true. It rejects when the permission is refused or there is no microphone, with the browser's error (NotAllowedError, NotFoundError…).
enableElement(el)methodAnalyses an <audio> or <video> element: enableElement(el) returns true. The element keeps playing to the speakers. Web Audio takes an element in only once, so a second enableElement() for the same element throws a browser error.
input()methodReturns the AnalyserNode (creating the context first), so you can bring your own sound: node.connect(audio.input()). Any node of audio.ctx works; for Tone.js, connect its raw node. Nothing is routed to the speakers by this.
update()methodCall it once per frame. Reads the analyser, works out the numbers, publishes the signals if there is a bus, and returns the object { rms, peak, low, mid, high, centroid, onset, kick, snare, hat }, or null when no source is enabled yet. It also resumes a suspended context.

Notes

  • It makes its own AudioContext, so p5.sound or Tone.js can run beside it. To analyse a sound that lives in another context, connect a node of audio.ctx into input(), or use enableElement().
  • enableMic() turns off echo cancellation, noise suppression and automatic gain, because they change the loudness you want to measure. On a laptop that plays the sound it listens to, expect the speakers to leak into the microphone.

Examples

To be confirmed

Typical rms values for speech differ between the notes of this project: the handbook (docs/inputs.md) says speech often sits around 0.05 to 0.2, a comment in oav-p5 says 0.01 to 0.05. They depend on the microphone and the room, and have not been measured here, so no typical number is given.

Whether notes are being heard right now: true once startSound() has finished, false before and after.

startSound()#

functionoav-p5
startSound([id])

Also: OAVp5.sound.start

Makes the keys you play heard through an instrument you name, and returns a promise that says whether sound is on.

Call it once in setup(): startSound('organ'). From then on every note you play is heard: a MIDI keyboard, the 🎹 on screen, a phone, midi.play(60, 0.8). Your own notePressed() still gets the note, and the sound is made before the sketch is told, so a slow callback never delays it. Pads on MIDI channel 10 (the General MIDI drum channel) play the drum kit instead of the instrument, and the sustain pedal holds notes.

The instrument ids are piano, epiano, organ, strings, choir, harp, marimba, vibraphone, xylophone, glockenspiel, music-box and the synth presets synth/pad, synth/saw-lead, synth/square-lead, synth/pluck, synth/supersaw, synth/bass, synth/acid, synth/brass, synth/bell, synth/sub and synth/chip. Calling startSound(id) while sound plays switches the instrument. An id that does not exist is listed in the console together with the real ones: an instrument that is already playing stays, and at the first call the warm pad synth/pad plays.

Nothing is loaded before the first call (or before 🔊 in the 🎹 panel): @openav/sound comes from next to oav-p5.js and Tone.js 15 from jsDelivr (the tone option points it somewhere else). Only the piano plays recorded samples, about 2 MB the first time; the electric piano sounds meanwhile (or, when you switch from another instrument, that one keeps sounding), and OAVp5.sound.instrument changes to piano when the samples are in. Every other instrument is made by Tone.js and has no files to load.

Before you call it

A browser lets a page make sound only after a click or a key press on the page, and a key on a MIDI keyboard does not count. Calling startSound() in setup() is fine: OAVp5.sound.state is 'waiting' and a card beside the 🎹 says "Sound is ready but silent"; the first click or key press turns sound on. soundIsOn tells when it has.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
idStringAn instrument id, for example 'organ' or 'synth/pluck' (the list is in the description). Leave it out to keep the instrument chosen before; at the very first call that is the piano. A value that is not a non-empty string counts as left out. optional default 'piano'

Returns

Promise<Boolean> Resolves to true once sound is on. When the browser wants a click first, that is after the first click or key press on the page. Resolves to false when the loading option sound is off, when stopSound() came first, or when Tone.js could not be loaded.

Notes

  • No code at all: ?oav_sound=piano on the page address (any instrument id; on OpenProcessing ?sketch_oav_sound=piano) makes any sketch heard from the first click, and ?oav_sound=off keeps it silent: startSound() then does nothing and resolves to false. In the 🎹 panel, 🔊 turns sound on and off and shows a picker with every instrument.
  • Sound is separate from the drum machine: startDrums() has its own kit and is heard from the first click without startSound().

Examples

Related

  • stopSound() Turns sound off and lets every ringing note go; the instrument stays loaded, so startSound() brings it back at once.
  • soundIsOn Whether notes are being heard right now: true once startSound() has finished, false before and after.

stopSound()#

functionoav-p5
stopSound()

Also: OAVp5.sound.stop

Turns sound off and lets every ringing note go; the instrument stays loaded, so startSound() brings it back at once.

It releases every note that is ringing, sets soundIsOn to false and OAVp5.sound.state to 'off'. Notes you play afterwards are not heard (the sketch's notePressed() is still called). Tone.js and the instrument stay loaded: startSound() afterwards is on again at once, without a new download and without waiting for another click.

It also works while sound is still loading or waiting for the first click: the pending startSound() then resolves to false.

Returns

Promise<Boolean> A promise that is already resolved to false, the new state of the sound.

Notes

  • It does not touch the drum machine (use stopDrums()) or the microphone (stopMic()).

OAVp5.sound.state#

variableoav-p5
OAVp5.sound.state

Where sound is: 'off', 'waiting' (for a click), 'loading', 'on' or 'error'.

'off' is where it starts and where stopSound() leaves it. startSound() moves it to 'loading' while @openav/sound and Tone.js arrive, to 'waiting' when everything is ready but the browser has not yet had its click, and to 'on' when notes are heard. 'error' means the sound parts could not be loaded (a network, a school firewall or an ad blocker); the message is in OAVp5.sound.error, and calling startSound() again tries once more.

soundIsOn is the same thing reduced to state === 'on'.

Type
String
Range

Starts as 'off' and changes whenever the sound moves to another stage.

OAVp5.sound.status#

OAVp5.sound.status

How the instrument is loading: { id, state, progress, error }, with progress from 0 to 1.

It is about the instrument, not about the whole sound: OAVp5.sound.state is the whole sound. Only the piano has files to load, so for every other instrument progress is 1 almost at once. While a sampler loads, OAVp5.sound.instrument is still the one you hear and status.id is the one on its way (at the very first call it may name the electric piano that stands in, and then the piano).

Type
Object
Range

A new object on every read. id is the instrument the loader is working on, state is 'idle' before anything loads, 'loading', 'ready' or 'error', and progress is the fraction of the files loaded.

modalInstrument()#

function@openav/sound
modalInstrument({ id, name, category = 'mallets', credit = null, params, defaults = { cutoff: 8000 }, partials, strike = null, damp = 0, pitchDecay = 0.6, transpose = 0, gain = 0, attack = 0.0015, tremolo = null, maxVoices = 40, set = null, })

Makes a struck-bar or tine instrument from data: a list of partials that ring and die away, and a short noise for the mallet.

A xylophone bar, a glockenspiel bar and a music-box tine are the same physics with different numbers: a strike excites a few modes, each rings at its own multiple of the pitch and dies at its own rate. So a mallet instrument here is data, not code. The built-in xylophone is this short:

js
modalInstrument({
  id: 'xylophone', name: { en: 'Xylophone', zh: '…' }, transpose: 12,
  partials: [{ ratio: 1, gain: 1, decay: 0.9 }, { ratio: 3, gain: 0.32, decay: 0.32 }, { ratio: 6.1, gain: 0.1, decay: 0.1 }],
  strike: { ratio: 5, q: 1.1, gain: 0.35, decay: 0.012 },
  pitchDecay: 0.75,
});

Harder strikes brighten: the upper partials grow faster with velocity, as a real mallet does. The voices are raw Web Audio nodes built for each strike and left to the garbage collector.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
idStringThe instrument id (see registerInstrument()).
nameString | ObjectThe name: a string, or { en, zh }.
categoryStringThe picker group. optional default 'mallets'
creditString | ObjectA credit line, a string or { text, url }. optional default null
paramsObject[]Params of its own: [{ key, label, min, max, def }]. Handled by the set function. optional
defaultsObjectStarting values for the shared params. The default opens the filter, because bars are bright. optional default { cutoff: 8000 }
partialsObject[]The modes of the bar: [{ ratio, gain, decay }]. ratio is the frequency as a multiple of the note (1 is the note itself, 3 a twelfth above it), gain the level relative to the others and decay the seconds to near silence at middle C. High notes die faster than low ones. A partial above 45% of the sample rate is skipped. Required: without it this throws.
strikeObjectThe mallet, a few milliseconds of band-passed noise: { ratio, q, gain, decay }, where ratio sets its pitch as a multiple of the note, q its width, gain its level and decay its length in seconds. optional default null
dampNumberSeconds in which letting go of a key mutes the bar. 0 lets the bars ring free (xylophone, glockenspiel); a vibraphone has a damper. optional default 0
pitchDecayNumberHow much faster high notes die than low ones. The decay is scaled by (261.63 / frequency) ^ pitchDecay, held between 0.2 and 3. 0 makes every note last the same. optional default 0.6
transposeNumberSemitones to shift what is played (the xylophone sounds an octave up: 12). optional default 0
gainNumberThe instrument's level, in dB. optional default 0
attackNumberSeconds the partials take to reach full level. optional default 0.0015
tremoloObjectA level wobble over all voices, the vibraphone's motor: { frequency, depth, spread }. optional default null
maxVoicesNumberHow many notes can ring at once. The oldest is faded out in 30 ms when it is exceeded. optional default 40
setFunctionset({ key, value, tremolo, Tone }), called when one of the instrument's own params changes, so it can change the tremolo or anything else. optional default null

Returns

Object An instrument definition, not yet registered: pass it to registerInstrument(). tail is set to min(8, longest decay × 1.5 + 0.2) seconds.

A native <select> with one <optgroup> per category (CATEGORIES), so it works with a keyboard and on a phone and needs no styling to be usable. registerInstrument()#

function@openav/sound
registerInstrument(def, { replace = false } = {})

Adds a sound to every picker on the page: an id, a name, a category and one create() function that builds the instrument.

A sound you can pick is plain data plus one factory. Registering it is all it takes: import the file before you start, and every mountSoundPicker() on the page lists it under its category, with no change to the package. The registry lives on globalThis, so two copies of this module on one page share one list. Built-in instruments only fill empty slots: register your own 'piano' first and you keep it. The definition:

text
id          lowercase letters, digits and "-", at most one "/": 'kalimba', 'me/kalimba'
name        a string, or { en, zh }
category    keys · mallets · strings · plucked · organ · voice · synth · drums · other, or your own
create      create(Tone, ctx) → { noteOn(note, vel01, time), noteOff(note, time), set?(key, v),
                                  releaseAll?(time), ready?: Promise, dispose() }
params      your own knobs [{ key, label, min, max, def }], shown as sound/<key> while it plays
defaults    starting values for the shared params: { cutoff, space, volume }
credit      a string, or { text, url }, shown in the picker
gain        level in dB      transpose   semitones      tail   seconds the old one may ring after a switch
fallback    the id of an instrument to play if `ready` rejects

create(Tone, ctx) runs on enable and on every switch to the instrument, with Tone.js already loaded. ctx is { output, rawOutput, rawContext, baseUrl, options, onProgress }: connect Tone nodes to output (raw Web Audio nodes to rawOutput), baseUrl is where sample folders live, options is what was passed in toneEngine({ instruments: { <id>: … } }), and onProgress(0..1) shows a loading bar. If ready is a promise, the picker shows progress and the old sound keeps playing until it resolves. An instrument that makes mallet sounds from data can use modalInstrument(), and one that is a Tone synth with settings, registerSynthPreset().

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
defObjectThe instrument definition, see the table below.
replaceBooleanIn the options { replace }: allow replacing an instrument that has the same id. Without it a duplicate id throws. optional default false

Returns

Object The definition you gave. It throws a TypeError listing everything wrong if the definition is not valid (see validateInstrument()), and an Error for a duplicate id.

registerSynthPreset()#

function@openav/sound
registerSynthPreset(preset, opts)

Adds a synth preset to every picker as synth/ plus its id: describe the voice, the envelope and the effects as data.

A preset names a voice, its settings in Tone.js's vocabulary, and an optional effects chain, and nothing else. id is lowercase letters, digits and - (it becomes synth/<id>), name is a string or { en, zh }. voice is 'synth' (oscillator and envelope), 'mono' (adds a resonant filter with its own envelope), 'fm' or 'am'. The Tone settings are oscillator, envelope, filter, filterEnvelope, harmonicity, modulationIndex, modulation, modulationEnvelope, detune and portamento. The rest: octave (a whole number of octaves, -1 for a bass), gain (dB, to level it against the others), polyphony, defaults (starting cutoff, space, volume), params, category and credit, as in registerInstrument().

effects is a list of { type, …settings } that the sound passes through in order. The types are chorus, delay, pingpong, distortion, vibrato, tremolo, phaser, autofilter, filter, eq, compressor, chebyshev and widener; the other keys are the effect's own Tone settings, including wet. A preset that is wrong throws a TypeError with the reasons.

Parameters

presetObjectThe preset: { id, name, voice, … }, see below.
optsObjectThe options of registerInstrument(): { replace: true } swaps an existing one. optional

Returns

Object The instrument definition that was registered (synthInstrument() of the preset).

Sound#

class@openav/sound
new Sound({ signals, params = null, engine, instrument = null, remember = true, picker = true })

Makes every midi/note/on and midi/note/off on a bus audible through a sound engine, and puts the engine's params on the bus as sound/*.

Sound is the shell that wires an engine into an app. Once await sound.enable() has run, every midi/note/on and midi/note/off on the bus is played, whatever sent it: a MIDI keyboard, the on-screen piano (mountKeys()), a SimPlayer, a TakePlayer or a phone. Notes on a channel in the engine's skipChannels are left out (the Tone engine skips channel 10, which belongs to the drum machine).

The engine's params become sound/* params, so a knob, the timeline or a hand can play the filter the same way it plays the visuals: sound is performable state, not a side effect. Every frame, call sound.update(state) with the resolved param values, and the sound/* ones are pushed into the engine. The instrument is a discrete choice (setInstrument() or the picker); what you perform continuously stays a param.

Before you call it

sound.enable() from a click: browsers start audio only after a user gesture. With toneEngine() it also loads Tone.js from the network (jsDelivr) the first time. Before enable() nothing is heard, and the bus is not listened to.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsThe Signals bus. Sound listens to midi/note/on { note, vel, ch }, midi/note/off { note, ch } and midi/cc/64 (the sustain pedal, down at 0.5 or more), and pulses sound/instrument { id, name } when the instrument changes.
paramsParamsA Params registry to add the engine's params to, named sound/<key> (sound/cutoff, sound/space, sound/volume and the instrument's own). Left out, no params are registered. optional default null
engineObjectThe sound engine, such as toneEngine() or drumEngine(). The contract is { params, enable(), noteOn(note, vel01), noteOff(note), set(key, value), dispose() }, and optionally setInstrument, instrument, status, subscribe, sustain(down) and skipChannels.
instrumentStringThe instrument to start with, for an engine that has instruments ('piano', 'synth/pluck'). An unknown id is warned about in the console and ignored. optional default null
rememberBoolean | StringKeep the instrument the picker last chose, per page, in localStorage, and let it win over instrument the next time. A string is your own storage key; the default key is openav:sound:<page path>. false turns it off. Choices made from code are not remembered unless you ask (setInstrument(id, { remember: true })). optional default true
pickerBooleanWhether a console should show the instrument picker. It is stored as sound.picker for whoever builds the interface; Sound itself draws nothing. optional default true

Members

NameDescription
enable()methodStarts the engine and begins listening to the bus. Returns a promise of true. Call it from a click. Calling it again returns the same promise; if it fails you can try again. Emits { type: 'enabled', id } to onChange listeners.
update(state)methodPer frame: pushes every sound/<key> value of state into the engine's set(key, value). Other keys of state are ignored. Does nothing before enable().
instrumentgetterGetter. The id of the current instrument ('piano'), or null for an engine without instruments, such as the drum kit.
statusgetterGetter. { id, state, progress, error }: state is 'idle', 'loading', 'ready' or 'error' and progress is 0..1 while a sampler loads.
choosablegetterGetter. Whether the engine has instruments to choose from.
setInstrument(id, { remember = false } = {})methodSwitches instrument, live: setInstrument(id, { remember = false }). Held notes are released on the old one and the new one takes over once it is ready (a sampler keeps the old sound while its files load). Returns a promise: true once the instrument plays, false if the id is unknown, the engine has no instruments or the choice was replaced by a newer one. remember: true stores the choice for this page.
onChange(cb)methodListens for what happens: cb({ type, id, progress, error }) with type 'instrument', 'loading', 'ready', 'error' or 'enabled'. Returns a function that stops listening.
dispose()methodStops listening to the bus, drops the listeners and disposes the engine.

Notes

  • From a p5 sketch you do not build this: startSound() does it, loading this package only when it is called.

SOUND_PARAMS#

constant@openav/sound
SOUND_PARAMS = array, 3 items

The three params every instrument shares: cutoff (the filter), space (the reverb) and volume.

cutoff is the low-pass filter's frequency in Hz, space is how much reverb is mixed in (the wet amount, 0..1), volume is the level in dB. They sit after the instrument on the output chain, so the timeline, a knob or a hand keep performing them across instrument switches. In a show they are the params sound/cutoff, sound/space and sound/volume. An instrument may suggest other starting values through its defaults, and automation and overrides always win over a suggestion. An instrument's own params cannot use these keys.

Type
Object[]

[{ key: 'cutoff', min: 100, max: 8000, def: 2500 }, { key: 'space', min: 0, max: 1, def: 0.3 }, { key: 'volume', min: -36, max: 0, def: -8 }], each also with a label.

toneEngine()#

function@openav/sound
toneEngine({ cdn = TONE_CDN, instrument = DEFAULT_INSTRUMENT, baseUrl = SAMPLES_URL, instruments: perInstrument = {}, drumChannel = 10, } = {})

The sound engine that plays the registered instruments with Tone.js through a filter, a reverb and a limiter.

Tone.js stays a neighbour, not a dependency: it is loaded from the network the first time enable() runs, so an app that never turns the sound on pays nothing. After enable() the instrument's output goes through a low-pass filter (cutoff, starting at 2500 Hz), a reverb (space, the wet amount, starting at 0.3), a volume (volume, in dB, starting at -8) and a limiter at -1 dB, so a loud organ never clips the room. These three are the SOUND_PARAMS shared by every instrument. Their starting values can follow the instrument (a piano wants the filter open), and the instrument may add params of its own.

setInstrument(id) switches live and returns a promise of whether it worked. Before enable() it only remembers the choice. Held notes are released on the old instrument and its tail is left to ring for a few seconds. A sampler (the piano) keeps the old sound until its files are in; if they cannot load, the engine plays the instrument's fallback (the piano falls back to the electric piano), so a performance never goes silent because of one failed download. subscribe(cb) tells you about instrument, loading, ready and error events. sustain(down) is the pedal: note-offs wait until it comes up. releaseAll() is a panic button.

You usually pass the engine to a Sound, which is what listens to the bus. Used on its own, noteOn(60, 0.8) plays a note.

Before you call it

await engine.enable() from a click: it loads Tone.js from the network, then starts its audio. Before that, noteOn() does nothing and setInstrument() only remembers the choice.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
cdnStringWhere Tone.js is imported from when the engine is enabled. The default is TONE_CDN. A module URL, so you can host your own copy. optional default TONE_CDN
instrumentStringThe instrument to start with. An unknown id is warned about and synth/pad is used. optional default 'synth/pad'
baseUrlStringThe folder that holds the built-in sample sets (salamander/…). The default is SAMPLES_URL. optional default SAMPLES_URL
instrumentsObjectOptions for single instruments, handed to their create() as ctx.options: { piano: { baseUrl: '/my/salamander/' } }. optional default {}
drumChannelNumber | nullNotes on this MIDI channel belong to a drum engine (the drum machine sends General MIDI channel 10) and are not played here. null plays everything. optional default 10

Returns

Object An engine: { params, sharedParams, instrument, status, skipChannels, hasInstrument(id), subscribe(cb), setInstrument(id), enable(), noteOn(note, vel01, time), noteOff(note, time), sustain(down), releaseAll(), set(key, value), dispose() }.

Checks an instrument definition and lists everything wrong with it as readable sentences. An empty list means it is valid.

beatPhase#

variableoav-p5
beatPhase

Also: OAVp5.drums.beatPhase

How far through the current beat the drum machine is, smoothly from 0 up to just below 1, four times per bar.

A beat is a quarter note (four steps). 1 - beatPhase is biggest right on the beat and shrinks until the next one, so circle(width / 2, height / 2, 60 + (1 - beatPhase) * 80) pulses with the tempo, with no callback needed. drumPhase is the same thing across a whole bar.

Type
Number
Range
0..1

Read fresh each time you look at it. 0 on the beat, close to 1 just before the next one, then 0 again. It is 0 before the machine has played and holds still while it is stopped.

Before it has a value

Start the machine with startDrums(); until it plays, beatPhase is 0.

drawRhythm()#

functionoav-p5
drawRhythm([x], [y], [w], [h], [style], [o])

Also: OAVp5.drums.draw

Draws the rhythm on the canvas as a grid, a circle or a spiral, with a playhead and the hits lighting up, so a recording has it too.

Call it in draw() after background(): drawRhythm(20, 100, 360, 100). Each row is one drum that plays in the pattern, a hit lights up the moment it is heard (the clock drumPhase reads), and a hit between two steps, such as a triplet, sits where it falls. The grid card is part of the page and a recording never shows it, but the canvas is what a recording takes, so this is how the rhythm gets into the video.

With no box it draws a strip along the bottom for 'grid' and a square in the middle for the other two. It draws with p5's own shapes between push() and pop(), so it leaves your styles alone and works in 2D and in WEBGL, in p5 1.x and 2.x. In WEBGL the origin is the middle of the canvas: drawRhythm(-width / 2, -height / 2, width, height, 'circle') fills it.

Before you call it

Start the machine with startDrums() first. Before it plays you get an empty four-lane grid.

drumHit()#

eventoav-p5
function drumHit(lane, velocity) {}

An event you define: it is called for every hit of the drum machine, with the drum that sounded and how hard.

Define function drumHit(lane, velocity) { … } and oav-p5 calls it for every hit of every drum, the way it calls notePressed() for a key. It is called in the frame in which the hit is heard, right before draw().

The same hit also calls the microphone's functions, so you can pick the grain you want: kickDetected() for the kick, snareDetected() for snare, clap and rim, hatDetected() for the three hats, and beatDetected() (with beat true for a frame) for kick, snare, clap and rim, once per step. Toms, crash, ride and cowbell reach only drumHit(). On one step the order is: cueFired(), barStarted(), stepStarted(), then the hits.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
laneStringThe drum that sounded: 'kick', 'snare', 'hat' or 'clap' for the grid, and also 'openhat', 'pedalhat', 'rim', 'lowtom', 'tom', 'hightom', 'crash', 'ride' or 'cowbell' for a line of rhythm.
velocityNumberHow hard, from 0.15 to 1. It varies a little from hit to hit, because the machine plays slightly softer or louder on purpose.

Notes

  • While the tab is hidden nobody sees a frame: the clock keeps counting, but no hit is told, and nothing is told twice when the tab comes back. An error thrown inside drumHit() is printed, with its file and line, and the next hit still comes.

startDrums()#

functionoav-p5
startDrums([pattern], [bpm])

Also: OAVp5.drums.start

Starts a drum machine: a 16-step grid on the page that plays a preset, your own grid or one line of rhythm, and counts the bars for your sketch.

Call it once in setup(): startDrums('breakbeat', 120). A grid of 16 steps by 4 lanes (kick, snare, hat, clap) appears at the top of the page, with the tempo and the bar it is in, and plays a synthesized drum kit (no sample files). The grid is part of the page, not of the canvas: a recording never shows it, so use drawRhythm() to draw the rhythm on the canvas. A click on a cell changes the beat, and 🥁 in the 🎹 panel starts and stops the machine with no code at all.

The machine is also a clock and a source of events. Every hit calls drumHit() and the microphone's own functions (kickDetected(), snareDetected(), hatDetected(), beatDetected()), so a sketch written for the microphone moves over unchanged. drumStep, drumBar, drumPhase and beatPhase say where the machine is, and cue() lets you plan what happens at which bar.

Calling it again while it plays changes the pattern or the tempo without restarting: startDrums(90) only changes the tempo, startDrums('latin') only the pattern. A line of rhythm is any text that is not a preset name. A word is a drum (bd kick, sd snare, hh hat, oh open hat, cp clap, rim, lt mt ht toms, cr crash, rd ride, cb cowbell), ~ is a rest, words separated by spaces share the bar evenly, [ ] groups, *4 repeats, , puts another line on top, < > takes one per bar and bd(3,8) spreads 3 hits over 8 steps. A mistake shows a card that points at the character and says how to fix it, and 'four on floor' plays meanwhile.

A line copied from strudel.cc works too: startDrums('s("bd*4, [~ sd]*2").fast(2)'). s("…") and sound("…") with .fast(n) and .slow(n) are read, setcpm(110/4) sets the tempo if you give none, .bank(…) is left out (oav-p5 plays its own kit), and any other call in the chain gets a card that says it is not supported yet. The rest plays.

Before you call it

Nothing before the call. The counting, drumHit() and the other callbacks start at once, but a browser lets the page make sound only after a click or key press on it, so the drums are silent until the first one. A card at the top says so after a moment.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
patternString | Object | NumberWhat to play. A preset name ('four on floor', 'breakbeat', 'half time', 'latin', 'sparse'). A line of rhythm such as 'bd*4, [~ sd]*2, hh*8', or one copied from strudel.cc. Your own grid { kick: 'x...x...x...x...', snare, hat, clap } (x or 1 is a hit, a lane you leave out is silent, {} is a silent clock). A number alone is the tempo. Leave it out to keep what plays now ('four on floor' at the start). optional
bpmNumberThe tempo in beats per minute (a beat is four steps). Kept between 30 and 300. Leave it out to keep the current tempo: 112 at the start, or the one a copied Strudel line sets with setcpm(…). optional

Returns

Promise<Boolean> Resolves to true once the machine plays (or when a later startDrums() took over). Resolves to false when stopDrums() came first, when there is no page to put the grid on, or when @openav/drums could not be loaded.

Notes

  • Drum sound does not need startSound(): the machine has its own kit. Pads on MIDI channel 10 play the same kit once startSound() is on.
  • The card has – to fold the grid away and × to stop the machine. A tab in the background keeps counting and playing. The loading options drums (lookahead or frame) and drumlatency tune the clock.

stopDrums()#

functionoav-p5
stopDrums()

Also: OAVp5.drums.stop

Stops the drum machine and hides its card.

The machine stops playing, the grid disappears and drumsAreOn becomes false. The numbers keep the last value they had: drumStep, drumBar and cueName stay where they were, and drumPhase and beatPhase hold still. startDrums() afterwards begins again from bar 1.

It also works while the machine is still loading: the pending startDrums() then resolves to false. The × on the card does the same thing.

Returns

Promise<Boolean> A promise that is already resolved to false, the new state of the machine.

OAVp5.drums#

objectoav-p5
OAVp5.drums

The object behind the drum names: the state of the machine, its counters, the line of rhythm, its history and the loaded machine.

OAVp5.drums (also reachable as midi.drums) is what startDrums(), drumStep and the rest are built on. It holds the numbers (state, step, bar, count, bpm, phase, beatPhase), the rhythm (pattern, src, copyText, strudelUrl, history, edit(), undo()), the cues (cue(), cues, lastCue), a way to listen (on()), what the machine hears right now (now) and handles for the curious (machine, clock).

start, stop and draw are the same as startDrums(), stopDrums() and drawRhythm(). For a sketch the global names are enough. This object is for tools, libraries (Hydra, for one), the console and debugging.

functionoav-p5
OAVp5.drums.on(name, fn)

Listens to the drum machine from anywhere: OAVp5.drums.on('hit', fn) calls fn like drumHit does, and returns a function that stops listening.

The functions you define (drumHit, barStarted …) are one listener each. on() is for the cases where that does not fit: several listeners for one event, a library or a Hydra sketch that has no drumHit() of its own, a listener you want to remove again. It is the same idea as midi.on(). An error thrown inside fn is printed and the other listeners still run.

fnFunctionCalled with the same arguments as the function it matches: (lane, velocity), (step, bar), (bar), (name, bar) or (src, how).

Function A function: call it to stop listening.

@openav/drums

drumEngine()#

function@openav/drums
drumEngine({ samples = null } = {})

A drum kit made of Web Audio synthesis, with no sample files: General MIDI drum notes go in, drum sounds come out.

It follows the small engine contract of @openav/sound, so the same shell and the same signals drive it: enable() makes the AudioContext, noteOn(note, vel01, time) plays a drum, set(key, value) sets a param. The kit has thirteen voices (see GM): kick, rim, snare, clap, low tom, hat, pedal hat, tom, open hat, high tom, crash, ride and cowbell. A note the kit does not know (any melodic note) plays nothing and returns null.

noteOn(note, vel01, time) returns { time, cancel() }, or null before enable() or for a note it does not play. time is on the kit's own clock (engine.context.currentTime); left out, or already past, the hit sounds now. cancel() silences a hit that has not started, which is how DrumTransport takes back what it scheduled when the tempo changes. hit('crash', 0.9) plays a voice by name (or a note number) for code that is not a MIDI pad. There is one param, kitVolume, from −30 to 0 dB (default −6).

Once enabled, engine.context is its AudioContext and engine.output is the node that goes to the speakers, which a recorder can tap. Before that both are null. noteOff() does nothing (drums ring out) and dispose() closes the context.

Before you call it

await kit.enable() from a click: browsers start audio only after a user gesture. mountDrums() and DrumTransport with autoEnable do that for you on the first hit.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
samplesObjectPlay audio files instead of the synthesis: { 36: 'kick.wav', 38: 'snare.wav' }, MIDI note number to URL. They are fetched and decoded by enable(); a file that fails to load is skipped without an error, and a note of the kit then plays its synthesized sound instead. optional default null

Returns

Object An engine: { params, context, output, enable(), noteOn(note, vel01, time), hit(what, vel01, time), noteOff(), set(key, value), dispose() }.

Examples

DrumScheduler#

class@openav/drums
new DrumScheduler({ bpm = 112, swing = 0, humanize = 0.35, lookahead = 0.1, pattern = 'four on floor', seed = 0, random = Math.random } = {})

Pure drum logic with no timers and no audio: a grid or a line of rhythm goes in, timed events come out, ahead of time, on any clock you pass.

A DrumScheduler knows what plays in which bar, and when a bar happens, but it owns no clock: every time you give it is in seconds on one clock of your choosing, so it runs the same under a fake clock in a test as under the audio clock in a page. DrumTransport is the runtime that feeds it the real one. Use the scheduler on its own when you want drum events as data, for your own sound engine or a test.

The loop is: start(at) puts the downbeat of bar 1 at time at. Then, again and again, advance(now) schedules everything up to now + lookahead and returns the new events, in order. due(t) hands out the events whose time has come (they stay in queue until then). Two kinds of event come out: a step { kind: 'step', i, n, bar, pos, time } for every 16th, and a hit { kind: 'hit', voice, vel, pos, n, bar, token, word, layer, dur, time }. pos counts bars from the start (0 is the downbeat of bar 1, 1.5 is half way through bar 2), time is in your seconds, i is the step 0..15 and n counts steps since the start. For a grid, the step comes before its hits. token, word, layer and dur come from a line of rhythm and are null or undefined for a grid.

Positions turn into seconds by multiplication from the last tempo anchor, never by adding up frame times, so a thousand bars later nothing has drifted (the test measures under a microsecond). A tempo change adds an anchor, so the past keeps the tempo it had.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
bpmNumberThe tempo, in beats per minute. A value that is not above 0 becomes 112. optional default 112
swingNumber0 to 0.5: every odd 16th is that share of a 16th late. 0 is straight. optional default 0
humanizeNumber0..1: a few milliseconds late and a little softer or louder, so it grooves instead of ticking. Use 0 for exact, repeatable times. optional default 0.35
lookaheadNumberSeconds advance() schedules beyond now. optional default 0.1
patternString | ObjectA preset name from PATTERNS, your own grid, or a compiled line of rhythm (see setPattern()). optional default 'four on floor'
seedNumberPassed to the rhythm line as eventsInBar(bar, { seed }), so each ? decides the same way every time. optional default 0
randomFunctionWhere humanize gets its randomness: a function that returns a number from 0 up to 1. Pass your own for repeatable output. optional default Math.random

DrumSequencer#

class@openav/drums
new DrumSequencer({ onHit, onStep = null, bpm = 112, swing = 0.12, humanize = 0.35, pattern = 'four on floor' } = {})

A 16-step, four-lane drum pattern clock that you move forward with update(dt) every frame and that calls your function for each hit.

It is the simplest clock: no audio, no timers, no DOM. Make it with an onHit that does something, call toggle(true), then call update(dt) once per frame with the seconds since the last frame. It walks through the 16 steps of a bar (a 16th lasts 60 / bpm / 4 seconds) and calls onHit(lane, velocity) for each hit in the four lanes kick, snare, hat and clap. A hit is told in the frame in which it is due, so it can be late by up to a frame, and nothing happens in a hidden tab. For a steady beat under a heavy frame, use DrumTransport.

The grid is seq.grid: { kick: [0|1 × 16], snare, hat, clap }. seq.pattern is the preset name, or 'custom' once you changed a cell or gave your own grid. seq.playing, seq.bpm, seq.swing and seq.humanize are plain properties you can read and set.

bpmNumberThe tempo, in beats per minute. It can be changed later: seq.bpm = 90. optional default 112
swingNumber0 to 0.5: every odd 16th is that share of a 16th late. 0 is straight. optional default 0.12
humanizeNumber0..1: some hits a few milliseconds late and a little softer or louder. Use 0 for exact, repeatable velocities (0.9 on the beat, 0.6 between). optional default 0.35
patternString | ObjectA preset name from PATTERNS or your own grid. optional default 'four on floor'
