DrumTransport#

class@openav/drums
new DrumTransport({ scheduler = new DrumScheduler(), engine = null, onStep = null, onHit = null, onLate = null, autoEnable = false, now = perfNow, hidden = pageHidden, heartbeat = 'auto', tick = 0.025, latency = 'auto', stale = 0.25, startDelay = 0.05 } = {})

The runtime around a DrumScheduler: it hands every hit to the kit ahead of time on its audio clock, and tells the page each step and hit when it is heard.

A page that plays a hit in the frame it is due is late by up to a frame, and silent when its tab is hidden. DrumTransport fixes both. A timer (the heartbeat, from a Web Worker, 25 ms by default) looks 0.1 seconds ahead on the kit's own audio clock and hands the kit every hit with its exact start time. The page is told separately, in the frame in which each step and hit is heard: its time plus the output latency the browser reports. So the beat stays steady under a heavy draw() and in a hidden tab, and the callbacks still arrive in order: a step before its hits, hits in time order.

Call start(), then frame() once per animation frame. The heartbeat calls pump() for you. Tempo and pattern changes (setBpm(), setPattern(), toggleCell()) take back what was already handed over after now and make it again, so no hit is doubled or lost. Before the kit's AudioContext runs (no click yet) the clock runs on now() and the callbacks run but nothing sounds; once it runs, the hits from then on sound, and none from before.

A hidden page, or a frame loop that catches up more than stale seconds late, tells its steps quietly: ev.quiet is true, the clock moves and cues fire, but onHit is not called, and of several bar starts at once only the last has ev.announce. Nothing floods the page when the tab comes back. If a draw() ever holds the thread longer than the lookahead, the lookahead grows to 0.3 seconds (info().extended).

It has the getters playing, pattern, grid, mode, text, bpm, swing, humanize and lookahead of its scheduler; bpm, swing and humanize can also be set. You usually get one through mountDrums() with clock: 'lookahead'; build your own when you want the clock without the card.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
schedulerDrumSchedulerThe DrumScheduler that decides what is played when. optional default new DrumScheduler()
engineObjectThe sound engine, usually a drumEngine(). If it has a context property (an AudioContext, or null before it is enabled), hits are scheduled ahead on that clock. If not, each hit is played by calling engine.noteOn(note, vel) at the moment it is heard. optional default null
onStepFunctiononStep(i, n, ev) for every 16th step when it is heard. ev.quiet and ev.announce say whether it was told quietly (below). optional default null
onHitFunctiononHit(voice, vel, ev) for every drum hit when it is heard. optional default null
onLateFunctiononLate(margin, transport): a hit was handed to the kit after its time, because the page held the main thread longer than the lookahead. margin is how many seconds early it was (negative or tiny). optional default null
autoEnableBooleanCall engine.enable() by start() when the engine has no AudioContext yet. optional default false
nowFunctionA function that returns the time in seconds. Pass your own to drive the transport from a fake clock in a test. optional default performance.now() / 1000
hiddenFunctionA function that returns true while nobody can see the page. optional default checks document.visibilityState
heartbeat'auto' | 'interval' | falseWho calls pump(): 'auto' a Web Worker timer (a hidden tab does not slow a worker), falling back to setInterval; 'interval' always setInterval; false (or 'none') nobody, and you call pump() or frame() yourself. optional default 'auto'
tickNumberSeconds between two heartbeats. optional default 0.025
latency'auto' | NumberSeconds between a hit being scheduled and being heard. 'auto' asks the browser (getOutputTimestamp(), outputLatency); a number sets it by hand. optional default 'auto'
staleNumberA step that is told more than this many seconds late (a frame loop catching up) is told quietly. optional default 0.25
startDelayNumberWhen the audio clock is running, the first downbeat is put this many seconds after start(), so the first hit is not already late. optional default 0.05

The General MIDI drum note each drum of the kit plays: GM.kick is 36, GM.snare is 38.

mountDrums()#

function@openav/drums
mountDrums(container, { signals, engine = null, autoEnableEngine = true, onStep = null, onHit = null, onTakeover = null, bpm = 112, pattern = 'four on floor', clock = 'frame', lang = 'en', heartbeat = 'auto', latency = 'auto', now, hidden, rhythm = null, onRhythm = null, onLossy = null, onEditError = null, copyText = null, strudelComment = '' } = {})

Puts a drum machine on the page: a step grid, a transport and a line of rhythm you can type into. It publishes every hit as drum/* signals.

mountDrums(el, { signals }) builds a drum machine card inside el: a play checkbox, a preset menu, a tempo slider, the bar it is in, and a grid with a lane per drum (kick, snare, hat, clap, and a row of their own for the crash, ride, toms and open hat that a line of rhythm uses). A click on a cell toggles it. The returned object lets you do from code what the card does with the mouse: play(true), setPattern('breakbeat'), setBpm(96).

You must call drums.update(dt) every frame, with the seconds since the last one. It moves the machine (with the frame clock), tells your onStep and onHit what is heard, paints the grid and lets the drum/*/env signals decay. A machine that is never updated does not move.

Hits travel the same road as a drummer heard through the microphone, so a sketch written for the microphone moves over unchanged: drum/kick, drum/snare, drum/hat, drum/clap as pulses with { level }, drum/<voice>/env as continuous 0..1 values, and midi/note/on { note, vel, ch: 10 } with the General MIDI drum note (see GM). A voice a line of rhythm adds, like drum/crash, is defined the first time it is hit.

Give it the pattern module (rhythm) and the line of rhythm is always shown over the grid: a preset shows the line its grid is ('four on floor' is bd*4, [~ sd]*2, hh*8), and the word that sounds lights up. Then the two edit each other. A click on a cell rewrites the line (with fromGrid()). Typing in the line changes the cells: Enter, or 400 ms without a key, plays what was typed. A mistake is marked red, onEditError is told, and the last line that worked keeps playing. Escape drops what was not played yet. Every change is kept in history; ↶ on the card, or Cmd/Ctrl+Z after touching the card, goes back one. Copy puts the line on the clipboard and Open in Strudel opens it at strudel.cc in a new tab (strudelUrl()).

What the returned object offers:

text
play(on)               start (true) or stop (false) like the checkbox; no argument flips; returns whether it plays
setPattern(p, {text})  a preset name, your own grid, or a compiled line (text: the line it came from); the card follows
setBpm(bpm)            the tempo, like the slider; returns the tempo
update(dt)             call every frame
deliver()              tell onStep/onHit what is heard by now without painting (call it right before you draw)
phase()                { bar, beat, pos }: how far through the bar and the beat the listener is, 0..1
now()                  { bar, step, phase, beatPhase, tokens, mode, text } for the display
info()                 { clock, heartbeat, lookahead, late, extended, audio, latency, ... } the health of the clock
useRhythm(mod)         hand over @openav/pattern later (it can load on its own)
src()                  the line that plays now ('' with a grid and no rhythm module)
strudelUrl()           the line as a strudel.cc link, or ''
edit(text)             play a line as if typed: { ok, error }; a mistake keeps the last line playing
history, undo()        the lines before, oldest first; undo goes back one and returns whether it did
copy()                 put copyText() on the clipboard: Promise<{ ok, text }>
barEvents(bar)         the hits of a bar: [{ voice, pos, ... }]
voices()               the rows on the grid now
seq, engine, root      the DrumSequencer or DrumTransport, the sound engine, the card's element
dispose()              stop, release the kit and take the card out

Before you call it

A page with a DOM, and update(dt) called every frame. Sound waits for the browser: the kit's AudioContext is made by the first hit (or by play() with the lookahead clock), and until the page has had a click it stays suspended. Callbacks and signals run from the start; the sound comes in on the first click, and nothing from before it is played late.

engineObjectThe sound engine. Left out, the machine makes its own drumEngine(). Anything with enable() and noteOn(note, vel01, time) works. optional default null
autoEnableEngineBooleanSwitch the engine on by the first hit (or by play() with the lookahead clock), so no extra click is needed beyond the one the browser wants. optional default true
onStepFunctiononStep(i, n, ev), once for every 16th step when it is heard. i is 0..15 in the bar, n counts steps since the start, before that step's hits. It is the clock a timeline counts bars on. optional default null

clock'frame' | 'lookahead''frame': the machine moves in update(dt) and each hit sounds in the frame it is due. 'lookahead': hits are handed to the kit ahead of time on its audio clock, so the beat is steady under a heavy frame and in a hidden tab ('audio' means the same). See DrumTransport. optional default 'frame'
lang'en' | 'zh''zh' names the lanes and the buttons in Chinese. Anything else is English. optional default 'en'
heartbeat'auto' | 'interval' | falseOnly for clock: 'lookahead'. Who wakes the scheduler: 'auto' a Web Worker timer (falls back to setInterval where a worker cannot start), 'interval' always setInterval, false nobody (you call drums.update() often enough). optional default 'auto'
latency'auto' | NumberOnly for clock: 'lookahead'. How long after a hit is scheduled it is heard, in seconds. 'auto' asks the browser for its output latency; a number sets it by hand (a Bluetooth speaker is 0.15 to 0.25). optional default 'auto'
nowFunctionOnly for clock: 'lookahead'. A function that returns the time in seconds. The default is performance.now() / 1000. Replace it to run the machine on a fake clock in a test. optional
hiddenFunctionOnly for clock: 'lookahead'. A function that returns true while nobody can see the page. The default looks at document.visibilityState. optional
rhythmModuleThe @openav/pattern module (import * as rhythm from '@openav/pattern', anything with compile and fromGrid). With it the line of rhythm over the grid is always there and editable, and the cells and the line rewrite each other. It can also be handed over later with drums.useRhythm(mod). optional default null
onRhythmFunctiononRhythm(line, { how, prev }), once for every new line. how is 'code', 'cell', 'type', 'undo' or 'menu'. optional default null
onLossyFunctiononLossy({ text, bar, lost }): a click on a cell would lose something the 16 steps cannot hold (triplets, < >, ?, bd:2). lost is the same as in toGrid(). Left out, a note appears on the card. The next click rewrites the line anyway. optional default null

copyTextFunctioncopyText(line, bpm) returns what the Copy button puts on the clipboard. The default is the line itself. optional default null

Returns

Object { seq, engine, root, clock, play(on), setPattern(p, { text }), setBpm(bpm), update(dt), deliver(), phase(), now(), info(), dispose(), useRhythm(mod), src(), strudelUrl(), history, undo(), edit(text), copy(), copyText(), barEvents(bar), voices() } (and the getters rhythm and copied).

Notes

  • With clock: 'frame' the first bar of a compiled line is played on the 16-step grid of four lanes: hits between steps move to the nearest step, and drums with no lane (crash, ride, toms, open hat) are left out. The console says so. clock: 'lookahead' plays a line exactly as written.
  • In a p5 sketch you do not call it: startDrums() builds this card for you, with the lookahead clock, and calls update() every frame.

PATTERNS#

constant@openav/drums
PATTERNS = object, 5 keys

The five preset grids of the drum machine: 'four on floor', breakbeat, 'half time', latin and sparse.

The preset names are what startDrums(), DrumSequencer and mountDrums() accept as a pattern. A preset is just data, so you can start from one: { ...PATTERNS.latin, clap: 'x...x...x...x...' } is latin with a clap on every beat.

The five presets as text, one lane per column:

text
                  kick              snare             hat               clap
four on floor     1000100010001000  0000100000001000  1010101010101010  0000000000000000
breakbeat         1000000110100000  0000100000001001  1010101010101010  0000100000000000
half time         1000000000001000  0000000010000000  1010101010101010  0000000010000000
latin             1000001000100000  0010010000100100  1011101110111011  0000000000000000
sparse            1000000000100000  0000000000000000  0010001000100010  0000000010000000
Type
Object

Five presets, each { kick, snare, hat, clap } as 16-character strings of 1 and 0.

voiceForNote()#

function@openav/drums
voiceForNote(note)

Tells which drum of the kit a General MIDI drum note plays, or null for a note it does not play.

Pads and drum machines send notes on channel 10, and several notes map to the same drum: 35 and 36 are kicks, 38 and 40 snares, 41 and 43 low toms, 45 and 47 toms, 48 and 50 high toms, 49, 52, 55 and 57 crashes, 51, 53 and 59 rides. A note that is not in the table, such as a melodic 60, gives null: the kit stays silent instead of guessing, because a wrong cymbal on a kick pad is worse than nothing.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
noteNumberA MIDI note number.

Returns

String | null The drum name ('kick', 'crash'…), or null.

@openav/pattern

compile()#

function@openav/pattern
compile(src, { words = WORDS } = {})

Reads one line of rhythm text, like 'bd*4, [~ sd]*2, hh*8', and gives back the drum hits of any bar you ask for. It never throws.

compile() is the one function you need to turn a line of rhythm into hits. compile('bd sd hh').eventsInBar(1) answers "what happens in bar 1?" with a list of hits, sorted by pos. Bars count from 1, and one bar is one cycle of the line: the words share the bar equally, so bd sd hh puts a kick at 0, a snare at 1/3 and a hat at 2/3.

Each hit from eventsInBar(bar, { seed }) is { word, voice, n, pos, dur, vel, layer, token }. word is what was written, voice the drum it plays ('kick'), pos where in the bar, 0 up to (not including) 1. dur is how long it lasts, in bars, and may run past the bar (bd/2 lasts two). vel is always 1. layer is the index of the comma part it came from. token is { start, end }, the character range of the word in src, so you can light the word while it sounds. n is the sample number from bd:2, or null. n is kept for you but does not change the sound.

It never throws. A line it cannot read comes back as { ok: false, error }, and eventsInBar() returns [] for every bar, so check ok before you trust the hits. error.index and error.length mark the characters that are wrong, error.message and error.hint are English sentences, and error.code is one of empty, unclosed, unexpected, bad-number, bad-euclid, unknown-word or unsupported. An unknown-word error also carries suggestion, the closest word or null. The words and the symbols you can write are listed below.

text
bd sd hh      steps share the bar equally
~  or  -       a rest
[bd sd]        a group takes one step and splits it again
bd*4           faster: 4 times in its step (decimals work: bd*1.5)
bd/2           slower: once every 2 bars
<bd sd>        one per bar, in turn
bd, hh*8       a comma stacks layers
bd(3,8)        Euclidean: 3 hits spread over 8 steps
bd(3,8,2)      the same, starting 2 steps later
bd!2  bd !     repeat the step (each copy takes a step)
bd@3  bd _ _   make the step 3 times as long
hh*8?  hh*8?0.3   drop each hit by chance (1/2, or 0.3)
bd:2           sample number, kept in n

Modifiers chain in the order written (bd(3,8)*2, hh*8?). Word case does not matter (BD is bd). ? is decided by seed and the time of the hit, so the same seed and bar always give the same hits, while other bars and other seeds differ. Not supported, and refused with an unsupported error and a hint: . (Strudel's grouping), |, { }, %, .. and ^. A dot matters most: lane strings like 'x...x...' are not a line of rhythm, and a rest is ~.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
srcStringThe line of rhythm, for example 'bd sd hh'. Anything that is not a string is turned into one (null and undefined become an empty line, which is an error).
wordsObjectWhich words mean which drum: { word: voice }. The default is WORDS. To add a word, spread the default: { ...WORDS, boom: 'kick' }. The voice should be one the drum kit plays, see GM. optional default WORDS

Returns

Object { ok, error, src, voices, layers, period, eventsInBar(bar, { seed }) }. ok is true when the line was read. error is null, or { code, index, length, message, hint }. voices lists the drums the line uses, in the order they first appear. layers counts the comma parts. period is the number of bars until the written rhythm repeats.

Notes

  • Time inside is exact fractions, and each bar is computed on its own. Bar 1 000 000 of [bd sd sn]*3 lands on the same ninths as bar 1, and asking for bar 500 is as cheap as asking for bar 2.
  • From a p5 sketch you do not call it: startDrums() takes the line and compiles it for you. Use compile() yourself when you want the hits as data, for a score, a drawing or a test.
  • The way of writing comes from TidalCycles and Strudel. This is an independent implementation written from their public documentation. Where it differs from strudel.cc on purpose (a rotation of n steps or more wraps around, *0 and (9,8) are errors, unknown names are errors), the package README says so.

Examples

euclid()#

function@openav/pattern
euclid(pulses, steps, rotate = 0)

Spreads a number of hits as evenly as possible over a number of steps, the Euclidean rhythm. euclid(3, 8) is the tresillo.

It is the function behind bd(3,8) in a line of rhythm: compile() calls it for every (k,n). Use it on its own when you want the pattern as data, for a drawing or your own sequencer. euclid(3, 8) is x..x..x., and euclid(5, 8) is x.xx.xx..

It follows Bjorklund's procedure as Toussaint (2005) describes it. rotate moves the pattern later, the direction strudel.cc plays: euclid(3, 8, 2) is x.x..x.., the hits of euclid(3, 8) moved two steps to the right.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
pulsesNumberHow many hits. A negative number plays the gaps instead: euclid(-3, 8) is the five steps euclid(3, 8) leaves out. More hits than steps fills every step. The number is cut to a whole number.
stepsNumberHow many steps. Fewer than 1 gives an empty array.
rotateNumberStart the pattern this many steps later. Negative starts earlier, and a number of steps or more wraps around. optional default 0

Returns

Boolean[] An array of steps booleans, true where there is a hit.

Examples

Related

  • compile() Reads one line of rhythm text, like 'bd*4, [~ sd]*2, hh*8', and gives back the drum hits of any bar you ask for. It never throws.

fromGrid()#

function@openav/pattern
fromGrid(grid, { steps = 16, words = null, order = null } = {})

Turns a grid of steps, like the drum machine card, into the one line of rhythm a person would write for it.

It is what happens when you click a cell of the drum machine card: the grid has to come back as text. Each lane becomes one layer, joined with , , and it picks the shortest honest spelling. Steady hits become bd*4 or hh*8, one hit per group [~ sd]*2, a Euclidean rhythm bd(3,8), and anything else is written beat by beat, like bd [~ ~ ~ bd] bd*2 ~. It never throws.

The line is exact: compile() of the result lands on the same steps, in every bar. The rules are in the package README, and the tests check a thousand random grids.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
gridObjectThe steps: { lane: 'x...x...' } or { lane: [1, 0, 0, 0, …] }. A lane is named by its drum (kick) or its word (bd). x, X, 1 and true are hits, | and spaces are ignored. A lane with no name the kit knows is left out.
stepsNumberHow many steps each lane has. optional default 16
wordsObjectKeep your own spelling: { kick: 'kick' } writes kick*4 instead of bd*4. optional default null
orderString[]Drums to put first, in this order, for example ['kick', 'snare']. The rest follow in the order of the grid's keys. optional default null

Returns

String One line of rhythm that plays exactly the grid. A grid with no hit anywhere gives '~'.

Examples

Related

fromStrudel()#

function@openav/pattern
fromStrudel(code)

Reads code copied from strudel.cc, like s("bd*4").fast(2), into the line of rhythm OAV plays, plus the tempo it found.

It lets someone paste what they made in Strudel. It reads s("…") and sound("…") with ", ' or backtick quotes. Several of them (also with a label like $: or name: in front) become layers. A .fast(n) or .slow(n) is folded into the line as […]*n or […]/n. setcpm(x) gives bpm as x times 4, setcps(x) as x times 240. .bank(…) goes to ignored, because OAV plays its own kit. Any other call or statement goes to unsupported, and the rest still plays. It never throws.

It only reshapes text: it does not check the words. fromStrudel('s("bd kik")') gives ok: true with src: 'bd kik', so pass src to compile() and look at its ok. startDrums() accepts Strudel code directly and does all of this for you.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
codeStringThe Strudel code, as copied from the strudel.cc editor.

Returns

Object { strudel, ok, src, bpm, ignored, unsupported }. strudel is false when the text has no s(…) or sound(…) in it. ok is true when there is a line of rhythm in src. bpm is the tempo from setcpm() or setcps(), else null. ignored lists what was left out on purpose (.bank(…)), unsupported what OAV does not do (.jux(rev), .gain(…)).

parse()#

function@openav/pattern
parse(src)

Reads a line of rhythm into a tree of nodes, each with its character range. It does not look words up in the drum kit.

parse() is the first half of compile(): it checks the grammar and builds the tree, and stops there. Use it when you want to look at the structure of a line, for example to colour its words or find a mistake. For the hits, call compile().

The root is always a layer whose layers are the top-level comma parts, and each of those is a seq. The node types are step { word, n }, rest, seq { steps: [{ node, weight }] }, layer { layers }, alt { steps } (one per bar), fast and slow { factor, node }, euclid { pulses, slots, rotate, node } and maybe { chance, id, node }. Every node has start and end, its character range in src. Weights and factors are fractions [numerator, denominator], so bd*1.5 has the factor [3, 2].

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
srcStringThe line of rhythm, for example 'bd [sd sd]'.

Returns

Object { ok: true, tree, error: null }, or { ok: false, tree: null, error } with the same { code, index, length, message, hint } error as compile().

Notes

  • Because parse() never looks at the drum kit, parse('kik') succeeds while compile('kik') fails with unknown-word. Everything else (an unclosed bracket, *0, (9,8)) fails in both.

Examples

Related

  • compile() Reads one line of rhythm text, like 'bd*4, [~ sd]*2, hh*8', and gives back the drum hits of any bar you ask for. It never throws.

toGrid()#

function@openav/pattern
toGrid(p, { bar = 1, steps = 16, seed = 0, bars = 16, words = WORDS } = {})

Shows one bar of a line of rhythm on a grid of steps, and tells you what the grid cannot hold.

It is the way back from fromGrid(), and what the drum machine card uses to draw the cells of a line. Each hit goes to the step it is nearest to. The lost fields say what that cost: offGrid is the number of hits that sit between steps (triplets) and were moved to the nearest one. stacked counts two hits of one drum on one step. varies is true when other bars differ (< >, /2). random is true when the line has a ?. samples is true when it has a sample number like bd:2. exact is true only when none of these happened.

A line that fails to compile does not throw: you get ok: false.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
pString | ObjectA line of rhythm, or the result of compile().
barNumberWhich bar to show, counting from 1. optional default 1
stepsNumberHow many steps the grid has. optional default 16
seedNumberDecides each ?, the same way as in eventsInBar(). optional default 0
barsNumberHow many bars to look through to find out whether the other bars differ (lost.varies). At most the line's period, and never more than 64. optional default 16
wordsObjectWhich words mean which drum, the same as in compile(). optional default WORDS

Returns

Object { ok, grid, words, voices, exact, lost }. grid is { voice: [0 or 1 × steps] }. words is the word the line used for each drum. voices lists the drums. exact is true when the grid holds the bar completely. lost counts what it cannot: { offGrid, stacked, varies, random, samples }. If the line cannot be read, ok is false and the rest is empty.

toStrudel()#

function@openav/pattern
toStrudel(src, { bpm = null, comment = '', words = WORDS } = {})

Turns a line of rhythm into Strudel code: OAV's drum words become Strudel's, with a tempo line and a comment if you give them.

The words become the names Strudel's drum sounds use: kick becomes bd, pedalhat becomes hh. A rotation of n steps or more in a Euclidean part, like bd(3,8,10), is written as the rotation OAV plays (bd(3,8,2)), because strudel.cc would play it unrotated. A line that does not read is passed through unchanged, so the result may not play in Strudel: check it with compile() first. It never throws.

To open the result in the Strudel editor, use strudelUrl().

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
srcStringThe line of rhythm.
bpmNumberThe tempo. When it is above 0 a setcpm(bpm/4) line is written, because one OAV bar is one Strudel cycle of four beats. optional default null
commentStringA line to put first as a // comment. optional default ''
wordsObjectWhich words mean which drum, the same as in compile(). optional default WORDS

Returns

String The Strudel code, one to three lines, ending in s("…").

Examples

WORDS#

constant@openav/pattern
WORDS = object, 26 keys

The drum words a line of rhythm may use and the drum each one plays: bd is kick, sd is snare, hh is hat.

The short words are the ones TidalCycles and Strudel use: bd kick, sd and sn snare, hh hat, oh open hat, cp clap, rim and rs rim, lt low tom, mt tom, ht high tom, cr crash, rd ride, cb cowbell. cue()#

functionoav-p5
cue(bar, name, [every])

Plans something for a bar: at bar bar the function cueFired(name, bar) is called and cueName becomes name; with every, again every that many bars.

The drum machine counts the bars, so it can run a plan: cue(1, 'calm', 12); cue(5, 'bloom', 12); cue(9, 'storm', 12); in setup() makes three scenes that come round every 12 bars. When a cue is due, cueFired(name, bar) is called and cueName holds the name; read it in draw() if you prefer that to a callback. Several cues on one step fire in the order you declared them, before barStarted(), stepStarted() and the hits of that step.

Calling cue() twice with the same values adds nothing, so it is safe in draw() too. Counting starts with startDrums(), and a cue only fires when the machine passes its place: declare the cues right after startDrums() in setup() so that a cue at bar 1 is not missed. After the machine is stopped and started again, the cues fire again from bar 1.

barNumberThe bar, counted from 1 (the first bar). A fraction is a place inside a bar: 4.5 is halfway through bar 4 (the nearest of the 16 steps is used). A value below 1, or one that is not a number, prints a warning in the console and adds nothing.
nameAnyWhat to call it, usually a string. It is passed to cueFired() and becomes cueName.
everyNumberRepeat every this many bars after the first time (fractions work, at least one step). 0 or left out: only once. optional default 0

Returns

undefined Nothing. OAVp5.drums.cue() is the same function and returns the cue it made.

Notes

  • A cue declared after its bar has passed fires at its next repeat if it has an every, otherwise never until the machine is started again. Without a running machine no cue fires at all.

@openav/score

Director#

class@openav/score
new Director({ score, modules = [], api = {}, onStatus = null, onCue = null, maxStep = 2 } = {})

Runs a score's segment modules: enters each once, updates it every frame, exits it once, fires cues, and switches off a module that crashes without stopping the show.

A segment module is the code that performs one segment (the dawn, the storm, the finale). The director calls its hooks as the show moves through the score:

js
{
  id: 'dusk',                                  // the id of the segment it performs
  enter(api, ctx)  {},                         // the segment began, or a seek landed inside it
  update(api, ctx) {},                         // every frame while the segment (and its linger) is current
  exit(api, ctx)   {},                         // it ended, or a seek left it: give back what you took
  param(key, value, ctx) { return value; },    // optional: rewrite a timeline param meanwhile
  cue(name, ctx)   {},                         // optional: one of its cues was just passed
  reset(api)       {},                         // optional: R was pressed, forget everything
}

Every hook gets a ctx: p (progress through the segment, 0 to 1; above 1 during linger; exactly 1 while holding), t (seconds into the segment), dt, dur, T (show time), segment, cue(name) and cueT(name) (where a cue sits, as a progress and in show seconds), phase ('active', 'linger', or 'failed' inside exit() after a crash), holding, held (seconds waited at a hold: a clock for ambient motion while T is frozen), playing and api.

A module is entered once and exited once, however the show got there: a seek into the middle of a segment calls enter with the right p, so a module must be able to start from the middle. A module that throws is switched off alone: the director calls its exit() once with phase: 'failed', logs one console.error, and never calls it again; the other modules and the show carry on. Reset brings it back.

In a show, createShow() builds the director from its score option and calls update() every frame after the timeline has advanced; the director's param() plugs into timeline.layer. Without createShow() you do that wiring yourself: director.update(timeline.t, dt, { holding: timeline.holding, playing: timeline.playing }).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
scoreScoreThe Score to perform. Required: without it the constructor throws "Director needs a score".
modulesArray | ObjectThe segment modules: an array (matched to segments by each module's id) or an object keyed by segment id. A segment with no module is simply not performed. optional default []
apiObject | FunctionWhat every module hook receives as its first argument (also ctx.api). A function is called once, the first time it is needed, and its result is used. optional default {}
onStatusFunction | nullCalled with status() when the segment, the holding state or the list of switched-off modules changes, not every frame. optional default null
onCueFunction | nullCalled for each cue the playhead passes: { name, cue, T, n, segment }. optional default null
maxStepNumberA jump bigger than this many seconds between two update() calls counts as a seek, so the cues in between are not fired. Raise it if you rehearse at a very high timeline.rate. optional default 2

Members

NameDescription
apigetterThe api object the modules receive (a function given as api is called on first use).
register(mod)methodAdd a segment module (it replaces one with the same id). Throws when the module has no string id. Returns the director.
moduleFor(seg)methodThe module that performs a segment: the one named by its module field, else the one with its own id, else null.
holdinggetterWhether the show is parked at a hold, as told by the last update().
update(T, dt = 0, state = {})methodCall once per frame, after the timeline advanced: update(T, dt, { holding, playing }) with T the show time. Enters, updates and exits the modules and fires the cues passed since the previous call.
param(key, value, T = this._T)methodThe timeline's param layer: param(key, value, T) lets the modules of the current segments rewrite the value (a module returns a number to replace it). A performer's override still wins afterwards.
seek(T)methodThe playhead jumped to T: modules whose segment no longer covers T exit now, and the next update() enters the new ones with the right p.
reset()methodBack to the start: every active module exits, every module hears reset(api), and switched-off modules come back.
status()methodFor the desk and the backstage: { cut, T, total, segment, next, holding, held, active, failed, errors, missing }, with the current segment's progress and time remaining, the next segment and its countdown, and who is switched off.

Notes

  • The last segment is never exited by time: while the show sits at its end (or past it), the last module stays entered. It exits on a seek that leaves it, or on reset().
  • A new segment's module is entered before the old one exits, and during linger both run at the same time.
  • A module whose module or id matches no segment, or a segment that names a module nobody registered (listed in status().missing), is simply not performed. The show keeps going.

Score#

class@openav/score
new Score({ cuts, cut } = {})

A show written as segments with lengths, never as absolute seconds: it works out every start, end, cue and countdown, for every version (cut) of the show.

A timeline written as a table of absolute seconds cannot grow: make one scene longer and every later cue, curve and if (t > 466) is wrong. In a score you write only how long each segment is, and Score computes every start, end, cue time, countdown and scene from those lengths. Change one dur and everything after it moves; a second version of the show is a few lines of data.

A cut is one version of the show; a segment is one stretch of it:

js
{ id: 'full', title: 'A day', segments: [
  { id: 'standby', dur: 6, hold: true, acts: ['Press Space when the room is ready'] },
  { id: 'dawn',    dur: 24, cues: { birds: 0.3 } },          // a ratio of the segment
  { id: 'noon',    dur: 30, cues: { flare: { s: 8 } } },     // or seconds into it
  { id: 'dusk',    dur: 24, linger: 8 },
] }
{ id: 'short', from: 'full', scale: 0.5 }                     // the same show at half the length

dur is the only time a segment has. cues are named moments (a ratio 0 <= r < 1, or { s: seconds }), acts is what the human operator does (strings shown on the desk), linger keeps a segment's module running for some seconds after it ends, hold stops playback at the end of the segment until the operator releases it, and module names the module that performs it when that is not the segment's own id. A derived cut scales dur, linger and { s } cues, so a cue keeps its place in the music.

Everything is checked when the score is built. Duplicate ids, a dur of 0 or below, a from that is not a cut, a cut derived from itself, a cue outside its segment: each throws a ScoreError that lists every problem at once. In a show, createShow() builds the score from its score option and hands it to a Timeline and a Director; ?cut=<id> in the page address picks the cut.

NameTypeDescription
cutsArray | ObjectThe cuts this show can be performed as: an array of cuts, or an object keyed by cut id. A cut is { id, title?, start?, segments: [...] }, or a derived one, { id, title?, from, scale }. Required: without a cut it throws.
cutStringThe id of the cut to perform. Defaults to the first one; an id that is not in cuts is an error. optional default the first cut

cutsgetterEvery cut, for a version picker: [{ id, title, total, from, scale, base }].

segment(id)methodThe segment with this id, or undefined.

cues()methodEvery cue of the cut in time order: [{ name, cue, T, p, n, segment }], where n is its place in that order.

@openav/timeline

CURVES#

constant@openav/timeline
CURVES = object, 5 keys

The curve names a keyframe can use to say how its segment gets there: linear, ease, in, out, step, each a function from 0..1 to 0..1.

In a Timeline, the third item of a keyframe names the curve of the segment that ends at that keyframe: [30, 320, 'ease'] means "arrive at 320 at second 30 the ease way". linear is the default, and an unknown name or a typo also falls back to linear, so a mistake never stops a show. You can pass your own function instead of a name.

linear goes straight. ease is a smoothstep: slow, fast, slow. in starts slowly (f²). out starts fast and lands softly (1 − (1 − f)²). step is special: the segment holds the old value until the keyframe, then jumps. The step function stored here returns 0 and is never called to interpolate; it is listed so that the object is the whole vocabulary.

A param declared with step in its Params schema holds each keyframe whatever curve you name.

Examples

HOLD_EPS#

constant@openav/timeline
HOLD_EPS = 0.000001

How far before the boundary the playhead parks when a hold stops the show: one microsecond, so it still belongs to the scene that is waiting.

A scene with hold: true stops playback at its end. The Timeline parks HOLD_EPS (0.000001 seconds) before the boundary rather than on it, so sceneIndexAt(t) and the director still say "the held scene", timeline.t reads 5.999999 for a hold at 6, and the next scene has not started. release() then moves the playhead onto the boundary itself.

You only need it when you compare the playhead with a boundary yourself: while holding, timeline.t is boundary - HOLD_EPS, not exactly boundary.

Examples

Related

  • Director Runs a score's segment modules: enters each once, updates it every frame, exits it once, fires cues, and switches off a module that crashes without stopping the show.
  • Score A show written as segments with lengths, never as absolute seconds: it works out every start, end, cue and countdown, for every version (cut) of the show.

Timeline#

class@openav/timeline
new Timeline({ params, automation = {}, scenes = [], total = 600, score = null, start = null, loop = false, onCue = null })

Answers "what is every param at time t?" from keyframes, and runs the transport around it: play, seek, scenes, holds, loops, cues and recording.

timeline.state(t) returns { key: value } for every param at time t, interpolated from automation. That is the whole job: the timeline owns time, and a world never reads the clock. In a show, createShow() builds the timeline from its timeline option, Loop calls advance(dt) every frame, and what state() returns goes into params.resolve(), where a hand or a knob that has overridden a param still wins.

Between two keyframes the value moves in a straight line. The optional third item of a keyframe says how the segment that ends at that keyframe gets there: 'linear', 'ease', 'in', 'out', 'step', or your own function of 0..1 (see CURVES). Before the first keyframe the value is the first one, after the last it is the last one, and a param with no keyframes stays at its def. A param declared with step holds each keyframe instead of interpolating.

Scenes give the show its shape: { id: 'storm', t: 90, title: 'Storm', note: 'clusters welcome' }. onSceneChange is the hook to fire sound, lights or prompts, and the console shows the title and note to the performer. A scene with hold: true stops playback at its end until someone calls release(). Scene cues are { name, t } with t in show seconds (not seconds into the scene), and they fire only when playback passes them: a seek, a jump or a reset never does.

Before you call it

Time only moves when you call play() and then advance(dt) every frame (a show does this for you). state(t) and valueAt(key, t) work at any moment, playing or not. The callbacks do not fire for the starting scene until the first advance() or seek().

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
paramsParams | ArrayThe Params of the show, or a plain schema array. The timeline reads the schema to know which params to resolve. Required.
automationObjectThe keyframes of each param: { hue: [[0, 200], [30, 320, 'ease'], [60, 40]] }. A keyframe is [seconds, value, curve?], sorted by time. optional default {}
scenesArrayThe scenes: { id, t, title?, note?, acts?, hold?, cues? }, sorted by t. A negative t is a pre-show standby. Ignored when a score is given. optional default []
totalNumberThe length of the show in seconds. Playback stops by itself there. (createShow() passes 120 unless you say otherwise.) Ignored when a score is given. optional default 600
scoreScore | nullA Score: the scenes, the total and the start then come from it, and automation is read at score.baseTime(t), so a derived cut stretches the curves with it. optional default null
startNumber | 'first' | nullWhere reset() goes and where the playhead starts: a number of seconds, or 'first' for the start of the first scene (a standby at −30, say). null means 0, or the score's start. optional default null
loopBoolean | String | Objecttrue wraps the show at its end and plays on; 'scene' repeats the scene the playhead is in; a scene id repeats that scene; { from, to } repeats a range (seconds or scene ids). It is a plain property: set timeline.loop any time. optional default false
onCueFunction | nullThe same as calling timeline.onCue(cb) once: cb(cue, { cause }). optional default null

Members

  • These are plain fields you can read and set: t, playing, holding, rate (1 is real time; 4 rehearses at four times the speed), total, start, scenes, automation, score, loop, loops (laps since the last reset), and layer.
  • layer is (key, value, t) => value. A Director plugs in here so segment modules can bend a param; the performer's override is still applied afterwards and wins.
  • With a score, anything you pass as scenes or total is ignored, and reset() goes to the score's start.

lag(), env(), spring(), trail(): the way TouchDesigner shapes a value. 28

count()#

functionoav-p5
count(on, [limit], [name])

Also: OAVp5.chop.count

Counts how often on has turned on, or how many 'kick' (or any other event) have happened; with a limit it loops 0, 1, … limit − 1.

A counter you do not have to keep yourself: count(mouseIsPressed) is the number of clicks so far, count(beat, 4) walks 0 1 2 3 0 1 … on the beat, and count('kick') counts the kicks of the drum machine. A switch has to go off and on again to be counted twice.

Event counts start when count('kick') is first called, so earlier kicks are not counted. An event of your own fired with trigger() is counted from its first firing, whenever count() is first called.

Before you call it

The event names work like env(): 'kick', 'snare', 'hat' and 'beat' come from the microphone, or from the drum machine once startDrums() has been called, and the first count('kick') asks for the microphone if the drum machine is not on. The first call loads @openav/chop, which takes a few frames.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
onBoolean | Number | StringA switch: a boolean, or a number above 0.5, and each time it goes from off to on counts one. Or an event name ('kick', 'beat', 'note', or one of your own fired with trigger()): how many of those events have happened.
limitNumberLoop at this number: 4 gives 0 1 2 3 0 1 … Left out, or 0 or less, it keeps counting up. optional default 0
nameString | NumberOnly for the switch form (count(beat, 4, 'a')): a name for its memory, as the last argument. The event-name form needs none. optional read from arguments

Returns

Number The count, a whole number from 0. It is 0 until @openav/chop has loaded (a few frames), and for an unnamed switch outside draw().

Notes

  • Unnamed calls find their memory by their order in draw(): the first lag() is the first lag, the second is the second. Put one inside an if, or in a loop whose length changes, and the order slips: a card says so, and from then on oav-p5 matches each call by the line it is written on. A name at the end is the sure way. Outside draw() an unnamed call has nothing to remember by: it returns what Returns says and a card says so.
  • A sketch with its own variable or function called count keeps it. OAVp5.chop.count(…) is this function under another name.

Examples

drawTrail()#

Draws a line through values on the canvas, so it is in the work and in a recording: the oldest at x, lo at the bottom of the box, hi at the top.

The picture scope() shows in the corner, but drawn on the canvas: stroke(255); drawTrail(trail(micLevel, 3), 0, height - 100, width, 100). The line is one shape in the sketch's own stroke() colour and weight (white while noStroke() is in effect), with no fill, and the style you had before is put back afterwards.

The oldest value is at the left edge x, the newest at x + w. A number instead of an array is the shortcut: drawTrail(micLevel, 0, 0, width, 100) draws the last 2 seconds without a separate trail() call.

Call it in draw() after createCanvas(). With a number, the first call loads @openav/chop, which takes a few frames, and nothing is drawn until then.

env()#

functionoav-p5
env([event], [attack], [decay], [name])

Also: OAVp5.chop.env

A 0..1 pulse that jumps up after each event (a kick, a beat, a key, a press) and then fades out: TouchDesigner's Trigger CHOP.

Call it every frame and use the number like a size or a brightness: circle(width / 2, height / 2, 60 + env('kick', 0.01, 0.3) * 200) swells on every kick. The number rises to 1 in attack seconds after an event and falls back to 0 in decay seconds, quick at first and landing softly, the way a bass drum's swell looks right.

An event that arrives while the last pulse is still sounding restarts from where the pulse is, never from zero, so fast hits pile up into a plateau instead of flickering. The attack is measured from 0: a retrigger from halfway up takes half the attack.

The events: 'kick', 'snare' and 'hat' are the hits kickDetected() hears (from the microphone, or from the drum machine when it plays), 'beat' is beat, 'note' is any key going down, 'bar' and 'step' come from the drum machine, a cue's name fires when cue() does, and any other name is yours to fire with trigger(). The switch form, env(mouseIsPressed, 0.02, 0.5), fires on every press.

Before you call it

'kick', 'snare', 'hat' and 'beat' need something that makes them. If the sketch has not started the drum machine (startDrums()), the first env('kick') asks for the microphone, like reading micLevel, and ?oav_mic=off means nothing ever fires. Once the drum machine is started, the microphone is not opened for it. 'note' needs a key: play one, press 🎹, or call OAVp5.play(). A name of your own needs trigger(): if nothing fires it within 4 seconds, a card says so.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
eventString | Boolean | NumberWhat to react to. A name: 'kick', 'snare', 'hat', 'beat' (from the microphone or the drum machine), 'note' (any key), 'bar', 'step' (the drum machine), a cue's name, or an event of your own fired with trigger(). Or a switch: a boolean, or a number above 0.5, and each time it turns on counts as an event. Left out: 'beat'. optional default 'beat'
attackNumberSeconds the rise from 0 to 1 takes. optional default 0.01
decayNumberSeconds the fall from 1 back to 0 takes. optional default 0.3
nameString | NumberOnly for the switch form (env(mouseIsPressed, …, 'a')): a name for its memory, as the last argument. A named event such as 'kick' needs none. optional read from arguments

Returns

Number 0..1: 0 when nothing has happened, 1 at the top of the pulse. Until @openav/chop has loaded (a few frames) it returns 0.

Notes

  • A named event needs no place in draw(): env('kick') works in setup() or mousePressed() too. Only the switch form remembers anything between frames, and an unnamed switch outside draw() returns 0. Calls in draw() are matched by order, like lag().
  • OAVp5.chop.env(…) is this function under another name.

lag()#

functionoav-p5
lag(value, [up], [down], [name])

Also: OAVp5.chop.lag

Follows value smoothly instead of jumping: up in up seconds, down in down seconds (TouchDesigner's Lag CHOP).

Wrap any number that jumps: circle(width / 2, height / 2, 50 + lag(micLevel, 0.03, 0.4) * 300) is a VU meter. It opens within 0.03 seconds when someone speaks and takes 0.4 seconds to close. up is the time to follow a rise, down the time to follow a fall. Leave down out and both are up. Leave both out and they are 0.1.

The seconds are TouchDesigner's: lag(x, 0.1) moves like a Lag CHOP set to 0.1, so the numbers you learn here carry over. That is about the time the output takes to cover 90% of a jump (underneath, a one-pole lag whose time constant is the seconds divided by 2.3). The curve is the same at 30 and at 144 frames per second.

The first value it sees is taken as it is, so nothing glides in from 0. A boolean counts as 0 or 1: lag(mouseIsPressed, 0.2) is a soft switch.

Before you call it

Nothing to call or declare: write it in draw(). The first call loads @openav/chop from next to oav-p5.js, which takes a few frames.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
valueNumber | BooleanThe number to follow. A boolean counts as 0 or 1. Anything that is not a finite number (a string, NaN) goes straight through and the lag keeps what it had.
upNumberSeconds to follow a rise: about how long the output takes to cover 90% of a jump upward. Negative numbers count as 0. optional default 0.1
downNumberSeconds to follow a fall. Left out, it is the same as up. optional default up
nameString | NumberA name for this call's memory, written as the last argument. Optional. Without one, oav-p5 tells calls apart by their order in draw(); with one, the call is the same wherever it is made. optional read from arguments

Returns

Number The smoothed value. It returns value as it is until @openav/chop has loaded (a few frames), and for an unnamed call outside draw().

Notes

  • Unnamed calls find their memory by their order in draw(): the first lag() is the first lag, the second is the second. Put one inside an if, or in a loop whose length changes, and the order slips: a card says so, and from then on oav-p5 matches each call by the line it is written on. A name at the end is the sure way. Outside draw() an unnamed call has nothing to remember by: it returns what Returns says and a card says so.
  • A sketch with its own variable or function called lag keeps it. OAVp5.chop.lag(…) is this function under another name.

scope()#

functionoav-p5
scope(value, [label])

Also: OAVp5.chop.scope

Shows value in a small oscilloscope in the corner of the page and gives it back, so you can wrap any expression to watch it.

It is a CHOP's viewer: each label is one line in a small plot across the page from the 🎹, with the last 4 seconds of the value and its number now. Call it twice in a frame with two labels and you get two lines to compare, raw against smoothed. The scale is at least 0 to 1 and grows to hold whatever the values reach.

It lives on the page, not on the canvas: never in a recording or in 📷, and it never takes a click from the sketch. To draw the same line inside the work, use drawTrail().

Before you call it

Only inside draw(): anywhere else it just returns value. ?oav_scope=off hides it, and so does ?oav_hints=off, which is the one thing to know if it does not appear. See scope. The first call loads @openav/chop, which takes a few frames.

valueNumber | BooleanThe number to watch. A boolean is drawn as 0 or 1. Anything that is not a finite number is returned as it is and not drawn.
labelStringThe name of this line in the legend. Each label is one line, and a label longer than 9 characters is cut short there. Without one the line is numbered. optional

Returns

Number | Boolean Exactly value, so circle(x, y, scope(lag(micLevel, 0.03, 0.4), 'lag') * 300) works.

Notes

  • Unnamed calls find their memory by their order in draw(): the first lag() is the first lag, the second is the second. Put one inside an if, or in a loop whose length changes, and the order slips: a card says so, and from then on oav-p5 matches each call by the line it is written on. A name at the end is the sure way. Outside draw() an unnamed call has nothing to remember by: it returns what Returns says and a card says so.
  • OAVp5.chop.scope(…) is this function under another name. The lines keep coming from the last second: stop calling it for a second and its line leaves the plot.

How fast value is changing, per second: positive while it rises, negative while it falls, 0 while it holds still (TouchDesigner's Slope CHOP).

Adds rate to a running total every second, so rotate(speed(TWO_PI)) turns once a second and the rate can change without the total ever jumping.

Use the total to turn or move something: rotate(speed(TWO_PI)) is one turn a second, x = speed(60) % width slides 60 pixels a second and wraps around. You pass the rate, not the position, so the rate can follow a knob or the microphone (speed(micLevel * TWO_PI) spins faster the louder it gets) and the angle never jumps, which frameCount * rate would do.

Time is in seconds, the same at any frame rate. One frame counts for at most a quarter of a second, so coming back to a hidden tab does not make the shape leap.

Before you call it

Nothing to call or declare: write it in draw(). The first call loads @openav/chop, which takes a few frames.

Returns

Number The running total, 0 at the start. It is 0 until @openav/chop has loaded (a few frames), and for an unnamed call outside draw().

Notes

  • Unnamed calls find their memory by their order in draw(): the first lag() is the first lag, the second is the second. Put one inside an if, or in a loop whose length changes, and the order slips: a card says so, and from then on oav-p5 matches each call by the line it is written on. A name at the end is the sure way. Outside draw() an unnamed call has nothing to remember by: it returns what Returns says and a card says so.
  • Plenty of sketches have a variable called speed. If yours does, it keeps the name, and OAVp5.chop.speed(…) is this function under another name (third example).

Also: OAVp5.chop.spring

Follows value like a mass on a spring: it overshoots, bounces and settles (TouchDesigner's Spring CHOP).

Wrap a target that jumps: circle(width / 2, height / 2, spring(mouseIsPressed ? 300 : 100, 100, 6)). The size does not just glide to the new target (that is lag()): it swings past it, comes back and settles.

Stiffness and damping are the two knobs. A stiff, lightly damped spring rings like a ruler on a table. A soft, heavily damped one just eases. A big jump or a low frame rate does not break it: the motion is the same at any frame rate.

Also: OAVp5.chop.trail

The last few seconds of value as an array, 60 values a second, oldest first and newest last (TouchDesigner's Trail CHOP).

A history to draw or measure: drawTrail(trail(micLevel, 3), 20, 20, width - 40, 100) plots the last three seconds of the microphone level, and Math.max(...trail(x, 2)) is a two-second peak. The values are sampled 60 times a second whatever the frame rate, and the gaps between two frames are interpolated, so 30 fps and 144 fps give the same shape.

Change seconds between frames and the history is resized, keeping the newest values. The array you got last frame is never changed afterwards.

OAVp5.chop#

objectoav-p5
OAVp5.chop

The CHOP functions under one roof, plus the state of the module behind them: OAVp5.chop.lag(…), .state, .slots(), .reset().

Every function of this group is also here: OAVp5.chop.lag, .env, .trigger, .speed, .spring, .trail, .slope, .count, .scope and .drawTrail are the same functions as the plain names, for a sketch whose own speed or count keeps the plain name.

The rest is for looking inside: state says whether the module is loaded, module is the module itself, slots() lists every memory in use and reset() forgets them.

Notes

  • This is advanced: a sketch that only calls lag() and friends never needs it.

OAVp5.chop.reset()#

functionoav-p5
OAVp5.chop.reset([name])

Forgets the memory named name (a lag, a speed total, a count …), or every memory when you give no name: the next call starts fresh.

The call that follows starts from nothing, as if it were the first one: a speed() total is 0 again, a lag() takes its input as it is, a count() is back at 0. Use it to restart a named effect, for example on a key press.

Calling it with no name also drops the unnamed memories. They are made again by order on the next frame, so nothing breaks, but every unnamed value starts over too. Event counts from trigger() are not memories of a call and are not touched.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
nameStringThe name you gave a call as its last argument ('spin' in speed(1, 'spin')). The memory of that name is forgotten in every function that has one. Left out, every memory is forgotten, named or not. optional

Lists every memory the CHOP functions are using right now: its kind, how it is found, and its latest value.

approach()#

function@openav/chop
approach(current, target, seconds, dt)

One step of a one-pole lag: moves current toward target, closing 63% of the gap after seconds.

The smallest piece of smoothing. Call it once per frame, value = approach(value, target, 0.2, dt), and value chases target: 63% of the way after seconds, 90% after 2.3 × seconds, 99% after 4.6 × seconds. It is exact for any dt, so a sketch at 30 fps and one at 144 fps draw the same curve.

seconds here is a time constant, which is shorter than the "seconds" of TouchDesigner's Lag CHOP. Lag takes the TouchDesigner kind and divides it by TD_LAG_RATIO before calling this function. @openav/mapping's smooth steps with approach and means the time constant too.

Before you call it

Nothing. It is pure arithmetic with no memory: you keep current yourself and pass in the seconds since the last call. For a value with its own memory use Lag.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
currentNumberWhere the value is now.
targetNumberWhere it is heading.
secondsNumberThe time constant: after this many seconds the gap to target has closed by 63% (1 − 1/e). 0, a negative number or NaN jumps straight to target, whatever dt is.
dtNumberSeconds since the last step. 0, a negative number or NaN leaves current where it is.

Returns

Number The new value, between current and target.

Examples

Related

Count#

class@openav/chop
new Count({ threshold = 0.5 } = {})

Counts how many times its input turned on (true, or a number above threshold); with a limit it loops 0 … limit − 1. The Count CHOP.

count.step(input, limit) counts a rising edge, the moment the input goes from off to on, not the time it stays on. Hold a button for ten seconds and that is one. With limit 4 the result walks 0 1 2 3 0 1 …, which is how a beat becomes "beat 1 of 4".

The counter keeps counting underneath even when you pass a limit, so you can change the limit later without losing your place. A value that is not a number counts as off.

In a p5 sketch use count(): count(beat, 4), or count('kick') to count the drum machine's kicks.

Before you call it

Nothing to load. Call step every frame, even while the input is off: it has to see the "off" to notice the next "on". It has no dt, because a count does not depend on time.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
thresholdNumberA number counts as "on" when it is above this. A boolean true is 1, false is 0. optional default 0.5

step(input, limit = 0)methodstep(input, limit?): look at the input and return the count, looped to 0 … limit − 1 if limit is above 0 (a fraction is rounded down).
reset(value = 0)methodreset(value?): set the counter to value (0 if left out; a fraction is cut to a whole number) and forget whether the input was on. Returns the Count.

envelope()#

function@openav/chop
envelope(times, t, attack = 0.01, decay = 0.3, peak = 1)

The level, 0 to peak, of an attack-and-decay envelope at time t, for events that happened at the given times; the Trigger CHOP.

Keep a list of the times something happened (a kick, a key press, a cue) and ask for the level at the time you are drawing: scale(1 + envelope(kicks, now, 0.01, 0.3)). It rises in a straight line to 1 in attack seconds, then falls to 0 in decay seconds, quick at first and landing softly.

It is a pure function of the times and of t: ask twice, or at 30 fps and at 144 fps, and the same moment gives the same level; attack and decay may change every frame (a knob on the decay). A new event while the last one still sounds restarts from where the envelope is, never from 0, so fast hits pile up into a plateau instead of flickering. The attack counts from 0 to the peak, so a retrigger from halfway up takes half the attack.

In a p5 sketch you do not import it: env() and trigger() keep the event list for you and read the drum machine and the microphone.

Before you call it

Nothing to load. You record the event times yourself (for example kicks.push(performance.now() / 1000) when a kick arrives) and pass the same clock as t.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
timesNumber[]When the events happened, in seconds on any clock you like, oldest first. An empty array (or none) gives 0. Events later than t have not happened yet and are ignored. Only the last few matter, so you can trim the list.
tNumberThe moment to read, on the same clock as times.
attackNumberSeconds to rise from 0 to the peak. 0 starts at the peak at once. optional default 0.01
decayNumberSeconds to fall back to 0 after the peak: it is exactly 0 from attack + decay seconds after an event. optional default 0.3
peakNumberThe top of the envelope. optional default 1

Returns

Number 0 to peak: peak just after an event, 0 once it has died away.

envelopeStage()#

envelopeStage(elapsed, attack, decay, from = 0, peak = 1)

The level of one envelope elapsed seconds after its trigger: a straight rise to peak, then a fall to 0 in decay seconds.

The building block of envelope(), which strings several of these together for a list of events. On its own it answers: "how high is a kick that happened elapsed seconds ago?" With the defaults of envelope() (attack 0.01, decay 0.3) it is 0.5 at 5 ms, 1 at 10 ms, 0.49 at 100 ms and 0 from 310 ms on.

The fall is quick at first and lands softly: that is the shape a kick drum swell looks right with. It reaches 0 in exactly decay seconds, not asymptotically.

Lag#

class@openav/chop
new Lag({ up = 0.1, down = up, value = null } = {})

Follows its input with one speed while the input is above the output and another while it is below; the TouchDesigner Lag CHOP.

Make one Lag per value you want to smooth, then call step(input, dt) once per frame. new Lag({ up: 0.03, down: 0.4 }) is a VU meter: it opens almost at once and closes slowly. up and down are in TouchDesigner's seconds: with up: 1, a jump from 0 to 1 is at 0.9 one second later, at 30, 60 or 144 fps alike.

Each step is the exact answer for an input held at its new value over dt seconds, so the frame rate does not change the curve. A boolean counts as 0 or 1 (lag.step(mouseIsPressed, dt) is a soft switch). A value that is not a number, such as NaN, comes back untouched and leaves the memory as it was.

In a p5 sketch you do not import this: lag() keeps one Lag per call for you.

Before you call it

Nothing to load or start. Pass the seconds since the previous frame as dt (in a browser: the difference of two performance.now() / 1000). The first step only stores the input, so the output equals the input on frame one.

Parameters

upNumberSeconds to follow a rise, while the input is above the output. TouchDesigner's seconds: about the time to cover 90% of a jump. 0 follows at once. optional default 0.1
downNumberSeconds to follow a fall, while the input is below the output. Leave it out and it is the same as up. optional default up
valueNumberA starting value. Leave it out and the first input is taken as it is, so nothing glides in from 0. optional default null

NameDescription

Slope#

class@openav/chop
new Slope()

How fast the input is changing, in units per second; 0 on the first step. The Slope CHOP.

slope.step(value, dt) returns (value − previous value) / dt. A value rising by 3 every second gives 3 at any frame rate; a value that stands still gives 0; a falling one gives a negative number. Use it for "how hard did the knob just move": scale(1 + abs(slope.step(knob, dt))).

It has no smoothing: a single jump of the input is one big spike for one step. Put the result through a Lag if you want it to fade. A dt of 0 or less changes nothing and returns the last slope, and a value that is not a number returns the last slope too.

In a p5 sketch use slope().

Nothing to load. The first step only stores the value and returns 0, because there is no earlier value to compare with.

Speed#

class@openav/chop
new Speed({ value = 0 } = {})

Adds rate every second to a running total: a rate in units per second becomes a position; the Speed CHOP.

speed.step(rate, dt) adds rate * dt to the total and returns it. With rate 1 the total grows by 1 every second; rotate(speed.step(TWO_PI, dt)) is one turn a second. Feed it a rate that changes (a knob, micLevel) and the motion speeds up and slows down smoothly, without the jump you get from multiplying frameCount by it.

It is the integral of the rate, so it is the same at any frame rate. A boolean rate counts as 1 per second while true. A rate that is not a number, or a dt of 0 or less, adds nothing.

In a p5 sketch use speed(), which keeps one for each call.

Spring#

class@openav/chop
new Spring({ stiffness = 100, damping = 6, value = null } = {})

Follows its input like a mass on a spring: it overshoots, swings back and settles; the Spring CHOP with the input as position.

Make one Spring per value, call step(target, dt) once per frame and draw what it returns. With the defaults (stiffness 100, damping 6), a jump of the input from 0 to 1 sends the output to 1.37 after a third of a second, and it is within 1% of 1 from about 1.4 s on. Raise the damping to 20 and it glides to the target without overshooting.

Each step is the exact answer from springStep(), so 30 fps and 144 fps give the same motion and a long frame cannot blow it up. The input is the position it is pulled toward; a boolean counts as 0 or 1; a value that is not a number is returned as it is and changes nothing.

In a p5 sketch use spring().

springStep()#

function@openav/chop
springStep(x, v, target, stiffness, damping, dt)

One exact step of a damped spring of mass 1 pulled toward target; returns [position, velocity].

Solves x'' = −stiffness·(x − target) − damping·x' exactly over dt for a target that stays still during the step. It handles all three cases (under-damped: it bounces; critically damped; over-damped: it creeps) and a huge dt never blows up, which is why a sketch can fall behind for a whole second and the spring just lands on the target.

damping = 2 * Math.sqrt(stiffness) is the edge where it stops bouncing: with stiffness 100 that is a damping of 20. With no spring (stiffness 0) only the damping acts and the velocity just fades.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
xNumberThe position now.
vNumberThe velocity now, in units per second.
targetNumberWhere the other end of the spring is held.
stiffnessNumberHow hard it pulls. Negative counts as 0.
dampingNumberHow much friction slows it. Negative counts as 0.
dtNumberSeconds to advance. 0 or less (or NaN) returns [x, v] unchanged.

Returns

[Number, Number] The new position and velocity.

Notes

  • Advanced. The Spring class holds the position and the velocity for you and calls this.

TD_LAG_RATIO#

constant@openav/chop
TD_LAG_RATIO = 2.302585092994046

Math.LN10, about 2.303: how many time constants a lag needs to cover 90% of a jump, which is what TouchDesigner's Lag seconds mean.

TouchDesigner's Lag CHOP quotes its seconds as roughly the time the output takes to follow 90% of a change. A one-pole lag reaches 90% after ln 10 time constants, so seconds / TD_LAG_RATIO is the time constant to hand to approach(). Lag does exactly that, which is why lag(x, 0.1) in a p5 sketch moves like a Lag CHOP set to 0.1.

You only need it when you mix the two kinds of seconds: a time constant tau is tdSeconds / TD_LAG_RATIO, and tdSeconds is tau * TD_LAG_RATIO. Attack and decay of an envelope() are plain lengths and are not converted.

Type
Number

Exactly Math.LN10, 2.302585092994046. A fixed number: it never changes.

Examples

Remembers the input over the last few seconds as a list of values, oldest first, at a fixed 60 values a second; the Trail CHOP.

trail.step(value, dt) returns an array of seconds * rate past values followed by this step's input at the end, so the array is seconds * rate + 1 long (121 for the defaults). Draw it across the canvas as a line: that is a scope of the value.

The length is fixed from the first step, filled with the first value, so a sketch can draw the whole line from frame one. startRecording()#

functionoav-p5
startRecording([o])

Also: OAVp5.record.start

Records the canvas and the sound your sketch makes into one video file, and returns a promise that says whether the recording began.

Start it from a key or a click: if (key === 'r') startRecording();. What goes into the video is the canvas alone, at its own pixel size (a retina screen doubles it), and everything your sketch sounds like: the instrument of startSound(), the drum machine, the pads, the microphone while it is on, and p5.sound 1.x, mixed into one track while the speakers play as before. The 🎹, the drum grid and the cards are part of the page, not of the canvas, so they are never in the video. A sound that comes on during the take joins it.

The file is MP4 (H.264 + AAC, which Instagram, YouTube and every editor take) where the browser can write it, and WebM where not; a card says Instagram will not take a WebM. It is named oav-20261015-183005.mp4, with name in the middle when you give one. When the take is done it is downloaded, and on a phone that can share files a Share button appears on the card. After stopRecording(), or when seconds has run out, recordingSaved(info) is called with the details. Without seconds a take stops by itself at the longest length (300 seconds unless the reclimit option says otherwise).

Without bitrate the quality follows the canvas: 0.16 bits per pixel per frame, kept between 4 and 16 megabits a second (24 above 30 frames a second). Calling startRecording() while a take is running starts nothing new. After every take a card says what was recorded and, when something looks wrong, what and why: nothing reached the sound track although a sound was on, WebM, a file that is almost empty, a black video of a canvas that was not black.

Before you call it

A browser that has MediaRecorder: where it is missing, a card says so and the promise resolves to false. The picture is recorded at once, but the page can only make sound after a click or key press on it, so a take that begins before the first one has nothing to hear at first. A canvas that shows an image from another site (no CORS) cannot be recorded, and a card says so.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
oNumber | ObjectA number is the length in seconds: startRecording(10) stops by itself after ten. An object can hold seconds (the same, never more than the longest take, 300 by default), fps (frames a second, at most 60, 30 by default), mic (false keeps the microphone out of the video), name (a word for the file name), canvas (the canvas to record: a <canvas>, a p5 canvas or a createGraphics() buffer; the biggest p5 canvas on the page by default) and bitrate (bits a second). Leave it out to record until stopRecording(). optional

Returns

Promise<Boolean> Resolves to true once the recording is running (or when one already is). Resolves to false when the loading option record is off, when there is no canvas to record, when this browser has no MediaRecorder, or when it could not start; a card says why.

Notes

  • In the 🎹 panel, ⏺ starts and stops a take with no code, and 📷 saves the canvas as a PNG (see OAVp5.record.shot()). While a take runs the 🎹 button shows a red dot and the time. The loading options record (on, nomic or off), recfps, reclimit and title set the defaults.
  • The microphone is in the take while it is on: wear headphones, or the speakers are recorded twice. p5.sound for p5 2.x connects each sound straight to the speakers, so it cannot be recorded (a card says so); use p5 1.11, or startSound() and startDrums(). Sound that your sketch makes with its own Tone.js or Web Audio code is not recorded either.
  • Whatever you draw on the canvas is in the video, so show hints only while recordingIsOn is false.

Examples

OAVp5.record#

The object behind the recording names: the state, the time, the last file, the formats this browser can write and the screenshot function.

AudioTap#

class@openav/record
new AudioTap({ context = null, sources = [], captureDestination = false } = {})

Collects the sound of your work (and, if you add it, a microphone) into one recordable track, without sending anything to the speakers.

Recording the speakers with a microphone gives you the room. Tapping the Web Audio graph gives you the instrument exactly as it was synthesized, on the same clock as the canvas. An AudioTap has two buses and two outputs. The work bus is the sound of the piece; the extra bus is for things that belong in the video but not in the sound file, such as a microphone. tap.stream and tap.tracks are work and extras together (give them to the video Recorder); tap.workStream and tap.workTracks are the work alone (for the separate audio file). Both are a single track, on purpose: Chrome records only the first audio track of a stream.

The tap never routes anything to the speakers, so adding a microphone cannot feed back. To record a sketch you did not write (p5.sound, Tone.js, Sound), call captureDestination() before the work starts its sound: from then on every node that connects to a speaker destination is tapped too.

Before you call it

An AudioContext that is running. Browsers start audio only after a click, so call tap.resume() from a click handler. Without the click the tracks exist but carry silence.

contextAudioContextThe AudioContext to mix in, usually the work's own. One is made if you leave it out; it needs Web Audio to exist. optional default null
sourcesArrayThings to add to the work bus at once: AudioNodes, MediaStreams or MediaStreamTracks (see add()). optional default []
captureDestinationBooleanAlso call captureDestination() right away. optional default false

Members

workTracksgetterGetter. The audio tracks of workStream (one).

A node of this tap's context is connected directly, a node of another AudioContext is bridged through a MediaStream, and a MediaStream or MediaStreamTrack is brought in as a source node. bus: 'extra' reaches the video only. Returns a function that removes it. Throws a TypeError for anything else.

Install it before the work starts its sound: a node connected earlier is invisible. It can be called again without doubling. Returns a function that uninstalls it.

Returns a promise of the MediaStream. A microphone added before is replaced. Needs the user's permission.

cleanValue()#

function@openav/record
cleanValue(v, depth = 0)

Makes a copy of a signal value that is safe to write as JSON: rounded numbers, plain arrays, no functions, nothing too deep.

The rules: numbers are rounded to 6 decimals, and NaN and infinities become null. Typed arrays become plain arrays. A bigint becomes a number. Objects and arrays are copied down to depth 4 and anything deeper becomes null. A function, symbol or undefined becomes null in an array and the key is dropped from an object. EventLog runs every value through it.

Compositor#

class@openav/record
new Compositor({ size = 'vertical-1080p', layout = 'stack', layoutOptions = {}, getWorkCanvas = null, background = '#000', mirrorCam = true, maxFps = 60, onDraw = null, canvas = null } = {})

Draws your work and the performer's camera into one canvas of an exact size, every frame: the canvas that a Recorder records.

A performance video is two things in one picture: your work and the performer. The Compositor makes that picture. It owns a canvas (comp.canvas) of exactly the size of the file you want, whatever your window is, so a vertical 4K video from a laptop really is 4K. It is the canvas you hand to a Recorder. To show it on the page as a preview, put comp.canvas in the DOM and shrink it with CSS.

comp.start() redraws every animation frame (and, because a hidden tab freezes animation frames, from a Web Worker timer too, so a recording does not freeze with the tab). comp.draw() draws one frame now: call it yourself right after your work renders if you have your own loop. comp.rects is the last layout, { work, cam } in output pixels, and comp.fps is the rate it has been drawing at.

The camera is optional and never owned: setCamera(stream) shows it and setCamera(null) lets go, and you stop the tracks yourself. The camera's area can show a panel instead, anything with draw(ctx, rect, now), for example a drawing of the controller being played. The area for the camera is reserved before the camera arrives, so the picture does not jump.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
sizeString | Object | Number[]The size of the output, which is the size of the file. A preset id from PRESETS ('vertical-4k'), '1080x1920', [w, h] or { w, h }. Each side is rounded up to an even number. See resolveSize(). optional default 'vertical-1080p'
layoutStringWhere the work and the camera go: stack, pip, side or work (see LAYOUTS). optional default 'stack'
layoutOptionsObjectPassed on to layoutRects(): fit, camFit, camAnchor, minCam, split, pip. optional default {}
getWorkCanvasFunctionReturns the canvas of your work, or null. It is asked every frame, because a p5 sketch may replace its canvas and a WebGL work may resize it. The compositor never owns the work. optional default null
backgroundStringThe colour behind everything, any canvas colour string. optional default '#000'
mirrorCamBooleanShow the camera as a mirror, as performers expect. Keep it equal to the mirror of a hand tracker drawn on top. optional default true
maxFpsNumberDraw at most this often when running. A 120 Hz display does not need 120 composites a second. optional default 60
onDrawFunctiononDraw(ctx, rects, comp), called after the work and the camera are drawn, to put an overlay on top. A context state is saved and restored around it. An error in it is warned about once and does not stop the recording. optional default null
canvasHTMLCanvasElementDraw into this canvas instead of making a new one. Its width and height are set to the output size. optional default null

Members

NameDescription

panelgetterGetter. The panel drawn in the camera's area, or null (the camera is shown).

Call it from onDraw. Does nothing without a camera, or with a panel in its place.

stop()methodStops redrawing. Returns the compositor.
