Notes

  • A WebGL work: the compositor copies its canvas in the same animation frame it was drawn in, which works in Chrome. If you see black, create the WebGL context with preserveDrawingBuffer: true, or call comp.draw() right after your render and do not call start().
  • Webcams usually stop at 1080p30, so a 4K stack layout enlarges the camera about 1.6 times. The work above it stays sharp because it is drawn at the output size, as long as the work's own canvas is at least as large as its area.
  • In a p5 sketch you do not need this: startRecording() records the canvas and its sound for you. The Compositor is for a page that records the work together with a camera.

EventLog#

class@openav/record
new EventLog({ now = defaultNow, filter = null, throttleMs = 0 } = {})

Keeps a timestamped list of what happened during a take, such as notes and parameter changes, on the same clock as the recording.

A video keeps the picture and the sound. The log keeps the score of the take: every note, pad hit and (throttled) hand position, in milliseconds from the moment recording started. With it a take can be re-rendered at another size, re-synced to a better audio take, or turned into MIDI later. Start it with the recorder's start time so event times line up with the video's first frame: log.start(recorder.t0).

log.attach(signals) logs every signal a Signals bus publishes; pulses are always kept and continuous signals obey throttleMs. Or add events yourself with log.add(name, value). Values are cleaned into plain JSON data by cleanValue(). toJSON() gives { format: 'openav-eventlog', version: 1, startedAt, durationMs, count, events }, and EventLog.fromJSON(json) reads it back. toTake() turns the log into a MIDI take; TakeRecorder is a log that does exactly that on midi/*.

Properties: events is the list [{ t, name, value }] (t in ms, to a tenth), t0 the clock time of t = 0, startedAt the wall-clock time (ISO text) and durationMs is null until stop().

nowFunctionThe clock, in milliseconds. The default is the same clock as Recorder.t0. Pass your own in a test. optional default performance.now
filterFunctionfilter(name, value, meta), returns whether to keep an event. It applies to add() too. optional default null
throttleMsNumberFor continuous signals: keep at most one event per name in this many milliseconds. Pulses (note on, note off…) are never throttled. optional default 0

layoutRects()#

function@openav/record
layoutRects(layout, out, src = {}, opts = {})

Works out where the work and the camera go in an output frame, in whole pixels, for one of the four layouts.

It is pure arithmetic: no DOM, no clock. The Compositor calls it whenever a size changes. A 1080 by 1920 frame with a square work and stack splits into exactly 1080 by 1080 and 1080 by 840, with no seam row. The crop of a camera is in the displayed orientation, so with the mirror on, an anchor of x: 0.2 still means "keep the left of what you see".

stack puts the work across the full width at the top and the camera below. If that would leave the camera under minCam of the height (a square or landscape frame), the work gets split of the height and is letterboxed in it. side is the same turned sideways. pip fills the frame with the work and puts the camera in a corner as a rounded inset. work is the work alone.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
layoutStringOne of LAYOUTS. Any other name throws a TypeError.
outObjectThe output size { w, h } in pixels. It must be positive, or this throws.
srcObjectThe sizes of the sources: { workW, workH, camW, camH }. A missing or zero value means unknown. An unknown work counts as square. With an unknown camera the camera's area is still reserved, with crop: null and frame: null, so the frame does not jump when the camera arrives. optional default {}
optsObjectOptions: fit ('contain' default, or 'cover', for the work), camFit ('cover' default, or 'contain'), camAnchor ({ x, y }, 0..1, default the middle: which part a cover-crop keeps, in what you see), minCam (0.2: the share of the height in stack, or of the width in side, that the camera must keep), split (0.6: the work's share when it would leave the camera less than minCam) and pip ({ corner: 'br' | 'bl' | 'tr' | 'tl', size: 0.3, margin: 0.03, radius: 0.08, aspect: 0 }: the inset's width as a share of the frame, its distance from the corner as a share of the short side, its corner radius as a share of the inset's short side, and its shape, 0 being the camera's own). optional default {}

Returns

Object { layout, out, work, cam }. work and cam are { x, y, w, h, crop, frame, box } in output pixels (all whole numbers), and cam also has radius. crop is the part of the source that is drawn (source pixels, may be fractional) or null for the whole source. frame is where the whole source frame would land, cropped parts falling outside the rect, which is what overlays need. box is the area it was placed in. cam is null for the work layout.

normalizeTake()#

function@openav/record
normalizeTake(input)

Turns anything take-shaped, or its JSON text, into a valid take: events sorted by time, bad events dropped, nothing negative.

A take is what an EventLog filtered to midi/* records, as plain data: t is milliseconds from the start, name is a signal name such as midi/note/on, value is its payload, and meta holds free fields like { bpm, device, notes }. normalizeTake() makes any input safe: events that are not objects, have no name or have a t that is not a number are dropped; t is rounded to a tenth of a millisecond and held at 0 or more; the events are sorted by t (events with equal times keep their order); name defaults to 'take'; durationMs is at least the time of the last event. A new object is returned.

Every function in this package that takes a take runs it through here first, so you can pass raw data.

function@openav/record
noteOf(ev)

Tells whether a recorded event is a key going down or up, whatever its spelling, and which note on which channel.

A hardware keyboard publishes the same note under several names, and this function knows them all: midi/note/on and midi/note/off (family legacy, with value: { note, vel, ch }), midi/ch/<ch>/note/<note> (family channel, a number, 0 for off), midi/<device>/note/on|off (family slug:<device>) and raw bytes on midi/virtual (family virtual, { data: [status, note, vel] }). A key-down with velocity 0 in raw bytes counts as off. A channel of 0, as the on-screen piano says, counts as channel 1.

function@openav/record
quantizeTake(take, { bpm, grid = 4, strength = 1, offsetMs = 0 } = {})

Snaps the key presses of a take to a rhythmic grid, so a loose performance lands on the beat.

Each key-down moves to the nearest grid line (60000 / bpm / grid milliseconds apart). The key-up of a note moves with it, so the length of every note is kept. Everything that is not a note (controllers, pitch bend) stays where it was. A note written in two spellings at the same time (midi/note/on and midi/ch/1/note/60) moves by the same amount in both.

strengthNumberHow far to move, 0..1. 1 is all the way, 0.5 is half way to the grid, 0 changes nothing. optional default 1
offsetMsNumberShift the grid later by this many milliseconds, for a take that does not start on a beat. optional default 0

Recorder#

class@openav/record
new Recorder({ canvas = null, stream = null, fps = 60, audioTracks = [], audioOnly = false, videoBitsPerSecond, audioBitsPerSecond = 192000, mimeType, prefer = null } = {})

Records a canvas, together with the sound you give it, into one video file with one MediaRecorder, so picture and sound stay in sync.

new Recorder({ canvas, audioTracks }) then start() and, later, await stop(). The canvas track and the audio track go into the same MediaRecorder, which stamps both from one clock: nothing has to be lined up afterwards. stop() resolves, after the last chunk, with { mimeType, ext, bytes, chunks, durationMs, width, height, fps, audio, blob, error }: the blob is the file, ext the extension to give it (mp4, webm, m4a…), audio whether it has sound. Give the blob to URL.createObjectURL() for a download link.

Which file you get depends on the browser: it records MP4 (H.264 and AAC) when it can, WebM otherwise. A WebM from Chrome has no duration in its header; players cope, editors may want ffmpeg -i in.webm -c copy out.webm. The file is a master to edit, so the default bitrate is high.

To keep a long take out of the tab's memory, pass ondata(blob, seq) to start(): each chunk (every timeslice ms) is handed over in order, and a promise you return is awaited before the next chunk and before stop() resolves, so uploads stay ordered. With ondata the chunks are not kept and blob is null, unless you pass keep: true. To line a take up with an EventLog, start the log with recorder.t0, the performance.now() of the moment recording started.

Before you call it

A browser with MediaRecorder (Recorder.supported tells), and a canvas or a stream, or audioOnly: true: otherwise the constructor throws a TypeError. Mixing several audio tracks makes an AudioContext, which needs the page to have had a click. A camera or microphone in the stream needs the user's permission, as always.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
canvasHTMLCanvasElementWhat to record, usually compositor.canvas. optional default null
streamMediaStreamA ready video stream to record instead of a canvas. optional default null
fpsNumberThe capture rate of the canvas. Use recommendedFps(w, h): 30 for 2.7K and 4K. optional default 60
audioTracksMediaStreamTrack[]The sound, for example tap.tracks of an AudioTap. Several tracks are mixed into one, because Chrome records only the first audio track of a stream. optional default []
audioOnlyBooleanRecord only the audio tracks: the sound as a file of its own. Then canvas and stream are not needed. optional default false
videoBitsPerSecondNumberThe video bitrate. The default is recommendedBitrate() of the canvas size and fps (12 Mb/s when there is no canvas). optional
audioBitsPerSecondNumberThe audio bitrate. optional default 192000
mimeTypeStringForce one MIME type. The default is the first one the browser supports from VIDEO_MIMES or AUDIO_MIMES, see pickMime(). optional
prefer'mp4' | 'webm'Try this container first when picking the MIME type. optional default null

Members

recordinggetterGetter. Whether state is 'recording'.

TakePlayer#

class@openav/record
new TakePlayer({ signals = null, take = null, loop = true, speed = 1, yieldToLive = false, resumeAfter = 0, isLive = defaultIsLive, chase = true, clock, maxStepMs = 250, onEvent = null, onState = null, now = defaultNow } = {})

Plays a take back into a bus at the right times, so the work, its sound and its chord detector cannot tell it from you playing.

Give it a bus and a take, call play(), and it publishes the take's events into the bus at their times: the same signals a keyboard would have, so a work's visuals, its sound (Sound) and its chord detector respond exactly as to your hands. That is what lets a work's preview play itself. Pass clock: 'manual' and call player.update(dt) from your loop for full control.

No stuck notes, ever: the player remembers every key it pressed, in the spelling it pressed it, and the sustain pedal, and lets go of them on pause, stop, seek and every loop wrap. With yieldToLive, playing a key yourself makes the take fall silent; with resumeAfter: 8 it comes back 8 seconds after you stop. Its state is 'playing', 'paused', 'yielded' or 'stopped', and position (milliseconds), loops, playing and yielded are plain properties.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsThe Signals bus to publish into. It also defines take/playing (0 or 1) and take/position (0..1). optional default null
takeObject | StringA take or its JSON. You can load() another one later. optional default null
loopBooleanStart again at the end. Off, it stops there. optional default true
speedNumberPlayback speed: 0.5 is half speed. optional default 1
yieldToLiveBooleanFall silent when someone plays live: a key-down that the player did not send (hardware, the on-screen piano, a phone) pauses the take and releases its notes. optional default false
resumeAfterNumberSeconds without live playing before a take that gave way resumes. 0 means it stays paused. optional default 0
isLiveFunctionisLive(name, value), what counts as live playing. The default is any key-down that did not come from the player; knobs do not count. optional default any key-down
chaseBooleanWhen you seek(), send again the last value of every controller before that point (the sustain pedal, knobs), so the take is in the state it would have been in. optional default true
clock'raf' | 'timer' | 'manual'Who drives the time: 'raf' (requestAnimationFrame, the default in a page), 'timer' (a 10 ms timer: tighter for sound and it keeps going, slower, in a background tab) or 'manual' (you call update(dt) or tick(); the default where there is no requestAnimationFrame). optional
maxStepMsNumberThe longest time one step may move forward. After a gap (a frozen tab) the take slows down instead of firing a burst of notes. optional default 250
onEventFunctiononEvent({ t, name, value }, player), for every event as it is played. optional default null
onStateFunctiononState(state, reason), when it changes: 'playing', 'paused', 'yielded' or 'stopped'. optional default null
nowFunctionThe clock, in milliseconds. optional default performance.now

Members

NameDescription
durationgetterGetter. The length of the loaded take, in milliseconds (0 without one).
progressgetterGetter. How far through the take, 0..1.
stategetterGetter. 'playing', 'yielded' (gave way to live playing), 'paused' (anywhere after the start, also at the end of a take that does not loop) or 'stopped' (at the start). The onState callback still says 'stopped' with the reason 'end' when a take that does not loop ends.
load(take)methodReplaces the take (stopping the current one and releasing its notes) and goes back to the start. null clears it. Returns the player.
play({ from } = {})methodPlays from where it is, from the start after the end, or from from milliseconds: play({ from }). Returns false when there is nothing to play (no take, or an empty one), otherwise true.
pause(reason)methodPauses where it is and releases the sounding notes. Returns the player.
stop()methodStops, rewinds to the start and releases the sounding notes. Returns the player.
seek(ms)methodJumps to ms milliseconds (held between 0 and the length), releasing the sounding notes, and with chase sends the controllers' values at that point. Returns the player.
update(dt)methodAdvances by dt seconds. For clock: 'manual': call it with the seconds since the last frame from your loop.
tick(nowMs = this.now())methodAdvances to the clock time nowMs (default now()): what the raf and timer clocks call. The first call only records the time.

TakeRecorder#

class@openav/record
new TakeRecorder({ signals, filter = /^midi\//, name = 'take', meta = {}, overdub = false, throttleMs = 0, now = defaultNow } = {})

Records what you play: it listens to every midi/* signal on a bus from start() to stop() and gives you a take.

A TakeRecorder is an EventLog that listens to midi/* on a bus. Press record: rec.start(). Play. Press stop: const take = rec.stop(). The take is plain data, so it can be saved as JSON, turned into a .mid (toMidiFile()) or played back (TakePlayer). It has every member of EventLog (mark(), between(), toJSON()…).

No stuck notes: a recorder stopped in the middle of a chord closes the keys that are still held (and a sustain pedal that is still down) in the take itself, at the stop time. The events are the signals as they were published, so a take from hardware holds both naming families (midi/note/on and midi/ch/1/note/60) and the device names, and playback publishes all of them. Pass recorder.t0 of a video Recorder to start() to line the take up with the video.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsThe Signals bus to listen to.
filterRegExp | FunctionWhich signals are the take: a pattern for the name, or filter(name, value, meta). optional default /^midi\//
nameStringThe name of the take. optional default 'take'
metaObjectFree fields copied into the take: { bpm, device, notes }. The device is found from the events if you leave it out. optional default {}
overdubBooleanAlso record what a TakePlayer is playing back right now. Off, a recorder ignores playback. optional default false
throttleMsNumberFor continuous signals (knobs, aftertouch): at most one event per name in this many milliseconds. optional default 0
nowFunctionThe clock, in milliseconds. optional default performance.now

NameDescription
start(at = this.now())methodClears the take and starts listening. at is the clock time of t = 0 (default now), for example recorder.t0. Returns the recorder.
add(name, value = null, opts = {})methodAdds one event by hand, like EventLog.add() (see EventLog), and keeps track of which keys and pedals are held so stop() can release them.
stop(at = this.now())methodStops listening, releases the keys and pedal still down, and returns the take { v: 1, name, createdAt, durationMs, events, meta }.
toTake({ name = this.name, meta = this.meta } = {})methodThe take so far, as EventLog.toTake() does, with meta.device filled in from the events when it is missing.

toMidiFile()#

function@openav/record
toMidiFile(take, { ppq = 960, bpm } = {})

Writes a take as a Standard MIDI File (type 0) that opens in any DAW.

One track holds note on and off with velocity, controllers (the sustain pedal is CC 64), pitch bend, and channel and poly aftertouch, each on its own channel; channel 10 stays the drums. The take's name becomes the track name, and a 4/4 time signature is written only so a DAW's grid looks sane. Times are kept to the millisecond whatever the tempo, so the file plays like the take. Only one naming family of the take is used, so nothing doubles (midiEventsOf()). To save it, wrap it in a Blob of type audio/midi.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
takeObjectThe take.
ppqNumberTicks per quarter note. optional default 960
bpmNumberThe tempo written in the file. Left out, it is take.meta.bpm, and then 120. optional

Returns

Uint8Array The bytes of the .mid file.

trimSilence()#

function@openav/record
trimSilence(take, { keep = 0 } = {})

Cuts the silence before the first key press of a take, so the first note comes at the moment you choose.

Everything before the first key-down is cut away, but not lost: a controller value set during the silence, such as the sustain pedal or a knob, is kept and moved to the start (to t = 0 if it was before the cut), so the take still starts in the same state. If the take has no key-down at all, it is moved so its first event is at keep.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
takeObjectThe take.
keepNumberMilliseconds of lead-in to keep before the first key-down. optional default 0

Returns

Object A new take. Everything moved earlier by the same amount, and durationMs is shorter by that amount. A take that starts at once comes back as it is.

validateTake()#

function@openav/record
validateTake(take)

Checks a take and lists everything wrong with it as readable sentences. An empty list means it is valid.

It checks: v is TAKE_VERSION, name is a string, durationMs is a number from 0 up, events is an array, each event is an object with a signal name and a t of 0 or more, the events are in time order and none is after durationMs, and meta, if present, is an object. Use it on a take you read from a file; to repair one, use normalizeTake().

takeanyThe take to check.

Returns

String[] Sentences such as v must be 1 (got 2) or events[3] is out of order (t 100 < 200). [] when valid. It never throws.

VIDEO_MIMES#

constant@openav/record
VIDEO_MIMES = array, 6 items

The video MIME types the recorder tries, best first: MP4 with H.264 and AAC, then WebM.

MP4 comes first because it opens everywhere a performance video goes next (an editor, Instagram, a phone's gallery) without a remux, and Chrome encodes H.264 in hardware. The first string asks for a profile (avc1.640033, High profile level 5.1, enough for 4K at 30 and 1080 by 1920 at 60) because Chrome says no to the generic avc1,mp4a but yes to the qualified one, so both are in the list for other browsers. Plain video/mp4 is for Safari. pickMime() walks this list.

Type
String[]

A frozen list of 6 strings: video/mp4;codecs=avc1.640033,mp4a.40.2, video/mp4;codecs=avc1,mp4a, video/webm;codecs=vp9,opus, video/webm;codecs=vp8,opus, video/webm, video/mp4.

clock#

optionoav-p5
?oav_clock=follow | off

Whether an external MIDI clock (from a DAW, Strudel or a drum machine) moves drumPhase, drumBpm and the drum machine: follow or off.

With follow, an external MIDI clock (24 ticks a beat, plus start, stop and song position) is followed: drumPhase, beatPhase, drumBar, drumStep and drumBpm read it, and a drum machine that is up takes its tempo and its downbeat from it, starting and stopping with it. OAVp5.clock tells you what it hears. With nothing sending a clock, nothing changes.

off ignores every clock message: OAVp5.clock.info.state stays 'none'. Use it when something on the page or the machine sends a clock you do not want the sketch to follow.

default

Values in window.OAV_P5 are turned into text, so write 'off', not false. On OpenProcessing the page address takes ?sketch_oav_clock=… (the project's README says OpenProcessing forwards it to the sketch).

drums#

optionoav-p5

How the drum machine is clocked: lookahead (hits scheduled ahead on the audio clock) or frame (moved by animation frames, 0.5's way).

With lookahead, a heartbeat in a Web Worker hands the hits to the audio clock a little ahead of time, so the beat stays steady when frames stutter or the tab is busy, and the sketch is told when each hit is heard. With frame, the machine is moved by the animation frames instead, as it was in oav-p5 0.5. It is the safety net: where the lookahead machine misbehaves, frame brings the old behaviour back, and the timing is then only as steady as the frame rate.

link#

optionoav-p5
?oav_link=a room name

Joins a room: oav-p5 pages with the same room hear what each other's programs play, over the relay. A room name, or empty for none.

Every oav-p5 page with the same room (another tab, another computer) gets what this page's programs play into the virtual MIDI output (notes, controllers and the clock), over the phone relay, and plays it at the moment it sounds here. On the other side, OAVp5.last.source is 'link'. Nothing it receives is sent on, so two pages cannot loop. The room is also the phones' room, so one QR code plays every linked page.

OAVp5.link.info tells you the room, whether it is connected and how many other pages were heard. The 🎹 grows a 🔗: green when another page is there, yellow while connecting or alone, red when the relay is gone. linkdelay adds a buffer.

String

default
'' (no room)

Only letters, digits, _ and - are kept, and only the first 32 characters.

Before it has a value

shim#

optionoav-p5
?oav_shim=on | off

Whether oav-p5 replaces navigator.requestMIDIAccess so sketches with their own Web MIDI code also hear the 🎹 and phones: on or off.

With on, a sketch that calls navigator.requestMIDIAccess() itself (WebMidi.js does) gets the real ports and one more input called "OAV Virtual MIDI", which carries whatever the on-screen controller and the phone play. It also works in Safari and on iPad, where there is no Web MIDI: the sketch gets the virtual port alone, so a WebMidi.js sketch still runs there. Programs can play into its output as well (Strudel's .midi('OAV Virtual MIDI')).

off leaves the browser's own requestMIDIAccess alone. Use it when a page already has its own MIDI handling that must not see an extra port.

Type
String
Values
on | off
default
on

Only off turns it off.

Notes

  • Order matters: oav-p5 has to load before the code that asks for MIDI, which is why the loader line goes first. A page that opened MIDI earlier keeps the browser's own answer, and 🩺 says so.
  • Set it before oav-p5 loads. window.OAV_P5 = { shim: … }; above the loader line wins, then ?oav_shim=… on the page address, then ?shim=… on the script's own URL. Values in window.OAV_P5 are turned into text, so write 'off', not false. sound#

optionoav-p5
?oav_sound=click | off | an instrument id

Whether notes are heard: click (only after startSound() or 🔊), off (never), or an instrument id that starts at the first click.

With click, nothing makes a sound until the sketch calls startSound() or someone presses 🔊 in the 🎹 panel. With an instrument id, every key, pad, the on-screen controller and a phone are heard from the first click on the page, with no code at all, so any MIDI sketch becomes playable by adding the option to the page address: ?oav_sound=piano. off is a promise to the page: nothing sounds, startSound() resolves false and the 🔊 button is hidden.

Browsers let a page play sound only after a click, and a MIDI key is not a click, so the first sound waits for one: a card says "sound is ready but silent" until then.

The OAVp5 object (advanced)#

Everything oav-p5 exposes under OAVp5 and midi: state, subscriptions, the check-up. 13

oav-p5

OAVp5#

objectoav-p5
OAVp5

Also: midi oavMidi

The object oav-p5 hangs everything on: MIDI state, the panel, the microphone, the clock, the check-up. midi and oavMidi are the same object.

It is there as soon as oav-p5 has loaded, in setup() and draw() alike. The plain names of the p5 style (knob1, note, micLevel) are the easy way in. OAVp5 is the way in when you want more: the raw MIDI state (OAVp5.note, OAVp5.cc, OAVp5.bend, OAVp5.held, OAVp5.last), subscriptions (OAVp5.on()), a way to send bytes (OAVp5.input()), the microphone's numbers (OAVp5.mic), the external clock (OAVp5.clock), the link (OAVp5.link), the values over time (OAVp5.chop) and the check-up (OAVp5.check()).

Three names, one object. OAVp5 is always there. oavMidi is always there too. midi is there unless the page already had a midi of its own, in which case it is left alone and the console says to read OAVp5 instead. OAVp5.options holds the loading options as oav-p5 read them: OAVp5.options.mic, and so on for each of the loading options (for example mic).

Before it has a value

Only the loader line. If it has not loaded, OAVp5 is not defined, and a sketch that reads it stops with "OAVp5 is not defined".

Notes

  • midi and oavMidi are the same object under other names.

Examples

Related

Runs the 🩺 check-up: the version, page, browser, microphone, MIDI, sound, drums, recording, wiring and hints, as a card to screenshot and as an object.

The same thing the 🩺 button in the panel does. When something does not work for a student, OAVp5.check() in the console (or 🩺) gives a card that says what this browser did: whether the page is in an iframe, whether the microphone is on or blocked, whether Web MIDI exists and which devices it found, the last message, the sound and drum state, whether MP4 recording works, what the controller is wired to, which of the sketch's own names stepped in the way, and which cards have appeared. OAVp5.clock#

objectoav-p5
OAVp5.clock

What oav-p5 hears of an external MIDI clock: its state, tempo and where it is in the bar. Nothing until another program or device starts sending one.

Some programs keep the time and everyone else follows: Strudel (midicmd("clock*96, <start stop>/8")), a DAW over a virtual cable, a drum machine on a MIDI cable. They send 24 clock messages per beat, plus start, continue, stop and song position. oav-p5 counts them: OAVp5.clock.info says whether a clock is running, OAVp5.clock.bpm its tempo and OAVp5.clock.phase how far through the bar and the beat it is now.

When a clock is moving, drumPhase, beatPhase, drumBar, drumStep and drumBpm read it, and a drum machine that is up follows it. ?oav_clock=off turns all of that off. Clock messages are not delivered to midiMessage(): they belong to the clock.

Notes

  • The first clock message loads the counting code (@openav/midi's MidiClock) from next to oav-p5.js, which takes a few frames. Until then the members read none, null and null.
  • This is advanced: most sketches only read drumPhase and let it follow a clock.

Examples

Related

  • drumPhase How far through the current bar the drum machine is, smoothly from 0 up to just below 1, as it is heard.
  • beatPhase How far through the current beat the drum machine is, smoothly from 0 up to just below 1, four times per bar.

OAVp5.clock.info#

objectoav-p5
OAVp5.clock.info

A snapshot of the external clock: state (none, running, stopped or lost), bpm, whether the drums follow it, where it came from, and counts.

state is 'none' until a clock message has come, 'running' while the clock is going, 'stopped' after a MIDI stop (the position holds and clocks may still arrive), and 'lost' when no clock message has arrived for 0.6 seconds. bpm is the tempo fitted over the last 24 ticks, rounded to two decimals, or null before two ticks. running is true while the transport runs, which a stream of clocks with no start message counts as too (implicit is true then).

following is true when the drums read this clock: it is running, has a tempo and clock=off is not set. source says where the messages came from: 'hardware', 'screen', 'phone', 'virtual-out' (a program playing into OAV Virtual MIDI) or 'link'. clocks, dupes, starts, stops and continues count what arrived; a start sent three times with one timestamp counts once and adds to dupes.

Type
Object

A new object each time you read it: { state, bpm, running, following, source, implicit, clocks, dupes, starts, stops, continues }. Before any clock message it is { state: 'none', bpm: null, running: false, following: false, source: null, clocks: 0 }.

Examples

OAVp5.clock.phase#

variableoav-p5
OAVp5.clock.phase

Where the external clock is right now: { pos, bar, beat, bpm, running }, or null while there is no tempo.

A bar is four beats. bar and beat count up from 0 and fall back to 0 at the next downbeat, the same way drumPhase and beatPhase do. After a stop the position holds. A clock with no start message gets its downbeat from the first tick after a silence of half a second, so a phase is there anyway.

Type
Object | null

A new object each time you read it: pos is the number of bars since the start (0 is the downbeat of bar 1), bar and beat are 0..1 through the current bar and beat, bpm the tempo and running whether the transport is moving. null until a tempo is known.

OAVp5.drums.clock#

objectoav-p5
OAVp5.drums.clock

How the drum machine keeps time: which clock moves it, how far ahead it schedules and how long the callbacks wait for the speakers.

This is the diagnostic behind the 🩺 check-up. When drum hits feel late or early, look here first: the handbook puts a Bluetooth speaker at 0.15 to 0.25 seconds of latency, and ?oav_drumlatency=200 sets it by hand. late, skipped, warning and why are further notes the check-up reads.

Type
Object
Range
{ clock, heartbeat, lookahead, latency, audio, extended, preDraw, … }

A new object on every read. clock is 'lookahead' (hits are handed to the audio clock ahead of time, the default) or 'frame' (moved by the frames, the drums option). heartbeat is 'worker' (a Web Worker wakes it every 25 ms), 'interval' (the fallback), 'frame' with the frame clock, or 'none' before the machine exists. lookahead is the seconds scheduled ahead and extended is true when a slow draw() made it look further ahead. latency is the seconds the callbacks wait for the output of the speakers, audio whether the kit's audio clock is running, and preDraw the p5 hook that delivers the callbacks right before draw().

OAVp5.link

What the link to other oav-p5 pages in the same room is doing: only OAVp5.link.info, and null unless a room is set.

A link joins oav-p5 pages that share a room: what one page's programs play into OAV Virtual MIDI (notes, controllers and the clock) is heard by every other page in the room, at the moment it sounds there. OAVp5.link.info#

variableoav-p5
OAVp5.link.info

The state of the link: its room, state (connecting, open, closed), how many other pages are there, and the trip time. null when no room is set.

Read it in draw() for a status line, or look at the 🔗 on the 🎹, which turns green when another page is there, yellow while connecting or alone, and red when the relay is gone. The 🩺 check-up prints the same facts. A new object is made on every read.

Type
Object | null

null without a link room. With one: { room, state, peers, rtt, trip, late, sent, received, … }. state is 'connecting', 'open' or 'closed' (the relay is gone and it retries). peers is how many other pages were heard in the last 6 seconds. rtt is the shortest round trip to the relay in the last 30 seconds and trip the one-way trip estimated from it, both in milliseconds. late counts notes that arrived after the moment they should have sounded and were played at once. sent and received count messages. The object also has diff, lead, msgs, dupes and id, which explain the clock alignment (packages/relay/link.js).

bendToUnit()#

function@openav/midi
bendToUnit(v)

Turns a 14-bit pitch-bend value (0..16383) into −1..1, with the centre (8192) exactly 0.

MIDI centres pitch bend at 8192, so there are 8192 steps below the centre and 8191 above. Below the centre it divides by 8192 and above by 8191, so the bottom reaches exactly −1, the top exactly +1 and the rest position exactly 0. This is the number published as midi/bend and midi/ch/<ch>/bend.

A 2018 sketch that calls navigator.requestMIDIAccess() (or WebMidi.js) and waits for a keyboard shows nothing on a laptop without one, and on an iPad has no Web MIDI at all. Hand it this access instead and the on-screen controller becomes a real-looking MIDI input: the sketch's own unmodified code receives midimessage events with the same bytes a keyboard sends.

The virtual OUTPUT is a real-looking port too: a program that plays out to it (Strudel's .midi('OAV Virtual MIDI'), a WebMidi.js sketch) calls send(bytes, timestamp), and onOutput hears both. Real ports can be merged in with addReal(realAccess): they come FIRST in inputs, the virtual one last, so a sketch that only listens to inputs[0] takes the hardware when it is there and the virtual controller when it is not. Real ports pass through untouched, so nothing is delivered twice.

idStringThe port id prefix: the ports are <id>-in and <id>-out. optional default 'oav-virtual'
sysexBooleanWhat access.sysexEnabled reports. optional default false
onOutputFunction | null(bytes, timestamp) => … called when a program sends to the virtual OUTPUT. timestamp is when the bytes should sound (performance.now() milliseconds), or undefined for "now". optional default null
onClearFunction | nullCalled when the program calls output.clear() (Web MIDI: drop what is still waiting). optional default null

Returns

Notes

  • access.inputs and access.outputs are Maps, as in Web MIDI. input.listening counts the listeners a program put on the port, and requests counts how often virtualRequestMIDIAccess() handed the access out.

EchoGuard#

class@openav/midi
new EchoGuard({ window = 40, max = 256 } = {})

Recognises our own MIDI messages coming back: remember what was sent, and an identical message arriving within a short window is an echo, not a performer.

A virtual cable or a DAW can send your message straight back on an input, and the engine would treat it as a performer. sent(bytes) records a message and isEcho(bytes) asks whether an arriving one is that message returning. Each sent message cancels at most ONE echo, so two real identical messages are not both eaten.

A note-on with velocity 0 counts as a note-off, in both directions, because a DAW may rewrite one as the other. System messages (clock and the like) are never recorded. Midi has one (midi.echo, with the echoWindow option) and drops the echoes it finds, counted in midi.echoDropped.

windowNumberMilliseconds an echo may take to come back. 0 turns the guard off. optional default 40
maxNumberHow many sent messages to remember. Only the newest max are kept. optional default 256

isEcho(bytes, now = performance.now())methodGives true when this arriving message is a recorded one coming back within window ms, and uses that memory up. Older records are forgotten.

encodeMessage(ev)

Turns an event object back into MIDI bytes, the inverse of parseMessage(): { type: 'cc', ch: 1, cc: 74, value: 64 } becomes [0xb0, 74, 64].

genericSignals()#

function@openav/midi
genericSignals(ev, { device = null, legacy = true, channel = true } = {})

Lists the device-independent signals one MIDI event becomes: midi/cc/74, midi/note/on, midi/bend, and their per-channel twins such as midi/ch/2/cc/74.

Two families, both published for every hardware port and every virtual controller. The short ones are what most worlds read: a noteon becomes the pulse midi/note/on with { note, vel (0..1), velocity (1..127), ch, device }, a noteoff becomes midi/note/off with { note, ch, device }, a cc becomes midi/cc/<n> (0..1), and a pitchbend becomes midi/bend (−1..1).

The per-channel ones are for two devices that share a CC number, or a work that cares about the channel: midi/ch/<ch>/note/<n> (velocity 0..1 while held, 0 on release), midi/ch/<ch>/cc/<n>, midi/ch/<ch>/bend, midi/ch/<ch>/pressure (channel aftertouch) and midi/ch/<ch>/poly/<n> (polyphonic aftertouch). Pressure and poly exist only in this family. program, clock and the other system messages produce nothing.

There is deliberately no midi/cc/<ch>/<n>: under prefix subscriptions it would collide with "CC 1 on any channel".

linkControllers()#

function@openav/midi
linkControllers(relay, signals, controllers)

Links the on-screen controllers to phones over the room relay: tells phones which device is on screen, echoes this machine's moves to them, and mirrors theirs here.

A phone's MIDI tab publishes the device's signals itself (the controller lives there), so this side only does three things. When you select another device it tells the phones with relay.config('midi', { profile }). When a knob, fader, encoder, wheel, strip or toggle button on THIS machine moves from hardware or the screen, it queues relay.feedback('midi/<short>/<id>', value) so the phone's knobs follow. When a phone plays (midi/virtual) it mirrors that on this screen, state and view only, because the phone already published the signals.

This is what @openav/remote's show-side host and the lab's midi module call. You need it only when you wire phones into a page yourself.

matchProfile()#

function@openav/midi
matchProfile(portName, profiles)

Finds the device profile that owns a MIDI port name, such as 'Minilab3 MIDI', by testing each profile's match patterns.

Only device profiles are considered (a generic layout never matches by name). A profile matches when one of its match.ports regular expressions (case-insensitive) hits the name. The score starts at 1, gains 1 when a match.prefer pattern also hits, and loses 2 when a match.avoid pattern hits. The highest positive score wins, so a port a device only exposes for something else (Minilab3 DIN THRU, Minilab3 MCU/HUI) does not match.

This is how MidiControllers turns a plugged-in device into the right on-screen controller. When a device exposes several ports, pickPort() chooses which one to listen to.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
portNameStringThe name of a MIDI input port.
profilesObject[]The profiles to search, usually PROFILES.

Returns

{ profile, score } | null The best match, or null when no device profile fits.

Midi#

class@openav/midi
new Midi({ signals = null, filterOut = 'IAC', requestAccess = null, echoWindow = 40, prefer = [] } = {})

The Web MIDI engine: asks the browser for access, listens to every input, publishes what arrives as signals, and sends to one output port.

Create it, then await midi.enable(). It resolves true once the browser has given access and false when there is no Web MIDI (Safari, iPad) or the permission was refused; the reason is written to the log (onMessage). Nothing is listened to or sent before that.

In: every message from every listened input goes to the callbacks you added with listen(fn) (raw bytes, including clock), then is parsed and published as genericSignals() names. With two or more inputs it also publishes midi/<slug>/note/on, midi/<slug>/note/off, midi/<slug>/cc/<n> and midi/<slug>/bend, so devices do not collide. The slug comes from the port name (Minilab3 MIDI becomes minilab3-midi), so a device that drops and reconnects keeps its identity. Clock messages are not logged and publish nothing.

Out: send(bytes), noteOn(), noteOff() and cc() go to midi.out, the chosen output port, and are remembered for echo filtering. If that port is unplugged the engine moves to the next best live port (your choice by name, then prefer, then the first), moves back when your choice returns, and never lets an unrelated device steal the output. Every switch writes one line to the log and one console.warn, and calls the onOutput subscribers.

Hooks you can assign: onCC(cc, value01, ch), onNote(note, velocity01, on, ch), onMessage({ dir, text }) (the log), onSend(bytes) (sees everything sent, for a meter) and onDeviceChange(devices). Fields: enabled, inputs, outputs, out, access, echoDropped.

Before you call it

Call await midi.enable() first. Browsers with Web MIDI (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) ask the visitor for permission at that moment, so call it from a click when you can. Safari and iPad have no Web MIDI: enable() gives false.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignals | nullPublish every input message here as midi/… signals (see genericSignals()). Without it the engine still calls listen() callbacks and the on… hooks. optional default null
filterOutString | RegExp | nullInput port NAMES never to listen to, as a regular expression (a string is read as its source, case-insensitive). The default 'IAC' is the macOS bus you send into Ableton or TouchDesigner, so what you send never comes back as input. null listens to everything. optional default 'IAC'
requestAccessFunction | nullWhere the MIDIAccess comes from, called as requestAccess({ sysex: false }) and returning a promise. The default is navigator.requestMIDIAccess. Pass your own for a test, a shim, or a host that wraps Web MIDI for old sketches and hands the REAL one here. optional default null
echoWindowNumberMilliseconds. An input message identical to one just SENT within this window is our own echo and is dropped (counted in echoDropped). 0 turns it off. optional default 40
preferArray<String | RegExp>Output priority after the port you chose by name: the first entry that matches a live port wins (a string matches as a substring), else the first port. Example: ['IAC']. optional default []

MidiController#

class@openav/midi
new MidiController(profile, { signals = null, sink = null, short = null, onLed = null } = {})

One MIDI controller (a profile) as a live model: MIDI bytes go in, control values and signals come out, and a hand on screen sends the bytes the device would.

The one idea: the on-screen controller and the hardware speak the SAME language, MIDI bytes. setValue(), press() and the other virtual hands encode the exact message the real control would send and feed it through ingest(), the same door the hardware uses. So a virtual knob and a real one can never drift apart, and what your work receives is identical whichever hand moved it. Pass the bytes of a real device to ingest(bytes, { source: 'hw' }).

The source of a message decides what is published, so every event is published exactly once. 'hw': the device lives here, and Midi already published the generic midi/… names, so only midi/<short>/… is added. 'ui': a virtual hand, so it publishes midi/<short>/…, the generic names, and midi/virtual (the raw bytes, for Web MIDI shims). 'mirror': someone else published it (a phone, feedback), so only the state and the views move.

Signals per control (values are normalised, raw keeps the MIDI number): midi/<short>/<id> (0..1, −1..1 for a bipolar wheel) and /raw; an encoder's /delta; a pad's /hit pulse { vel, velocity, note, ch } and /pressure; a keys control's /on and /off pulses and midi/<short>/n<note> while a key is held; and midi/<short>/last, a pulse saying what was touched last. profileSignals() lists them for a profile.

Each control keeps a state { value, raw, held, pressure, pos } in controller.state (read it with get(id)). controller.keys maps each held key's note to its velocity. controller.profile is the working copy (learning changes it), controller.base the normalized profile before any learning, controller.lastEvent the last message with its text, and controller.learning and controller.learned track learn mode.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
profileObjectA raw or normalized profile (see PROFILES). It is copied, so changing the object later does nothing.
signalsSignals | nullPublish the controller's signals here. optional default null
sinkFunction | null(name, value, { pulse, min, max }) => … called for each signal instead of signals (a relay, a phone). When both are given, sink wins. optional default null
shortString | nullOverrides the signal namespace, so two controllers of the same device publish under different names. optional default null
onLedFunction | null(bytes) => … called with the MIDI that lights or dims a control's LED on the hardware, whenever its state changes. optional default null

MidiControllers#

class@openav/midi
new MidiControllers({ profiles, signals = null, sink = null, midi = null, initial = null, storage = safeStorage() } = {})

Ties hardware ports to controller profiles: plug in a MiniLab 3 and the on-screen one appears and moves with your hands; unplug it and it stays playable.

There is one MidiController per profile, created the first time it is asked for (get(id)), so a virtual MiniLab and a real MiniLab are the SAME object: whichever hand moves it, the work receives the same midi/minilab3/… signals. current is the controller the panel shows.

With a midi attached it matches every input port to a profile by name (matchProfile(), one port per device through pickPort()), switches current to the first device it recognises, sends the LED colours to its output port, and routes each port's messages to that profile's controller. A port nobody recognises can be given to a profile by hand with assign(slug, profileId); that choice is remembered per port name.

It remembers in storage under openav.midi.map.<profile id> (learned mappings, restored when the controller is created) and openav.midi.assign (manual port assignments).

midiMidi | nullAn enabled (or about-to-be-enabled) Midi to follow. Leave it out for no hardware, and call attach(midi) later. optional default null
initialString | nullThe profile id shown before any hardware arrives. optional default null
storageStorage | nullWhere learned mappings and manual port assignments are remembered: anything with getItem and setItem. The default is localStorage when the page has it, otherwise nothing is remembered. optional default safeStorage()

normalizeProfile()#

normalizeProfile(raw)

Validates a profile and returns a filled-in copy with defaults for channel, labels, groups, encoder mode and portrait layout; the input is not changed.

It throws invalid MIDI profile "<id>": followed by every problem when the profile is not valid. Otherwise it fills in: channel (1), learn (true for a generic layout), stack (true), sources and match (empty lists), and per control label (its id), group (its type), ch (the profile's channel), an encoder's relative (offset64), a button's mode (momentary) and a pitch-bend wheel's bipolar and spring (both true). Sections get label, flow (row) and spans, and portrait is built from the sections, top to bottom, with each section's height as its weight when you did not write one.

MidiController, ControllerCanvas and the view all work on the normalized form, which is what controller.profile gives you.

parseMessage()#

function@openav/midi
parseMessage(data)

Turns the bytes of one MIDI message into an event object such as { type: 'noteon', ch: 1, note: 60, vel: 100 }, or null for bytes it does not know.

parseMessage([0x90, 60, 100]) is { type: 'noteon', ch: 1, note: 60, vel: 100 }. Channels are numbered 1 to 16, the way they are printed on a device (the status byte stores 0 to 15), and data bytes are cut to 0..127. Every other function in this package that handles MIDI speaks these event objects.

The type is noteon and noteoff (note, vel), polyat (polyphonic aftertouch: note, value), cc (cc, value), program (value), chanat (channel pressure: value) or pitchbend (value 0..16383, centre 8192). System messages come back as clock, start, continue, stop, sysex (with data, the whole message) or system (with the status byte).

A note-on with velocity 0 comes back as noteoff, because that is how many devices say "released". Bytes that start with a data byte give null: the browser has already resolved running status before it hands you the message.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
dataArray | Uint8ArrayThe bytes of ONE message, the way Web MIDI hands them over (event.data): a status byte first, then up to two data bytes.

Returns

Object | null The event, or null when the input is empty, starts with a data byte (below 0x80) or is a channel status it has no case for.

Notes

  • It is pure: no DOM, no Web MIDI, no state. encodeMessage() is its inverse, and describe() turns the result into a line of text.

Chooses which MIDI output to send to from a list: the port you named, else the first match of a preference list, else the first live port.

The order is: 1) the port named preferred, 2) the first port that matches each entry of prefer, in order, 3) the first port. Only live ports (see isLive()) are considered, so a disconnected port is never picked.

It is a pure function over plain objects, so you can test the rules without any hardware. The Midi engine applies them through reselectOutput().

PROFILES#

constant@openav/midi
PROFILES = array, 27 items

Every controller profile that ships with the package, as an array of plain JSON objects: real devices first, then the generic layouts.

A profile describes one controller as data: what it looks like (the faceplate sections), every control on it (type and the exact MIDI message it sends), LED feedback where the device accepts it, how to recognise its port name, and the document each number came from. Each one is a JSON file in packages/midi/profiles/; the full field list is in the package README and the controllers page shows them all.

A device profile cites its sources and is matched to ports by name, so plugging the device in picks it automatically. A generic layout (generic-8k8p, generic-keys49 …) never auto-matches: you assign a device to it and it learns the controls in the order you move them.

Pick one with profileById() (by id or by the short name), and hand it to createController(), MidiController or MidiControllers. Do not edit these objects in place: copy first (structuredClone), as withChannel() does.

Type
Object[]

The order is the order a device picker shows. Each item is a raw profile (see normalizeProfile() for the filled-in form): id, short, name, kind ('device' or 'generic'), face, sections, controls and, for a device, match and sources.

Notes

  • A control marked verified: false (with a note saying why) has a message that comes from the manual or a guess and has not been confirmed on a real unit. The faceplate shows a small orange ? on its label, and Learn rebinds it in one move.

relativeDelta()#

function@openav/midi
relativeDelta(value, mode = 'offset64')

Turns the CC value an endless encoder sends into signed steps: with offset64, 65 is +1, 63 is −1 and 64 is no move.

An endless encoder has no position, so it sends how far it moved, and devices disagree on how to write it. offset64: 64 is no move, 65 is +1, 63 is −1. offset16: 16 is no move, 17 is +1, 15 is −1. twos: 1..63 are +1..+63 and 127..65 are −1..−63 (two's complement). signbit: 1..63 are positive, 65..127 are −1..−63 (sign and magnitude).

An unknown mode throws unknown relative mode "x". MidiController uses this for every encoder control whose profile says relative, and publishes the result as midi/<short>/<id>/delta.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
valueNumberThe CC value, 0..127 (only the low 7 bits are read).
modeStringHow the device writes a turn: one of RELATIVE_MODES. A profile names it in the control's relative field. optional default 'offset64'

Returns

Number The signed step count, positive for clockwise.

Examples

relativeValue()#

function@openav/midi
relativeValue(delta, mode = 'offset64')

The inverse of relativeDelta(): the CC value that says "turned by this many steps" in a given encoder encoding.

A virtual encoder sends the same encoding a hardware one does, so the on-screen controller and the real device look identical to everything downstream. relativeValue(-1) is 63 and relativeValue(3, 'twos') is 3. With offset16 the result is held at 0, so it can only go down to −16.

ScoreMidi#

class@openav/midi
new ScoreMidi({ midi, channel = 15, segment = { note: 36 }, cue = { note: 84 }, length = 0.15, scrub = false, enabled = true, timer = (fn, ms) => setTimeout(fn, ms) } = {})

Turns a show's segment changes and cues into MIDI notes and CCs on one channel, so a DAW or lighting desk can follow the show.

The score knows when a segment starts and when a cue passes. An outside program cannot read the score, but it can read MIDI: launch a clip on a note, jump a scene on a CC. Create a ScoreMidi, then call out.segment({ index, cause }) and out.cue({ name, n }) (createShow({ score: { …, midi: { channel: 15 } } }) does this for you).

Markers go out only while the show plays (cause is play or release). A reset never sends, and seek and jump send only with scrub: true. Everything goes through the engine's own noteOn, noteOff and cc, so the MIDI OUT meter shows it and panic() can silence it. Off unless you create it.

NameTypeDescription

channelNumberThe MIDI channel, 1..16 (anything else throws). optional default 15
segmentfalse | Object{ note, cc, velocity }: segment number i sends note note + i and/or CC cc with value i. velocity defaults to 100, note to 36 (give note: null to send only the CC). false sends no segment markers. optional default { note: 36 }
cuefalse | Object{ note, notes, cc, velocity }: every cue sends note (or its own note from the map notes, by cue name) and/or CC cc with the cue's number as value. note defaults to 84 (give note: null to send only the CC). false sends no cue markers. optional default { note: 84 }
lengthNumberSeconds before a marker note's note-off. A marker note is a trigger, not a held note. optional default 0.15
scrubBooleanAlso mark jumps the playhead made by hand (seek, jump). Off by default, so dragging the scrubber does not launch clips in the DAW. optional default false
enabledBooleanSet to false (or later, out.enabled = false) to send nothing. optional default true
timerFunction(fn, ms) => … used to schedule the note-offs. It is setTimeout; pass your own in a test. optional default (fn, ms) => setTimeout(fn, ms)

Checks a controller profile and returns every problem as a sentence; an empty array means it is valid.

It reports all problems at once, not just the first. It checks: id and short are lower-case [a-z0-9_-] and short is not a reserved family name (cc, note, bend, ch, virtual, raw, clock), name and kind exist, a device cites at least one source, match regexes compile, face has a size, every control has a unique non-reserved id (see RESERVED_IDS), a known type and msg, numbers in range and no two controls listening to the same message, encoders name their relative mode, and the sections (and portrait, if given) show every control exactly once, inside the faceplate and within their grid.

Builds the control event payload for one control change: id, value, raw, signal, the parsed message, its bytes and where it came from.

Always there: profile (the profile id), id, type, label, value, raw, signal, message, bytes, source and time (performance.now(), rounded). value is 0..1 (−1..1 for a bipolar wheel); a pad is its velocity while held and 0 on release; a button is 0 or 1; for keys it is that note's velocity. raw is the MIDI number (0..127, pitch bend 0..16383). signal is the name the rest of open-audiovisual uses (midi/lpd8/k1; for a key midi/minilab3/n60). message is the parsed MIDI ({ type: 'cc', ch: 1, cc: 70, value: 53 }) and bytes the raw bytes. source is 'ui' (a finger, a mouse, set()), 'hardware' (a real port, or bytes you ingest()) or 'mirror'.

Sometimes there: note and velocity (note messages, velocity 0 for a release), delta (a relative encoder: the signed steps), held (a pad or button), and pressure (a pad, when it is above 0). The control, noteon and noteoff events carry it as their detail.

ControllerCanvas#

class@openav/midi
new ControllerCanvas({ profile = 'arturia-minilab3', signals = null, controller = null, mapping = null, theme = {}, notes = 'auto', screen = true, padding = 0.05, now = defaultNow } = {})

Draws a controller's faceplate into any 2D canvas context, every frame, at any size: the bottom of a performance video, an overlay, a thumbnail.

The on-screen controller is DOM: perfect to play, impossible to record, because a page cannot capture its own DOM into a video. This draws the same faceplate, every section where it sits on the device and in the same colours, straight into a 2D context. It is vector and drawn at the output size, so a 4K frame is as sharp as a 1080 one, and it costs a few hundred path calls a frame. @openav/record's Compositor#setPanel takes one.

Call panel.draw(ctx, { x, y, w, h }) every frame, or panel.renderTo(canvas) to fill a canvas of its own. What a video needs that a screen does not: a touch has to stay visible for a few frames (30 fps is 33 ms; a staccato note can be shorter), so released keys and pads fade out instead of switching off, the control a hand just moved glows, and the keyboard follows the device's octave buttons. panel.aspect is the faceplate's width ÷ height, for reserving an area of that shape. With neither signals nor controller the panel just stays at rest.

NameTypeDescription
profileString | ObjectProfile id, short name or object. An unknown id throws ControllerCanvas: unknown profile "x". optional default 'arturia-minilab3'
signalsSignals | nullFollow the generic MIDI names on this bus (midi/ch/<ch>/…, midi/note/on|off, midi/cc/<n>, midi/bend): live hardware, the on-screen controller, the QWERTY piano, phones and a recorded take playing back all move the panel. controllerGeometry()#

function@openav/midi
controllerGeometry(profile, rect, { padding = 0.05, notes = 'auto' } = {})

Computes where everything goes when a profile's faceplate is drawn into a pixel rectangle: the face, every section, every control cell, and the notes strip.

The faceplate keeps its own proportions, centred in the rect. The sections are laid out the way the on-screen controller's CSS grid does (row or column flow, spans), so the canvas drawing and the DOM agree. It is pure, so it is the part to test, and the part to use when you want to draw something of your own on top of a control.

Returns

{ u, face, notes, sections, controls, deco } u is the pixel size of one face unit. face is { x, y, w, h }. notes is the strip or null. sections is a list with id, label, the box and its grid. controls is a Map from control id to { id, type, section, x, y, w, h }. deco lists the decorations (screen, logo, lettering) in pixels.

ControllerHost#

class@openav/midi
new ControllerHost(profile = 'arturia-minilab3', { profiles = PROFILES, signals = null, sink = null, channel = null, follow = false, midi = null, requestAccess = null, filterOut = 'IAC', storage = undefined, telemetry = true, embedKind = 'headless' } = {})

The object createController() returns: one controller with its events, its playable faceplate, its hardware connection and its MIDI output.

Events, with ctl.on(name, fn) (returns an unsubscribe function): control (every knob, pad, key or button change), noteon and noteoff (the same payload, for pads, keys and note buttons), connect and disconnect ({ port, profile }: a hardware port started or stopped driving it), status, profilechange ({ profile, name }) and '*', which gets (name, detail) for all of them. The control payload is the one described under controlDetail(). ready and error exist only on the <oav-controller> element.

ctl.status is { hardware, input, output, outputState }. hardware is off, asking, waiting (listening, but the device is not plugged in), connected, unavailable (the browser has no Web MIDI) or denied (permission refused). outputState is off, asking, open, missing (no port matches), unavailable or denied. ctl.profileId, ctl.controller and ctl.profile say which device is on screen; ctl.controllers, ctl.view, ctl.midi and ctl.output are the objects underneath.

What a hand plays on the screen leaves through the output port as real MIDI; moves of your real hardware are not forwarded (your software already hears the device), and input with the same name as the chosen output (the loopMIDI echo) is muted.

Before you call it

connectHardware(), setOutput() and requestMidi() are the only calls that ask the browser for MIDI. Chrome, Edge and Firefox show a permission prompt, so call them from a click when you can. Without Web MIDI (Safari, iPad) the controller still plays and fires events, and status says unavailable.

sinkFunction | nullPublish through this function instead (a relay), as in MidiController. optional default null
channelNumber | nullMove every control to this MIDI channel (your unit is set to another one). See withChannel(). optional default null
followBooleanWhen a different known device is plugged in, show that one. optional default false
midiMidi | nullUse this engine (a show's) instead of the page-shared one. optional default null
requestAccessFunction | nullWhere the MIDIAccess comes from, as in Midi. Giving it makes the controller use its own engine. optional default null
filterOutString | RegExpThe input-port filter of Midi. Anything but the default 'IAC' also gives the controller its own engine. optional default 'IAC'
storageStorage | nullWhere learned mappings are kept, as in MidiControllers. Default: localStorage when available. optional default undefined
telemetryBooleanfalse sends no anonymous page-load hit. optional default true
embedKindStringWhich kind of embed this is for the hit: 'headless' (default), 'element' or 'iframe'. optional default 'headless'

ControllerView#

class@openav/midi
new ControllerView(container, controller, { mode = 'auto', minTouch = 38 } = {})

The playable on-screen faceplate of a controller: knobs, faders, pads and keys you drive with a mouse, a finger or the keyboard, repainted from the controller's state.

Two shapes, chosen from the box it lives in. face: the device as it looks, sections where they sit on the real faceplate, scaled to fit (desktop, iPad, a phone held sideways). stack: the same controls re-gridded top to bottom for a tall box (a phone held upright), as the profile's portrait says. Nothing scrolls and nothing shrinks below a thumb. Square grid devices (Launchpad) stay face. mode fixes one; 'auto' follows the box.

Every control repaints from the controller's state, so a finger here and a knob on the desk look the same, and a move from hardware gets a brief glow ring so you can see your hand arrive. Touch: drag a knob (right or up raises it), drag or click a fader or strip, strike a pad (higher on the pad is softer, lower is harder), hold a button, play the keys (multi-touch works). The mouse wheel turns knobs and faders.

Keyboard: Tab reaches every control except the piano keys; the arrow keys, Page Up/Down, Home and End move knobs, faders and strips (Shift for fine steps); Space or Enter strikes pads and buttons, held while the key is held. Learn mode (setLearning(true)) turns every tap into "bind this control", and view.onLearnTap = (id) => … tells you which.

Before you call it

A browser DOM and a container with a height. createController(…).mount(el) is the usual way to get one.

modeString'auto', 'face' or 'stack' (below). optional default 'auto'
minTouchNumberPixels a control needs before face gives way to stack. optional default 38

dispose()methodStops listening, disconnects the resize observer and removes the view from the page.

createController()#

function@openav/midi
createController(profile = 'arturia-minilab3', o = {})

Makes one MIDI controller you can play, listen to, and point at hardware or a DAW, with no element and no framework: createController('akai-lpd8').

Four lines are enough: const ctl = createController('akai-lpd8'), ctl.mount(el) for the playable faceplate (optional, it works headless too), ctl.on('control', fn) to hear every knob, pad and key whether it came from the screen or the hardware, and ctl.connectHardware() to follow the real device. ctl.set(id, value) moves a control the way a hand would.

Controllers on one page share one Midi engine, so the browser asks for MIDI permission once. Nothing asks until you call connectHardware(), setOutput() or requestMidi(). Pass signals to publish midi/<short>/… into a show.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
profileString | ObjectA profile id ('akai-lpd8'), a short name ('lpd8') or a profile object. For a URL, load it first with loadProfile(). An unknown id throws unknown MIDI profile "x" (known: …). optional default 'arturia-minilab3'
oObjectOptions, the same as the second argument of ControllerHost: profiles, signals, sink, channel, follow, midi, requestAccess, filterOut, storage, telemetry, embedKind. optional default {}

Returns

ControllerHost The controller. Its methods are listed under ControllerHost.

Notes

  • Like <oav-controller>, it sends one anonymous hit per page load (which kind of embed and which device; nothing anyone plays) to the project's analytics, and nothing from localhost or the LAN. Turn it off with createController(profile, { telemetry: false }). The README's Telemetry section has the details.

The brightness of a fading touch: 1 at the moment it happened, 0 after ms, eased so it still reads on a 30 fps frame.

followMidiSignals()#

function@openav/midi
followMidiSignals(signals, onEvent, { channel = 1, defer = (fn) => queueMicrotask(fn) } = {})

Listens to a Signals bus and hands you each MIDI message back exactly once, as an event, although hardware publishes it under two names.

Hardware and the on-screen controllers publish every message twice: the legacy name (midi/note/on) and then the per-channel one (midi/ch/1/note/60) in one call. The QWERTY piano and some takes publish only the legacy name. A per-channel name counts at once; a legacy name waits for a microtask and is dropped if its per-channel twin shows up first. So a relative encoder never turns twice, a legacy CC (which has no channel) never lands on the wrong channel, and order is kept.

ControllerCanvas uses it. Use it yourself to turn a bus back into MIDI events, for example to drive your own visual from a recorded take.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsThe bus. It needs onAny(cb).
onEventFunction(ev) => … called with an event of parseMessage() for each message.
channelNumberThe channel given to legacy CC and bend names, which carry none. optional default 1
deferFunction(fn) => … that schedules the flush of legacy-only names. Default queueMicrotask; replaceable in tests. optional default (fn) => queueMicrotask(fn)

Returns

{ flush(), dispose() } flush() delivers legacy-only messages that are still waiting. dispose() stops listening and drops them.

fromParent()#

function@openav/midi
fromParent(data)

Frame side: validates a command from the page and returns a clean command, or null (the message is ignored).

It is strict, because anything on the web can post to an iframe. The message needs target: 'openav' and a type from FRAME_COMMANDS. Control ids must be lower-case [a-z0-9_-]. value must be a finite number. note must be an integer 0..127 (else null). keyWindow()#

Tells which note a drawn keyboard should start at after a note outside its printed range arrives, so it follows the device's octave buttons.

A keyboard control catches notes outside its printed range, because the device's Oct+/Oct− buttons shift what the keys send. When one arrives, the drawing moves and stays there, as the device does. The bar shows which device is on screen (the picker switches it), a chip saying whether a hardware port drives it, a port picker when hardware is attached, a Learn button (click a control, then move the one on the hardware; a second button resets the mapping), and a tiny monitor that prints the last message, so you see the hardware talking before you see what it moves. OavController#

class@openav/midi
new OavController()

The oav-controller custom element: a playable MIDI controller you paste into any page with one line, with no import map and no build.

Load @openav/midi/element (https://openaudiovisual.com/packages/midi/element.js) once and write <oav-controller profile="akai-lpd8" readout></oav-controller>. Importing the file registers the tag by itself. It is a shadow-DOM element, so the page's CSS cannot bend it and it cannot bend the page. It plays with a mouse, a finger, a pen and the keyboard, with or without Web MIDI: on Safari and iPad it still plays and fires events, and only the hardware and MIDI-out parts say they are unavailable.

Attributes, each also a property of the same name (midi-out is el.midiOut): profile (an id, a short name or a URL to a profile JSON; default arturia-minilab3), layout (auto, face as it looks, stack re-gridded for a tall box), hardware (off by default; bare or on follows the real device, ask shows a button so the permission prompt waits for a click, or a port name or /regex/), midi-out (off by default; bare or ask lets the visitor pick, or a port name, substring or /regex/ such as IAC or loopMIDI), channel (1 to 16: move every control to that channel), picker, readout (the last message under the faceplate), learn (a Learn button), follow (show whatever known device is plugged in), theme (dark or light: the toolbar only, the device stays the device), telemetry (off sends no anonymous hit) and lang (the toolbar language: zh… is Chinese, anything else English; it reads the nearest lang on the page).

Events are CustomEvents that bubble and cross the shadow root, so el.addEventListener('control', e => e.detail) works anywhere above it: ready { profile, name, controls }, control (see controlDetail()), noteon, noteoff, connect, disconnect, status, profilechange and error { message }. EMBED_EVENTS lists them. Methods: set(), get(), values(), reset(), press(), release(), ingest(), send(), on(), connectHardware(), disconnectHardware(), setOutput() and toggleLearn().

It fills its width, and its height follows the faceplate (a taller stack on a phone) unless you set one. CSS variables: --oav-bg, --oav-fg, --oav-accent, --oav-line, --oav-font, and --oav-ratio (width ÷ height). Parts: ::part(toolbar), ::part(body), ::part(readout).

Before you call it

Wait for the controller to exist: await el.ready (a promise that resolves with the element), or listen for the ready event. Before that, set(), press(), release() and ingest() return null and print one console warning, and get() also returns null. It never asks for MIDI permission unless hardware, midi-out or Learn is used.

Members

NameDescription

  • Like createController(), it sends one anonymous hit per page load, never from localhost or the LAN. telemetry="off" stops it.

parseEmbedOptions()#

function@openav/midi
parseEmbedOptions(src)

Reads the options of one embed from an element, a query string, an object or a getter function, and returns them cleaned up with defaults.

It is the one place that decides what the attributes and the iframe's query string mean, so the element and the iframe always agree. Defaults: profile is arturia-minilab3, layout auto, theme dark, hardware and midiOut off (so embedding never asks for MIDI permission), the booleans false, telemetry true, and channel, bg, frame, origin, lang are null.

Rules worth knowing: an unknown layout becomes auto; theme is light or dark; midi-out may also be written midiout or midiOut, and alone it means ask; frame may also be written id and is cut to 64 characters; origin is kept only as https://host or http://host with no path (anything else, such as javascript:, becomes null), lang is cut to 16 characters, and bg goes through embedColor().

srcElement | URLSearchParams | Object | FunctionWhere the options live: an element (read with getAttribute), a URLSearchParams (the iframe page passes its own), a plain object { profile: 'lpd8' }, or a function (name) => value | null.

setControl()#

Moves one control the way a hand would, whatever its type, and returns the MIDI bytes it sent: setControl(mc, 'k1', 0.5).

What value means depends on the type. Knob, fader, wheel, strip and encoder: 0..1 (−1..1 for a bipolar one). Pad and momentary button: above 0 presses (with that velocity, held to 1) and 0 releases. Toggle button: 0.5 or more is on. Keys: value is the velocity, above 0 presses that note and 0 releases it. This is what set() on ControllerHost and <oav-controller> call.

Keyboard (@openav/keys)#

The on-screen piano and the QWERTY fallback. 4

@openav/keys

KeysPiano#

class@openav/keys
new KeysPiano(container, opts = {})

An on-screen piano you can play with the mouse, a finger or the computer keyboard, that calls a function for every note.

new KeysPiano(el, { onNote }) builds the keys inside el. Whatever plays a key (a click or a touch on it, sweeping across the keys with the button held, the computer keyboard, or your own call to press()) ends up in onNote(note, vel01, on): on is true for a key going down and false for one coming up, and vel01 is 0..1 (0 on the way up). The black and white pattern follows the real pitch, so a piano can start on any note. A key that is already down ignores a second press().

The computer keyboard is off until you set piano.captureEnabled = true, and it is up to you to pass the page's keydown and keyup events to handleKeyDown(e) and handleKeyUp(e) (see PIANO_KEYMAP for which letter is which note). mountKeys() does all of that for you.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
containerHTMLElementThe element the keys are built in. It gets the class oav-keys and is emptied first.
optsObjectOptions: base (lowest key, default 48), octaves (default 2), semitones (the number of keys, default octaves × 12 + 1), velocity (0..127 for the mouse and the computer keyboard, default 100), onNote(note, vel01, on), onOctave(base), fill (size the keys in percent of the container, so it can be any width), keyWidth (px per white key when not filling, default 27), minBase (24) and maxBase (84), the range the octave keys can move base in. optional default {}

Members

NameDescription
noteName(n)methodThe name of a MIDI note with sharps: noteName(60) is 'C4', noteName(61) is 'C#4'.
setBase(n)methodMoves the piano to start on note n, held between minBase and maxBase. Sounding keys are released first, so no note sticks. onOctave(base) is called with the new value when it changed.
press(note, vel01)methodPresses a key as if it was played: press(60, 0.8). The key lights up and onNote(60, 0.8, true) is called. Pressing a key that is already down does nothing.
release(note)methodLets a key go: release(60) calls onNote(60, 0, false). A key that is not down does nothing.
releaseAll()methodReleases every key that is down, from the mouse, touch or computer keyboard. Call it when focus is lost so nothing sticks.
handleKeyDown(e)methodGive it a keydown event. Z and X move the piano an octave down and up, a letter in PIANO_KEYMAP presses its note (Shift adds 20 to the velocity), and the other letters are swallowed. Returns true when the event was used. A key held down (e.repeat) does not retrigger.
handleKeyUp(e)methodGive it a keyup event: it releases the note that key pressed. Returns true when the event was used.

Notes

  • handleKeyDown(e) returns true when the piano used the event, and then you should call e.preventDefault(). While capturing, every letter a–z counts as used, even those that play no note, so a stray letter cannot trigger a hotkey; digits, space and the arrows pass through. Held keys with Ctrl, Cmd or Alt are never used.

Examples

mountKeys()#

function@openav/keys
mountKeys(container, { signals, chord = null, base = 48, octaves = 2, sim = true, capture = true } = {})

Puts a playable piano on the page in one call, with a keyboard switch and a self-playing performer, and publishes every note as midi/note/on and midi/note/off.

mountKeys() is the whole keyboard department in one line: a KeysPiano you can play with the mouse, a finger or the computer keyboard, and a SimPlayer that plays by itself. Above the piano are two checkboxes, both off to begin with: keyboard (the QWERTY keys play, Z and X move an octave, Shift plays harder) and simulate performance.

Everything is published as the standard midi/note/on and midi/note/off, the same names a real MIDI keyboard uses, so a world, a sound engine or a chord detector cannot tell a QWERTY performance from hardware. Call keys.update(dt) once per frame, or the simulated performer does not move.

Before you call it

A page with a DOM. The keyboard checkbox must be ticked before the computer keyboard plays, on purpose: while it is on, every letter key is taken by the piano, so hotkeys on letters stop working. A key listener goes on window until dispose().

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
containerHTMLElementThe element to put the piano in. It gets a small bar of checkboxes and the piano under it. dispose() empties it again.
signalsSignalsThe Signals bus to publish into. Every key down is midi/note/on { note, vel, ch: 0 } (vel 0..1) and every key up midi/note/off { note, ch: 0 }. Without a bus the piano still works and calls chord. optional
chordChordDetectorAnything with noteOn(note, vel01) and noteOff(note), usually a chord detector from @openav/chord, to be fed every note directly. optional default null
baseNumberThe MIDI note of the lowest key (48 is C3). The simulated performer plays an octave above it. optional default 48
octavesNumberHow many octaves the piano shows. It has octaves × 12 + 1 keys, so two octaves end on a C. optional default 2
simBooleanShow the "simulate performance" checkbox. The performer exists either way: keys.sim.toggle(true) starts it from code. optional default true
captureBooleanShow the "keyboard" checkbox that lets the computer keyboard play the piano. With false there is no checkbox and captureBox is null; you can still set keys.piano.captureEnabled = true. optional default true

Returns

Object { piano, sim, update(dt), dispose(), captureBox }: the KeysPiano, the SimPlayer, a function to call every frame with the seconds since the last one (it drives the performer), a function that takes everything down again, and the "keyboard" checkbox (or null).

Notes

  • In a p5 sketch you do not need this: the 🎹 panel of oav-p5 is a piano like this one, and notePressed() hears it. mountKeys() is for a page that has no oav-p5.
