PIANO_KEYMAP#

constant@openav/keys
PIANO_KEYMAP = object, 17 keys

Which computer-keyboard letter plays which note: a is the base note, w a semitone higher, s two.

The layout the music software calls the DAW standard: the A S D F G H J K L ; row is the white keys and the W E T Y U O P row above it is the black keys, placed where they sit on a piano. With a piano that starts on C (base 48, 60…) it reads C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G, G♯, A, A♯, B, C, C♯, D, D♯, E. The keys are lowercase letters; KeysPiano.handleKeyDown(e) lowercases the key first. Z and X are not in the map: they move the octave.

Type

{ a: 0, w: 1, s: 2, e: 3, d: 4, f: 5, t: 6, g: 7, y: 8, h: 9, u: 10, j: 11, k: 12, o: 13, l: 14, p: 15, ';': 16 }: key to semitones above the piano's base.

SimPlayer#

class@openav/keys
new SimPlayer({ press, release, base = 60, scale = [0, 2, 4, 7, 9], density = 1 } = {})

A hands-free performer: it presses and releases notes on its own, in a scale, so a demo can play itself.

It plays like someone noodling. Every gesture it picks at random: mostly a step up or down the scale, sometimes a leap, now and then a triad stacked in the scale, and real rests. Notes last 0.18 to 0.68 seconds (a triad twice as long), the next gesture comes 0.22 to 0.77 seconds later (a rest lasts 0.6 to 2 seconds), all at the default density of 1, and the notes are kept between 36 and 96. Because it presses and releases through your own two functions, whatever listens downstream cannot tell it from a person.

It starts off. Call toggle(true) and then update(dt) once per frame with the seconds since the last frame; it does nothing while it is off. toggle(false) releases every note it is holding, so none sticks. The notes are random (it uses Math.random, there is no seed).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
pressFunctionpress(note, vel01): called when a note starts, with its MIDI number and a velocity between 0.45 and 0.85. Usually the press of a KeysPiano, so the keys light up.
releaseFunctionrelease(note): called when the note ends.
baseNumberThe MIDI note the scale starts on. optional default 60
scaleNumber[]The notes it may play, as semitones above base. The default is a pentatonic scale, which sounds fine whatever happens. optional default [0, 2, 4, 7, 9]
densityNumberHow busy it is. The gaps between notes are divided by it, so 2 plays about twice as often. optional default 1

Members

NameDescription
toggle(on = !this.enabled)methodTurns the performer on or off; with no argument it flips. Returns the new state. Turning it off releases every note it holds.
update(dt)methodAdvance by dt seconds: release the notes that are due and, when it is time, start the next gesture. Call it every frame. Does nothing while the performer is off.

Turns pinch and grab strengths into clean start and end events, per hand plus a both-hands pinch, using hysteresis so a wobbling value fires once.

A pinch strength hovers around any single threshold while the fingers are "almost touching", and one threshold then fires start, end, start, end sixty times a second. So every gesture is a trigger with two thresholds: it starts above on and only ends below off. The defaults are a pinch starting above 0.86 and ending below 0.5, a both-hands pinch entering when both hands are above 0.8 and leaving when either drops below 0.5, and a grab (fist) above 0.8 and below 0.5. A hand that disappears ends all of its gestures.

LeapInput already runs one (leap.gestures) and turns its events into the leap/…/pinch-start pulses. Use HandGestures on its own when you have hands from somewhere else.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
thresholdsObjectOverrides for the defaults in THRESHOLDS: { pinch: { on, off }, bothPinch: { on, off }, grab: { on, off } }. Keys you leave out keep their defaults. optional default THRESHOLDS

Members

NameDescription
update(hands)methodupdate(hands) takes [{ side: 'left' | 'right', pinch, grab, … }] and returns the events that just happened, in a stable order: { type: 'pinch-start' | 'pinch-end' | 'grab-start' | 'grab-end', side, hand }, then { type: 'both-pinch-start' | 'both-pinch-end', side: 'both', hands }. Call it once per frame.
stategetterWhat is held right now: { left: { pinch, grab }, right: { pinch, grab }, both }, all booleans.

Examples

handsOf()#

Reads either wire format (raw line or LeapJS v6 frame) into the one hand shape the rest of the package uses; anything else gives [].

This is the hand shape worlds draw from (leap.hands). A raw frame carries the fingers inline; a v6 frame carries them as pointables joined to their hand by handId, and handsOf() does that join. Both give the same hand, so code written against leap.hands does not care which URL the bridge was reached on.

Returns

Hysteresis#

class@openav/leap
new Hysteresis(on, off)

One Schmitt trigger: update(v) says 'start' when the value rises above on, and 'end' only when it falls below off.

The gap between on and off is what stops a value that hovers near one threshold from flickering. Each call to update() returns 'start' (it just became active), 'end' (it just stopped) or null (nothing changed). A missing or NaN value while active counts as an end, so a lost sensor lets go. active tells you whether it is on now.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
onNumberThe level the value must rise above to start.
offNumberThe level the value must fall below to end. It must be lower than on, or the constructor throws "Hysteresis: off must be below on".

Members

NameDescription
update(v)methodupdate(v) returns 'start', 'end' or null.
release()methodForce the end, for example when the hand is lost. Returns 'end' only if it was active, otherwise null.

Examples

INTERACTION_BOX#

constant@openav/leap
INTERACTION_BOX = object, 2 keys

The classic Leap interaction box, { center: [0, 200, 0], size: [235.247, 235.247, 147.751] } in millimetres, that positions are normalised against.

A frozen object: the centre sits 200 mm above the sensor, and the box measures 235.247 mm along x, 235.247 mm along y and 147.751 mm along z (the sensor's own axes: x across, y up, z toward the player). normalizePoint() maps it to 0..1, and the console panel draws it as an outline so you can see when a hand leaves it. Pass your own box to new LeapInput({ box }) to change where 0 and 1 are.

Related

LeapInput#

class@openav/leap
new LeapInput({ signals = null, url = DEFAULT_URL, reconnect = true, fingers = true, box = INTERACTION_BOX, thresholds = THRESHOLDS, WebSocket: WS = null } = {})

Reads Leap Motion hands from the local bridge and publishes them as leap/* signals, plus the joints (leap.hands) for drawing the hand itself.

Browsers cannot talk to the Leap Motion sensor directly, so a small program on the same machine, the bridge (startBridge(), ws://127.0.0.1:6437), reads it and serves the hands over a WebSocket. LeapInput connects to that bridge and does one job: it turns hands into normalised signals and never touches params or worlds. In a show, createShow({ modules: { leap: true } }) builds one and returns it as show.leap; the console's L1 panel shows which link is missing.

It publishes, for each side (left, right): leap/hand/<side>/present (0 or 1), x, y, z (the palm in the interaction box, 0..1, y up, z toward the player), pinch and grab (0..1), roll, pitch, yaw (−π..π radians), speed (0..1, 1 = 1 m/s), and <finger>/x|y|z for the five fingertips. Shared: leap/status (0 no bridge, 1 bridge but no tracking service, 2 service but no device, 3 tracking), leap/hands (0..2) and leap/both/distance (palm to palm, 1 = 40 cm). The full list with its ranges is what leapSignals() returns.

Gestures are pulses with a payload { side, x, y, z, strength }: leap/hand/<side>/pinch-start|pinch-end and grab-start|grab-end, and leap/both/pinch-start|pinch-end (payload { x, y, z, distance } at the midpoint). They use hysteresis, so a pinch hovering near the threshold fires once and not sixty times a second (see HandGestures). A hand that leaves the view lets go: its present, pinch, grab and speed go to 0 and its gestures end.

For continuous control, map a signal to a param ({ source: 'leap/hand/right/y', target: 'energy' }) so the timeline, a knob and a hand are interchangeable. Use leap.hands (joints in millimetres) only to draw the hand itself.

Before you call it

For real hands: the bridge must be running (node packages/leap/bridge/leap-bridge.mjs, or --mock for animated made-up hands) and you must call connect(). Nothing is published until the first frame arrives. No sensor and no bridge: feed it hands with ingest(), or call simulate() to turn the mouse into hands.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsThe Signals registry to publish into. Without one the input still works (hands, onFrame) but publishes nothing. optional default null
urlStringThe bridge address: the LeapJS protocol (the default, DEFAULT_URL) or …/raw for the raw line format. Any service that still speaks the LeapJS v6 protocol works too. optional default ws://127.0.0.1:6437/v6.json
reconnectBooleanWhether to try again after the connection drops, waiting 0.5 s, then 1 s, 2 s … up to 5 s between tries. optional default true
fingersBooleanPublish the fingertip signals (3 per finger, 30 across two hands). false leaves them out and keeps the signal list short. optional default true
boxObjectThe interaction box { center, size } in millimetres that positions are normalised against. The default is INTERACTION_BOX. optional default INTERACTION_BOX
thresholdsObjectOverrides for the gesture hysteresis, such as { pinch: { on: 0.9, off: 0.6 } } (see THRESHOLDS). Keys you leave out keep their defaults. optional default THRESHOLDS
WebSocketFunctionThe WebSocket constructor to use. Pass your own to test without a network. optional default globalThis.WebSocket

Members

NameDescription

disconnect()methodClose the connection and stop retrying. The status becomes 'closed' and every hand is let go.
connectedgetterWhether the socket to the bridge is open right now.

The palm and fingertips are dots and a pinch gets a ring. Points outside the box still draw.

Notes

  • Fields to read: status ('idle', 'connecting', 'bridge', 'no-service', 'no-device', 'tracking', 'simulated', 'closed'), hands (an array; each hand has id, side, palm, fingers (5 × 5 joints), pinch, grab, velocity, normal, direction … in millimetres), frame (the latest message as it came), frames, fps, device, serviceVersion, gestures and box.
  • While the simulator runs it owns the hands: real frames from the bridge are ignored, and what the bridge says is remembered and restored when the simulator stops.
  • The signals are normalised (y = 1 is up). leap.hands and the LeapJS frames keep the sensor's own millimetre units, with +z toward the player.
  • How the bridge talks, the formats and the troubleshooting table are in the package README.

mockFrame()#

function@openav/leap
mockFrame(t, id = Math.round(t * 60), { hands = 2 } = {})

One frame of made-up, animated hands at time t: a right hand circling and pinching every 3 seconds, a left hand rising, falling and slowly making a fist.

This is the bridge's --mock stream and the way to try Leap code without a sensor. The right hand pinches for about a second out of every 3, the left hand pinches once every 12 seconds, and at those moments (for example second 8) both are pinched, so the both-hands pinch fires too. The left fist comes and goes slowly. The output goes through exactly the same conversion and publishing as a real Leap Motion Controller.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
tNumberTime in seconds. The result depends only on t, so it is the same every time.
idNumberThe frame number written into the frame. optional default Math.round(t * 60)
handsNumberHow many hands: 2 (right and left), 1 (the right only) or 0. optional default 2

Returns

Object A frame in the raw line format: { t: 'f', id, fps: 60, hands: [hand, …] }, the right hand (side: 'R') first. Feed it to LeapInput.ingest() or handsOf().

mountLeapPanel()#

function@openav/leap
mountLeapPanel(el, leap, { width = 300, simulate = true, simTarget } = {})

Mounts a small panel that shows whether the Leap is alive (bridge, service, device, hands) and draws what it sees, with a button to simulate hands.

One status line says which link is the broken one, in order: no bridge, bridge but no tracking service, service but no device, tracking (with the number of hands and the frame rate). Under it, a small front view draws the interaction box (a hand outside it is visibly outside, its signals sitting clamped at the edge) and the hand skeletons. It redraws only on frames and status changes, so nothing runs while the sensor is idle.

In a show you do not call it: the console's L1 · Input panel mounts it when you declare modules: { leap: true }.

normalizePoint()#

function@openav/leap
normalizePoint(p, box = INTERACTION_BOX, clamp = true)

Maps a point in millimetres to 0..1 inside the interaction box, clamped by default: the same normalisation the leap/* signals use.

The classic box is centred 200 mm above the sensor and about 235 × 235 × 148 mm (INTERACTION_BOX). A palm at the centre reads [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]; a palm far outside it reads 0 or 1 on that axis, which is why the signals "sit clamped at the edge" when a hand leaves the box. Pass clamp = false when you want to know how far outside it is.

Returns

Array<Number> [x, y, z], each (p − center) / size + 0.5: 0.5 is the centre of the box, x grows to the right, y upward, z toward the player.

PROTOCOL_VERSION#

The highest LeapJS protocol version we speak: 6. LeapJS 1.1.1 and earlier throw "unrecognized version" above that.

v6Header() never reports more than this, and the bridge answers /v7.json as version 6. It is the default of the version argument there.

startBridge()#

function@openav/leap
startBridge({ port = DEFAULT_PORT, host = '127.0.0.1', mock = false, hz = 60, bin = null, log = () => {} } = {})

Starts the Leap bridge on this machine: a loopback WebSocket and HTTP server that serves the sensor's hands to every page (Node only).

This is what node packages/leap/bridge/leap-bridge.mjs runs (add --mock for made-up hands, --port, --hz, --bin, --quiet). It serves ws://127.0.0.1:6437/v6.json (the LeapJS protocol, which every 2014 to 2021 browser sketch speaks), ws://…/raw (the raw lines), the same lines as server-sent events on GET /raw and /hands, and GET /health (source, service, device, fps, hands, clients). Any page origin may read it, as the original Leap service allowed.

Call it from your own Node program when you want the bridge inside it, for example in a test. startBridge() throws at once for port 7457 (it belongs to The Last Input and the monitor) and for a non-loopback host; a port already in use rejects the returned promise with a message that suggests curl http://127.0.0.1:6437/health.

Before you call it

Node 22 or later, and for real hands the Ultraleap Hand Tracking service plus Xcode's clang to build the reader on first start. With mock: true neither is needed.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
portNumberThe port to listen on, DEFAULT_PORT unless you say otherwise. 0 picks any free one. The ports in RESERVED_PORTS (7457) are refused. optional default DEFAULT_PORT
hostStringThe address to bind. Only loopback (127.0.0.1, ::1, localhost) is allowed: hand data never leaves the machine. optional default '127.0.0.1'
mockBooleantrue serves two animated made-up hands (mockFrame()) instead of reading a sensor. optional default false
hzNumberThe most frames per second sent to each client (held to 1..120). A slow client skips frames; it never queues them. optional default 60
binString | nullThe path to the leap-stream reader program. By default the bridge compiles its C reader on first start (needs the Xcode command line tools) and caches it. optional default null
logFunctionCalled with a line of text for each event worth knowing (clients coming and going, status changes). optional default () => {}

Returns

Promise<Object> Resolves once listening, with { port, state, health(), close() }: the real port (useful with port: 0), the live state, a function returning the /health object, and a function that stops everything and returns a Promise.

Examples

STATUS#

constant@openav/leap
STATUS = object, 4 keys

The four levels of the leap/status signal by name: off 0, bridge 1, service 2, tracking 3.

A frozen object { off: 0, bridge: 1, service: 2, tracking: 3 }: 0 no bridge, 1 the bridge is there but the tracking service is not, 2 the service is there but no device, 3 tracking. Use it to read the signal without magic numbers: signals.get('leap/status') === STATUS.tracking. Note it is the number published as leap/status; leap.status is a different thing, a string ('tracking', 'no-device' …), and the simulator counts as 3.

Notes

  • The code in LeapInput writes the numbers itself and does not read this object, so STATUS is a convenience for your own code. The strings map as: tracking and simulated to 3, no-device to 2, bridge and no-service to 1, the rest to 0.

V6Converter#

class@openav/leap
new V6Converter({ box = INTERACTION_BOX, smoothing = 0.5 } = {})

Converts raw hand lines into LeapJS v6 frames, keeping the little state the protocol needs: time visible, smoothed positions and fingertip velocities.

Every browser sketch written for the old Leap service (LeapJS, 2014 to 2021) speaks the v6 protocol, so the bridge serves it on /v6.json. This class does the conversion: one converter per stream. It is stateful where the protocol is: a hand's timeVisible grows while it stays in view and starts over when it leaves, stabilized… positions are a light low-pass, and tipVelocity is a finite difference between two frames.

LeapC gives joints, not bone rotations, so the bone bases are rebuilt from the joints and the palm normal (boneBasis()). Gestures are not synthesised: gestures is always [].

NameTypeDescription
boxObjectThe interaction box written into every frame's interactionBox. optional default INTERACTION_BOX
smoothingNumber0..1: how strongly stabilizedPalmPosition and stabilizedTipPosition lag behind (0 follows exactly, close to 1 barely moves). optional default 0.5

Members

NameDescription
convert(raw, tUs = nowUs())methodconvert(raw, tUs = now): a raw frame { t: 'f', id, fps, hands } and its time in microseconds, to a v6 frame { id, timestamp, currentFrameRate, hands, pointables, interactionBox, gestures: [], r, s, t }. Pointable ids are handId × 10 + finger.

Body and hand pose (@openav/pose)#

Camera in, landmarks and pinches out. 2

@openav/pose

HandTracker#

class@openav/pose
new HandTracker({ signals = null, mirror = true } = {})

Tracks up to two hands from the camera with 21 landmarks each and publishes palm position and thumb-to-finger pinch distances as hand/* signals.

The fine-control tracker: each hand gives two precise continuous controllers, thumb to index and thumb to middle finger, so two hands are four controllers you can pinch. The distances are normalised by the size of your palm (wrist to the base of the middle finger), so moving toward or away from the camera does not change a pinch: stage-robust. It runs on the device with MediaPipe Tasks Vision and downloads nothing until enable(). In a show, createShow({ modules: { hands: true } }) builds one (show.hands) and the L1 panel gets a 🖐 hands button.

For each of left and right it publishes hand/<side>/present (0 or 1), hand/<side>/x and /y (the palm, 0..1; y flipped so 1 is raised), hand/<side>/pinch/index and hand/<side>/pinch/middle (0..1, 0 = touching, 1 = wide open) and hand/<side>/spread (index fingertip to little fingertip, 0..1). A side with no hand in view gets present 0 and keeps its other values. Note that these names do not start with pose/, and are different from the body tracker's.

A pinch is a distance, so for "pinch closes" use a route with invert: { source: 'hand/right/pinch/index', target: 'tightness', invert: true, smooth: 0.1 }. If you want pinch start and end as events, LeapInput's gestures do that; HandTracker only gives the continuous distances.

Before you call it

Call await hands.enable(): it loads the MediaPipe library from jsDelivr and the hand model from Google's model storage (so it needs the network), asks for the camera (https or localhost, and the user must allow it) and starts the loop. Until then the signals sit at their starting values.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignals | nullThe Signals registry to publish into. Without one the tracker still runs and keeps hands, but publishes nothing. optional default null
mirrorBooleanTreat the camera as a mirror: x is flipped, and the left and right labels MediaPipe gives are swapped so the signals match the body. optional default true

Members

NameDescription
enable({ videoEl = null } = {})methodenable({ videoEl = null } = {}): ask for the camera (640 × 360), load the model (up to two hands) and start detecting. videoEl is a <video> to use; without one an off-screen video is created. Resolves true; rejects if the camera is refused or the library or model cannot load.
stop()methodStop detecting and release the camera. Signals keep their last values.
skeleton(ctx, w, h, { colorLeft = 'rgba(55,201,120,0.9)', colorRight = 'rgba(255,209,102,0.9)', lineWidth = 2 } = {})methodDraw the hands onto a 2D canvas context: skeleton(ctx, w, h, { colorLeft, colorRight, lineWidth = 2 }), the 21 landmarks joined into finger bones, with bigger dots at the thumb, index and middle fingertips (the pinch control points). Left is green and right is yellow by default.

Notes

  • Fields to read: hands ([{ handed: 'left' | 'right', lm }], lm the 21 landmarks { x, y, z } in the camera image, y downward and not mirrored), running, mirror, video.
  • Landmark indexes used: wrist 0, thumb tip 4, index tip 8, middle tip 12, little finger tip 20, base of the middle finger 9 (the palm position and the size reference).

PoseTracker#

class@openav/pose
new PoseTracker({ signals = null, mirror = true } = {})

Tracks one body from the camera and publishes wrist positions, wrist speed, hand spread, height and lean as pose/* signals.

This is the body tracker: one person, 33 landmarks (the BlazePose set), run by MediaPipe Tasks Vision on the device. No video leaves the machine, and nothing is downloaded until you call enable(). For fine finger control use HandTracker instead. In a show, createShow({ modules: { pose: true } }) builds one and the console's L1 panel gets a 🕺 body button that calls enable(); it is show.pose.

Signals, all normalised, with y flipped so that 1 means raised and 0 means the bottom of the frame (performance meaning beats pixel meaning): pose/present (0 or 1: someone is visible), pose/hand/left/x and /y, pose/hand/right/x and /y (wrist positions, 0..1), pose/hand/left/v and pose/hand/right/v (wrist speed, 0..1, clamped), pose/hands/spread (distance between the wrists, 0..1), pose/height (nose height, 0..1: crouching to standing) and pose/lean (shoulder-line tilt, −1..1). When nobody is in view only pose/present goes to 0; the others keep their last values.

Map these to params ({ source: 'pose/hand/right/y', target: 'energy', smooth: 0.1 }) so a raised hand does what a knob would. The detection runs on every animation frame while running.

Before you call it

Call await pose.enable(): it loads the MediaPipe library from jsDelivr and the model from Google's model storage (so it needs the network), asks the browser for the camera (the page needs https or localhost, and the user must allow it), and starts the loop. Until then every signal sits at its starting value.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignals | nullThe Signals registry to publish into. Without one the tracker still runs and keeps landmarks, but publishes nothing. optional default null
mirrorBooleanTreat the camera as a mirror: x is flipped, so moving toward the viewer's right makes x grow. Natural for performers. false keeps the camera's own left and right. optional default true

Members

NameDescription
enable({ videoEl = null } = {})methodenable({ videoEl = null } = {}) asks for the camera (640 × 360), loads the model and starts detecting. videoEl is a <video> element to use; without one an off-screen video is created. Resolves true; rejects if the camera is refused or the library or model cannot be loaded.
stop()methodStop detecting and release the camera. Signals keep their last values. enable() can start it again.
skeleton(ctx, w, h, { color = 'rgba(122,166,255,0.9)', lineWidth = 2 } = {})methodDraw the body onto a 2D canvas context: skeleton(ctx, w, h, { color, lineWidth = 2 }), the bones of the torso, arms and legs plus dots at the nose, shoulders, wrists and hips. It follows the same mirroring as the signals but not the y flip (it draws in screen space). Does nothing without landmarks. Call it every frame after drawing the background.

Notes

  • Fields to read: landmarks (the latest 33 raw points { x, y, z, visibility }, x and y 0..1 in the camera image, y downward and not mirrored; null when nobody is seen), running, mirror, video.
  • Landmark indexes (BlazePose): nose 0, shoulders 11 and 12, wrists 15 and 16, hips 23 and 24.
  • The model is MediaPipe's "lite" pose landmarker on the GPU, one pose at a time. If two people are in view, only one is tracked.

Chords (@openav/chord)#

Held notes in, chord quality and consonance out. 1

@openav/chord

ChordDetector#

class@openav/chord
new ChordDetector({ window = 80, onChord = null, signals = null } = {})

Groups notes struck close together into one gesture and analyses it: chord type, consonance, triad and cluster flags, published as chord/* signals.

This is not a music-theory library. It is a performance semantics layer: raw notes in, one analysed event per gesture out, with features that are made to drive a work. A single note is a seed, a chord a colony, a consonant chord a flourish, a dissonant one decay; rename them for your own piece. In a show, createShow({ modules: { chord: true } }) builds one ({ chord: { window: 120 } } tunes it) and connects it to midi/note/on and midi/note/off, so a MIDI keyboard, the on-screen piano and phones all feed it.

Each closed gesture publishes chord/consonance (−1..1), chord/count (0..10), chord/root (the lowest note) and the pulse chord/event, whose payload is the whole analysis: { notes, count, root, vel, pcs, consonance, isConsonant, isDissonant, isTriad, thirdsFraction, dissonanceLevel, chordType }. chordType is one of single, major, minor, sus2, sus4, dim, aug, maj7, min7, dom7, halfdim7, maj9, min9, dom9, six, min6, cluster (a very dissonant pile) or chord (anything else). Inversions resolve to the root-position name.

consonance is the average of an interval weight for every pair of notes (an octave or fifth is high, a semitone or tritone is negative). isConsonant is consonance > 0.25 and isDissonant is consonance < −0.15, both only for two notes or more. dissonanceLevel is 0 for none, 1 for mild (a storm warning: foreshadow it) and 2 for severe (three or more notes that are a true cluster: commit to the decay). isTriad is true for major, minor, sus2, sus4, dim and aug, and thirdsFraction is the share of neighbouring notes exactly 3 or 4 semitones apart, so "genuinely stacked thirds" can be told from "some consonant notes".

Before you call it

Feed it with noteOn(note, vel) (and noteOff(note)), or let createShow do it from midi/note/on|off. Nothing is published until window milliseconds after the last noteOn, so the result is asynchronous. analyze() is the exception: it is instant and needs no setup.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
windowNumberHow many milliseconds after the last noteOn the gesture is closed and analysed. Notes struck within this time of each other are one chord. optional default 80
onChordFunction | nullCalled with the analysis object each time a gesture is closed. optional default null
signalsSignals | nullA Signals registry to publish chord/* into. The signals are declared when the detector is built. optional default null

Members

NameDescription
noteOn(note, vel = 0.8)methodA note was struck: noteOn(note, vel = 0.8), note a MIDI number and vel 0..1. Restarts the window timer; striking the same note twice in a gesture counts once, with the harder velocity.
noteOff(note)methodA note was released. It only updates the held map; a gesture is made of the notes struck inside the window, not of what is still held.
analyze(notes, vels = [])methodA pure function: analyze(notes, vels = []) takes MIDI note numbers (lowest first) and returns the analysis object at once, without timers or signals. vel is the mean of vels, or 0.8 without them.

Notes

  • Pass notes to analyze() lowest first: root is the first note, and the detector sorts for you but a direct call does not.
  • A major second like [60, 62] is typed cluster (no template fits and its consonance is below −0.3) even though its dissonanceLevel is only 1. Level 2 needs three or more notes.
  • The gesture window does not know about held notes: a note already down when you play two more does not join them.

Examples

OSC and outputs#

Send signals to TouchDesigner, Max or a hardware bridge. 9

@openav/osc

OscOut#

class@openav/osc
new OscOut(url = 'http://127.0.0.1:7456')

Sends OSC messages from the browser to TouchDesigner, Max, Reaper or a spatialiser, batched once per frame, through a small local bridge.

A browser cannot send UDP, so OscOut posts batches of messages to a ~100-line Node program, packages/osc/bridges/osc-bridge.js, which sends them on as OSC packets. Start it with node packages/osc/bridges/osc-bridge.js 7456 192.168.1.50 3456 (HTTP port, target host, UDP port; the defaults are 7456 127.0.0.1 3456). Then send(address, args) as often as you like and flush() once per frame: only the latest message per address survives a frame, because a position stream does not need its in-between values.

Numbers go out as OSC floats (what Spat, Reaper and TouchDesigner expect), and anything else as a string. createShow() does not create an OscOut: make one, call enable(), flush it from onFrame, and if you like hand it to the worlds as show.stage.io.osc and to the Layers panel as show.app.osc (which then shows the OSC rate).

Before you call it

The bridge must be running, and you must await osc.enable() first: it probes GET /health and answers false if nobody is there. Until it succeeds flush() just throws the queue away. On a public https page, Chrome asks permission before the page may reach 127.0.0.1.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
urlStringThe address of the OSC bridge (its HTTP port, not the UDP target). optional default 'http://127.0.0.1:7456'

Members

NameDescription
enable()methodProbe the bridge (GET /health) and, if it answers, switch on. Resolves true, or false when nothing is listening. Any HTTP answer counts as present. Calls onStatus(ok, info); info is the UDP target the bridge reports.
disable()methodSwitch off and throw away anything queued. Calls onStatus(false, 'disabled').
send(addr, args)methodQueue one message: send(address, args). args is an array, or a single value that is wrapped in one. Nothing leaves until flush(). Calls the onMsg(address, args) hook if you set one.
rate()methodMessages sent since the last call, which resets the count (so call it once a second for a rate). What the Layers panel shows.
flush()methodSend the queue as one POST, the latest message per address. Call once per frame. Async; it does nothing while a previous flush is still in flight, and throws the queue away when enabled is false.

Notes

  • Fields and hooks: enabled, udp (the target the bridge reported), onStatus = (ok, info) => {} and onMsg = (address, args) => {} (high frequency: use sparingly).
  • If the bridge disappears, the first failed flush calls onStatus(false, 'bridge lost'), and after more than 30 failed flushes in a row enabled turns false by itself, with no further message. Call enable() again to resume. The messages of a failed flush are lost.
  • Every number goes out as a 32-bit float, whole numbers included (the bridge's own header comment mentions integers, but its code only writes floats). If the receiver needs integers, convert there.

Examples

OutClient#

class@openav/out
new OutClient({ url = OUT_DEFAULT_URL, id = null, WebSocket: WS, schedule, maxBackoffMs = 5000, minBackoffMs = 250 } = {})

The page side of the out-bridge: set(channel, value) sends a number to a named hardware channel, at most once per frame, and keeps the connection alive.

Hardware needs a number, and a page has a number: out.set('light/0/r', 0.8). The channel name is yours (a-z A-Z 0-9 _ - . /, up to 128 characters) and the bridge (startBridge()) decides from its config where that channel goes: a WLED strip, a serial motor board, an OSC address. Values are plain numbers; the convention is 0..1. Several set() calls on one channel inside one frame leave as one value, the last. In a lab work lab.out is this class.

It keeps the connection alive on its own: it reconnects with a growing delay (250 ms doubling up to 5 s), resends everything it knows after a reconnect (a restarted bridge has forgotten it all), and while the socket is open it re-sends the held values every timeoutMs / 3 of the bridge's watchdog, so a slider that stands still is not mistaken for a frozen page. If the page really freezes, that heartbeat stops and the bridge puts the hardware on its safe values.

Before you call it

Call connect() (the bridge must be running: node packages/out/bridge/out-bridge.mjs --config out.json), or simulate() for no hardware at all. set() before the socket is open is not lost: it waits in last and goes out on open.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
urlStringThe bridge's WebSocket address. The default is OUT_DEFAULT_URL, ws://127.0.0.1:6450/out. optional default OUT_DEFAULT_URL
idString | nullA name for this page (the work's id), sent to the bridge in its "hello" and shown in its log. optional default null
WebSocketFunctionThe WebSocket constructor to use. Defaults to the global one (also in Node 22). Pass your own to test without a network. optional
scheduleFunctionA function that runs a callback once, on the next frame. The default is requestAnimationFrame (or a 16 ms timer when the tab is hidden or there is no requestAnimationFrame). optional
maxBackoffMsNumberThe longest wait between reconnection attempts, in milliseconds. optional default 5000
minBackoffMsNumberThe first wait between reconnection attempts. It doubles each time up to maxBackoffMs. optional default 250

Members

NameDescription
onStatus(fn)methodCall fn(status) when the status changes. Returns a function that unsubscribes.
connect()methodOpen the socket and keep it open (reconnects with a capped, doubling delay). Returns the client, so new OutClient(…).connect() chains. Does nothing in simulate mode, or when there is no WebSocket constructor.
simulate()methodNo socket: values are only recorded in last (for sketches without hardware; the lab does this for ?out=sim). The status becomes 'sim'.
close()methodClose the socket and stop reconnecting. The status becomes 'closed'. The bridge sees the last client leave and puts every channel with a safe value back on it.
set(ch, v)methodset(channel, value): send one number. The value goes through Number(); a channel that is not a string or a value that is not finite is ignored. Recorded in last at once, sent on the next frame.
batch(obj)methodbatch({ channel: value, … }): the same as one set() per entry.

Notes

  • On the wire a single value is { "type": "set", "ch", "v" } and several are { "type": "batch", "items": [{ "ch", "v" }, …] }, after a { "type": "hello", "id" }.
  • On a public https page, Chrome asks permission before the page may reach 127.0.0.1; if it is refused, the status stays 'connecting'.

startBridge()#

function@openav/out
startBridge({ port = DEFAULT_PORT, host = '127.0.0.1', config = null, watchdog = true, log = () => {}, print = (s) => console.log(s) } = {})

Starts the out-bridge: a loopback WebSocket server that routes channel values from the page to hardware sinks, with a watchdog that falls back to safe values (Node only).

This is what node packages/out/bridge/out-bridge.mjs --config out.json runs (also --port, --no-watchdog, --quiet; the environment variable OUT_BRIDGE_PORT). It serves ws://127.0.0.1:6450/out, which understands { type: 'hello', id }, { type: 'set', ch, v }, { type: 'batch', items } and { type: 'status' }, and answers with { type: 'status', … }; GET /health reports the sinks, the channel count, the clients and the time since the last value. Channel names are a-z A-Z 0-9 _ - . / up to 128 characters, values must be finite numbers, and there is room for 4096 channels.

The config routes channels: channels is a list of { match, sink, … } and the first rule whose match glob fits the channel name takes it (* means anything, slashes included); a channel no rule fits is counted and dropped. The sinks are log (stdout), udp-json (UDP, {"ch","v"}), osc (UDP, address "/" + channel, one float32), ddp (WLED over UDP 4048: light/<i>/r|g|b, 0..1, pixel index from 0, up to 10000 pixels) and serial (a device path, ch value lines or JSON, latest value only). safe maps a channel glob to its safe value, timeoutMs (default 500, at least 20) is the watchdog time, and allowOrigins lists the page origins that may connect (without it any page on this machine can).

The watchdog: a channel that has a safe value and gets no new value for timeoutMs is sent its safe value once (a new value re-arms it). When the last client disconnects, every channel the bridge has seen that has a safe value gets it at once, and so does a clean shutdown. It does not cover channels the bridge has never heard of, nor a bridge killed with SIGKILL.

It throws at once for port 7457 (it belongs to The Last Input and the monitor), for a host that is not loopback, and for a bad config (no channels, an unknown sink, a safe value that is not a number, a timeoutMs under 20). A port already in use rejects the returned promise.

Before you call it

Node 22 or later. The sinks need what they talk to: a WLED device for ddp, the device file for serial, a listener for osc.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
portNumberThe port to listen on, DEFAULT_PORT unless you say otherwise. 0 picks any free one. The ports in RESERVED_PORTS (7457) are refused. optional default DEFAULT_PORT
hostStringThe address to bind. Only loopback is allowed. optional default '127.0.0.1'
configObject | nullThe routing: { channels: [{ match, sink, … }], safe: { glob: value }, timeoutMs, allowOrigins } (see the description). null sends every channel to the log sink. loadConfig(file) reads it from a JSON file. optional default null
watchdogBooleanfalse switches the watchdog off: no safe values are ever sent (the tests use it to prove the watchdog is what does the work). optional default true
logFunctionCalled with a line of text for diagnostics: clients coming and going, safe values sent. optional default () => {}
printFunctionWhat the log sink prints each value with ("channel value"). The default is stdout. optional default (s) => console.log(s)

Returns

Promise<Object> Resolves once listening, with { port, state, health(), close() }: the real port, the counters (received, rejected, unrouted, safeSent …), a function returning the /health object, and a function that puts every known channel on its safe value, stops the server and returns a Promise.

Notes

  • The error messages the bridge throws and sends back to a page are written in Chinese in the code, so a page may show them in Chinese whatever its language.

LearnWizard#

class@openav/mapping
new LearnWizard({ mapper, keys, onChange = null })

Binds a list of params one after another: it arms learn for the first, you turn a knob, it binds it and arms the next. Skip, back and stop steer it.

Binding twelve params one by one with the learn chip means twelve clicks and twelve guesses about what to touch next. The wizard walks the list for you: start() arms learn for keys[0], wizard.current says which param it is waiting for ('Turn a knob for: hue (1/12)'), you move a control, it is bound and the next one is armed. At the end learn is disarmed. The console's 🎛 map knobs in order button is this class.

It is pure logic on top of the mapper, with no screen of its own. Learn only ever adds routes, so running the wizard twice puts a second control on a param instead of losing the first. While it runs, it owns learn mode: call sync() every frame so that a click on some other learn chip cannot leave it waiting for nothing.

keysArray<String> | FunctionThe param keys to bind, in order, or a function that returns them (it is called when start() runs).
onChangeFunction | nullCalled with the wizard whenever what a banner would show changes: the current param, the position, finished or not. optional default null

Members

NameDescription
totalgetterHow many params are in this run.
currentgetterThe param key being waited for, or null when the wizard is not running.
start()methodRead the keys, arm the first one and begin. Returns false (and does nothing) when the list is empty.
skip()methodLeave the current param unbound and wait for the next one. Skipping the last one finishes the run.
back()methodGo back to the previous param. It keeps what it already has; a turned knob adds one more.
stop()methodEnd the run now and disarm learn. done stays false.
sync()methodCall every frame: if learn mode was switched off or pointed elsewhere while the wizard runs, it re-arms the current param.

Notes

  • Fields to read: active, done (the run reached the end), index, total, order, and added ([{ key, source }], what was bound in this run).
  • While it runs the wizard wraps the mapper's onLearn and puts yours back when it ends, so your own onLearn keeps being called.

Fetches a map file from an address (what ?map= calls) and puts it on the mapper; it never throws and never blocks the show.

Fetches the address with credentials: 'omit', and importMap()s the text. Any failure (refused address, no fetch, the server answered 404, offline, a site that blocks cross-origin reads, a timeout, a file that is not a map) lands in the report and in mapper.report, where the console shows it, and the routes stay as they were. It is async, so createShow() does not wait for it and the show starts regardless.

A map on another site must be served with CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *); raw GitHub files and gists are. In a show you rarely call it: open the page with ?map=<url>, or pass map: 'maps/a.json' to createShow().

Mapper#

class@openav/mapping
new Mapper({ signals, params, profile = 'default', onChange = null, onLearn = null })

Connects signals to params: it holds a list of routes (a window, a curve, smoothing) and writes the matching param whenever a signal arrives.

The mapper is the only component that connects signals to params, and everything it knows is a list of routes, plain objects. mapper.addRoute({ source: 'midi/cc/74', target: 'bloom' }) makes the param bloom follow the signal midi/cc/74. One signal may drive several params, one param may listen to several signals (the last writer wins), and learn adds routes, it never replaces them. In a show, createShow() builds one, loads the saved routes (or adds the ones you declared in routes) and returns it as show.mapper.

A route needs only source and target; addRoute() fills in the rest and returns the stored route:

text
source, target      the signal name and the param key (required)
inMin, inMax        0, 1   the part of the signal that counts; outside it is clamped
outMin, outMax      the param's min and max AT THE MOMENT THE ROUTE IS ADDED (0 and 1 if the param does not exist yet)
curve               'linear' | 'exp' (x squared) | 'log' (square root) | 'smooth' (smoothstep); an unknown name is linear
invert              false   flip the value (1 - x) before the curve
smooth              0       glide time in seconds; 0 = instant
enabled             absent = on; false mutes the route
id                  assigned; used by removeRoute()

When a signal arrives, each enabled route with that source does five things in order: take the window ((value - inMin) / (inMax - inMin), clamped to 0..1), invert if asked, apply the curve, scale into outMin..outMax, and write. With smooth: 0 the param is overridden at once. With smooth > 0 the result becomes a target that update(dt) glides toward: after smooth seconds the param has covered about 63% of the way. If the target param is a pulse param, the route fires it instead: on every event of a pulse signal, or when a continuous source rises past 0.5.

Learn is generalised MIDI-learn: mapper.learn('bloom'), then move something. The first signal that moves by at least 5% of its declared range (a knob, a hand, a phone tilt), or the first pulse that fires (a key, a pad), becomes the source of a new route with the default settings. Calling learn('bloom') again cancels it. Because any pulse binds at once, stop the drum machine before you learn.

Before you call it

Create the signals and the params first, then the mapper. A smoothed route (smooth > 0) writes its param only inside update(dt), so call mapper.update(dt) every frame (createShow() does).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription

paramsParamsThe Params to write into. A route writes its target as an override.
profileStringThe name this mapper saves its routes under in localStorage (openav.map.<profile>), and the world name in an exported map file. createShow() uses the world's name. optional default 'default'
onChangeFunction | nullCalled with no arguments whenever the routes change or the import report changes (for a UI to redraw). optional default null
onLearnFunction | nullCalled as onLearn(route, signalName) when learn mode binds a signal. optional default null

Members

removeRoute(id)methodRemove the route with this id.

  • With createShow(), routes are added before the sound engine registers its sound/* params, so a route to sound/cutoff needs an explicit outMin: 100, outMax: 8000.
  • More, with the saved-profile rules: Mapping.

parseMap()#

function@openav/mapping
parseMap(input)

Reads and cleans a map file (JSON text or a parsed value) without touching any mapper; it never throws.

Use it to validate a file before you import it, or to show what is inside one. It refuses, with a plain-language error, text that is not JSON, text longer than MAP_MAX_BYTES, an object whose format is not MAP_FORMAT, a missing or newer version, no routes list, and more than 500 routes.

What it accepts is cleaned: a route without a string signal and param is dropped (and counted in dropped), unknown keys disappear, numbers must be finite, an unknown curve becomes 'linear', smooth is held to 0..60 seconds, and only invert: true inverts. A route is on unless it says enabled: false.

Decides whether a ?map= address may be fetched: same origin, or an absolute https URL, and nothing else.

A map file named in the page address is somebody else's data, so the rules are strict. Accepted: an address on the same origin as base (any scheme, so plain http://localhost works for a page served from there), or an absolute https: address. Refused: an empty address, one longer than 2048 characters, one that is not a URL, one carrying a user name or password, http: to another host, and data:, javascript:, file:, blob: and every other scheme. loadMapUrl() runs this check before it fetches anything.

Bus#

class@openav/core
new Bus()

A minimal event emitter: on(event, cb), emit(event, payload), off(event, cb). No wildcards, no async.

new Bus() is a tiny publish and subscribe helper for your own code: subscribe to an event name with on(), fire it with emit(), and every callback gets the one payload you pass. Callbacks run in the order they subscribed, synchronously, inside emit().

It is not the thing shows talk through. Inputs and worlds talk through Signals (named values with a range) and Params; nothing else in the framework uses a Bus, and createShow() does not create one.

Members

NameDescription
on(event, cb)methodSubscribe: on(event, cb). Returns a function that unsubscribes.
off(event, cb)methodUnsubscribe the callback you passed to on().
emit(event, payload)methodFire an event with one payload: emit(event, payload). A callback that throws is caught and logged as [bus] <event> handler:; the rest still run.

Loop#

class@openav/core
new Loop(onFrame, { maxDt = 0.1 } = {})

The frame clock: calls your function every animation frame with the seconds since the last one, and keeps ticking when the tab is hidden.

new Loop((dt) => { … }).start() runs your function once per requestAnimationFrame, with dt in seconds. It is the one clock a show has: the timeline advances, mapped signals settle, the world draws and the backstage feed is sent from inside it, in the order the architecture page lists. createShow() builds and starts one for you and returns it as show.loop.

Browsers freeze requestAnimationFrame in a hidden tab, but a performance must not stop because someone switched windows. So while the loop runs, a Web Worker beats every 33 ms; whenever no animation frame has arrived for 50 ms, the loop steps itself. A hidden tab therefore ticks at roughly 15 frames a second with a normal-sized dt, and show time stays real time. Where the page forbids workers (a strict content security policy) that fallback is simply absent.

loop.fps is the frame rate, rounded, refreshed about every half second (the very first value comes from the first frame alone); it is 0 before the first frame. loop.running says whether it is going.

Before you call it

Call start(): nothing ticks until you do. It needs a browser (requestAnimationFrame, performance); in Node there is no clock to run it.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
onFrameFunctionCalled as onFrame(dt, now): dt is the seconds since the previous frame (never more than maxDt), now the time in milliseconds. An error thrown inside is caught and logged as [loop]; the clock keeps going.
maxDtNumberThe longest dt you will ever be handed, in seconds. A stall (a long garbage collection, a dragged window) is cut to this, so a world never has to cope with a one-second jump. optional default 0.1

Members

NameDescription
start()methodStart the clock. Calling it while it already runs does nothing.
stop()methodStop the clock and shut the hidden-tab worker down. start() begins again.

Notes

  • Do not read the real clock inside a world: take time from dt (or from the timeline), so a show at 30 fps and one at 144 fps do the same thing.

Params#

class@openav/core
new Params(schema = [])

The values a world listens to: a list of declared params, each resolved every frame from the timeline, unless a hand, a knob or a route has overridden it.

A param is the way a world takes continuous control: { key: 'bloom', min: 0, max: 1, def: 0.5 }. The world never asks who set it. Every frame each param resolves to one number: the override if there is one, otherwise the base value (usually the Timeline's automation at the current time), otherwise def. resolve() does exactly that and hands the world a { key: value } object.

An override is sticky. After params.override('bloom', 0.8) (what a slider, a MIDI knob or a mapped route does) the timeline stops moving bloom until clearOverride('bloom'). That matches the stage: when a person grabs a control, the score gives way. Overrides are clamped into min..max and snapped to step when they are written.

A param with pulse: true is a trigger, not a level: nobody reads a value from it. Fire it with firePulse(key) (a pad, a route from a pulse signal, a console button) and listen with onPulse(key, cb).

In a show, createShow() builds one Params and registers every world's schema into it with add(), then returns it as show.params.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
schemaArrayThe param declarations: { key, label?, min, max, def, step?, pulse?, group? }. key is required; min, max and def give the range and the value when nothing else sets it. The array is kept, not copied. optional default []

Members

NameDescription
add(entries)methodRegister more params: add(entries). A key that already exists is skipped, so the first declaration wins. Returns the Params itself.
get(key)methodThe declaration of a param ({ key, min, max, def, … }), or undefined. It is not the current value: read that from resolve().
clamp(key, v)methodclamp(key, v) holds v inside the param's min..max and rounds it to a multiple of step. An unknown key returns v unchanged.
override(key, v)methodoverride(key, v) sets a sticky override, clamped like clamp(). A key that was never declared is ignored without a word.
clearOverride(key)methodGive one param back to the timeline.
clearAllOverrides()methodGive every param back to the timeline.
isOverridden(key)methodWhether a param currently has an override (the console shows these labels in yellow).
firePulse(key)methodFire a pulse param: every callback registered with onPulse(key, …) runs with the key.
onPulse(key, cb)methodonPulse(key, cb) runs cb(key) each time that pulse param fires. Returns a function that stops listening.
resolve(base = {})methodresolve(base = {}) gives { key: value } for every declared param: the override, else base[key] (for example timeline.state()), else def. A pulse param has no def, so its value is undefined.

Notes

  • step snaps with ordinary floating-point arithmetic: with step: 0.1, an override of 0.3 reads back as 0.30000000000000004. On a timeline a stepped param also holds each keyframe instead of interpolating.
  • resolve() does not clamp the base value, only overrides are clamped when written. Keep your automation inside min..max.
  • The fields a world may declare (label, options, surface, group …) are listed in Writing a world.

Signals#

class@openav/core
new Signals()

The registry every input writes into and everything else reads from: named values that are either a level (continuous) or an event (pulse).

new Signals() makes an empty registry. In a show you rarely build it yourself: createShow() creates one and returns it as show.signals. A signal is a name plus a value. Input packages publish with set() and pulse(); everything else reads with get() and norm(), or subscribes with on() and onAny().

There are two kinds. A continuous signal (the default) always holds a current value, usually between 0 and 1: a knob, the loudness of the room, the height of a wrist. A pulse signal (kind: 'pulse') is an event: its value is the payload of the last firing and it is null until the first one: a key struck, a kick heard, a pinch started. Read a level whenever you like; subscribe to an event with on().

Names are paths with the source first: midi/cc/74, audio/rms, pose/hand/right/y, breath/pressure. Declare a signal with its range before you publish it: signals.define('breath/pressure', { min: 0, max: 1 }). set() on a name nobody declared defines it on the spot as a continuous signal from 0 to 1, so declare first whenever your numbers are in degrees, MIDI notes or any other range.

A knob, a raised hand and a chord are equal citizens here. Whoever reads a signal (the Mapper, a world that listens for events, the monitor) does not know and does not care what produced it.

Members

NameDescription
define(name, meta = {})methodDeclare a signal and its range: define(name, { kind, min, max, unit, description, source }). Safe to call again: later declarations merge into earlier ones. A continuous signal starts at min, a pulse at null. Returns the registry.
set(name, value)methodPublish a value: set(name, value). Subscribers run every time, even when the value did not change. An undeclared name is defined on the spot as continuous 0..1.
pulse(name, payload = 1)methodFire an event: pulse(name, payload = 1). It is set() under another name; declare the signal with kind: 'pulse' first, or it is registered as continuous.
get(name)methodThe last value of a signal, or undefined for a name that was never declared or set. A pulse that has not fired yet is null.
norm(name)methodThe value as 0..1 inside the declared min and max, clamped. An unknown name, or a signal whose min equals its max, gives 0.
on(name, cb)methodSubscribe to one signal: on(name, cb), where cb(value, name) runs on every set() or pulse(). Returns a function that unsubscribes.
onAny(cb)methodSubscribe to every signal: cb(name, value, meta) runs for each one. The mapper's learn mode and the monitor use it. Returns a function that unsubscribes.
list()methodEvery signal as [{ name, value, at, kind, min, max, unit, description, source }]; at is the time of the last set() (performance.now(), 0 if never). What the monitor and meters read.

Notes

  • signals.meta is a Map of name → declaration and signals.values a Map of name → last value. Read them if you must; write through define() and set() so subscribers hear about it.
  • A subscriber that throws is caught and logged as [signals] <name>; the other subscribers still run and set() does not throw.
  • The names every built-in package publishes are listed in the signals reference.

@openav/show

createShow()#

function@openav/show
async createShow({ world = null, worlds = [], timeline: timelineCfg = { total: 120 }, routes = [], modules = {}, artwork = null, hint = '', profile = null, map = null, onFrame = null, mount = null, telemetry = true, score: scoreCfg = null, } = {})

Builds a whole show around a world in one call: signals, params, stage, timeline, mapper, the modules you switch on, the console, the backstage feed and the frame loop.

Every example is a world plus one createShow() call. It builds the Signals registry, the Params, the Stage with your world, the Timeline, the Mapper (with your routes), the inputs and outputs you declare in modules, the director's desk (mountConsole()), the backstage feed (MonitorFeed) and the frame Loop, starts the loop, and hands you every part. Nothing is hidden: show.signals, show.params, show.timeline, show.mapper, show.stage and the rest are the very objects the frame loop runs. When the framework grows a module, every show can have it just by declaring it.

The modules keys: midi (on by default, false turns it off, { controllers: true } or { controllers: { profile, profiles, open } } docks an on-screen MIDI controller), keys (the on-screen piano, QWERTY and the simulated performer: on by default, false turns them off, { base, octaves, sim, capture } tunes them), drums (true or { engine, autoEnableEngine }), audio (any truthy value: the microphone analyser, started from the 🎤 button), chord (true or { window }: a ChordDetector wired to every played note), hands (true: HandTracker), pose (true: PoseTracker), leap (true or { url, simulate, fingers, box }: LeapInput; ?leap=sim or ?leap=ws://… in the address overrides), remote (true or { room, … }: phones as controllers) and sound (true, an instrument id such as 'piano', or { instrument, remember, picker, engine }: instruments in the page, loaded only when declared). Parts that fetch things load lazily, so a show that does not declare them pays nothing.

The page shell is fixed once so every show is the same. Without mount, the page body becomes a two-column grid: the stage, and a 340 px side panel holding the piano and the console (an upright phone gets the stage on top and the panel below: see isStacked()). Every frame, in this order:

text
keys, drums, audio update   on-screen performers and the microphone
onFrame(dt, show)           your hook
timeline.advance(dt)        time moves
director.update(...)        with a score: segment modules enter, update, exit
mapper.update(dt)           smoothed routes settle
stage.frame(dt, state)      params resolve, world updates and renders
sound, remote               sound params reach the synth, values echo to phones
console.render(state)       the desk reflects reality
monitor.frame(snapshot)     the backstage hears about it

Before you call it

await it: it is async because it waits for the world's init() (and for lazily loaded modules). It needs a page (document, location, localStorage), and an import map or bundler that resolves every @openav/* package it imports (copy the one from examples/01-hello-particles/index.html). Browsers start audio only after a click, so sound and the microphone start from the console's buttons.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
worldObject | nullThe world to perform: { name, params, init, update, render, dispose } (see Stage). It is activated first, and createShow waits for its init(). optional default null
worldsArrayMore worlds to register, after world. All of their params are registered up front; switch with show.stage.activate(name). optional default []
timelineObjectThe options of the Timeline: { total, automation, scenes, start, loop, onCue }. With a score, its scenes and total win. optional default { total: 120 }
routesArrayRoutes for the Mapper. If a saved profile exists it is loaded, and any declared route whose source → target pair is missing from it is still added. optional default []
modulesObjectThe inputs and outputs to switch on, by key (see the description): midi, keys, drums, audio, chord, hands, pose, leap, remote, sound. optional default {}
artworkObject | null{ title, artist, year, note }: a credit line at the bottom right of the stage and a <meta name="artwork"> tag in the head. optional default null
hintStringA line of HTML at the bottom left of the stage, for example 'play the piano · Space plays the timeline'. It is inserted as HTML, so never put untrusted text in it. optional default ''
profileString | false | nullThe name the mapper saves its routes under in localStorage (default: the first world's name, else 'show'). false ignores the saved routes when the show starts, so the routes come from your code on every load. optional default null
mapString | false | nullA map file to load on start: a same-origin or https address (see loadMapUrl()). Left out, ?map=<url> in the page address is used; false ignores ?map=. optional default null

telemetryBooleanAllow one anonymous oav_show_start hit per page load. false sends nothing. optional default true

Returns

Promise<Object> The show: { signals, params, stage, timeline, mapper, midi, controllers, midiPanel, keys, drums, sound, audio, hands, pose, leap, chord, remote, score, director, scoreMidi, console, app, loop }. A part you did not ask for is null. With a score there is also show.show, the rehearsal controls. The same object is window.openav.

Notes

  • The mapper saves its routes under the profile name every 3 seconds, so a learned or edited route survives a reload and wins over a changed declaration in your code (the same source → target pair keeps its saved curve and smoothing). profile: false makes the routes come from code on every load, but the mapper still saves under the world's name from then on. To start clean, localStorage.removeItem('openav.map.<world name>').
  • Routes are added before the sound engine registers its sound/* params, so a declared route to sound/cutoff needs an explicit outMin: 100, outMax: 8000.
  • show.params.resolve() without an argument gives the def of every param. To read what the world sees this frame, pass the timeline's base state: show.params.resolve(show.timeline.state()).
  • Unless telemetry: false, one anonymous oav_show_start hit goes to Google Analytics per page load. Per the code it is silent on localhost, LAN addresses, file:// and openaudiovisual.com itself, and it honours Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control. Nothing played, no path, no cookie and no stable id is sent.
  • With a score, window.openav.show has table(), goto('dusk'), goto('dusk.glow'), goto(2), seek(T), cue(name), status(), next(), prev() and cuts, for rehearsal from the devtools console.

isStacked()#

function@openav/show
isStacked(width, height)

Whether a window of this size gets the stacked layout (stage on top, panel below): upright and no wider than 820 pixels.

The shell of createShow() has one layout rule: wide windows get the stage and a 340 px side panel next to each other, and an upright phone or small tablet gets the stage on top and the panel below it, scrolling. The rule is the media query STACK_QUERY, and isStacked() is the very same decision as a plain function, so a test (or your own layout code) can use it without a browser. A phone on its side is never taller than wide, so it stays in the wide layout.

NameTypeDescription
widthNumberThe window width in pixels.
heightNumberThe window height in pixels.

Returns

Boolean true when width <= 820 and height > width.

createCanvas()#

function@openav/stage
createCanvas(container, { alpha = false } = {})

Makes a 2D canvas that fills its container and keeps its size in step with it, at up to 2 times the device pixel ratio.

A convenience for worlds that draw with the 2D canvas API; a world may use it or ignore it. The canvas is display: block and as big as the container. fit() sets its pixel size to the container size times the device pixel ratio (never more than 2) and scales the context so you keep drawing in CSS pixels. Call fit() at the top of render(): it only does work when the size changed, and it returns { w, h } to draw with. A ResizeObserver also calls it when the container is resized.

Call dispose() in the world's dispose(): it stops the observer and removes the canvas.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
containerHTMLElementThe element to put the canvas in (a world's container, usually).

Stage#

class@openav/stage
new Stage({ container, params, signals, io = {} })

Runs one world at a time: registers worlds and their params, switches between them, and each frame resolves the params and calls the world's update and render.

A world is any system with this shape, and every method is optional:

js
{
  name: 'garden',                                   // unique: the stage registers worlds by name
  params: [{ key: 'growth', min: 0, max: 1, def: 0.5 }],   // what it can be performed with
  init({ container, signals, params }) {},           // when it becomes active (may be async)
  update(dt, state, io) {},                          // every frame: state = the resolved params
  render() {},                                       // every frame, right after update
  dispose() {},                                      // when another world is activated
}

The stage owns the lifecycle and the param aggregation and deliberately not a renderer: draw with a 2D canvas, p5, three.js, SVG, the DOM, whatever you like. The shell never knows the work: switching works means swapping the world and its data, and the shell stays.

A world takes continuous control from state (the params) and may subscribe to signals for discrete events (a note struck, a chord resolved). If it reads signals.get('midi/cc/74') inside update(), it works with your controller today, but the timeline, a hand or another controller can no longer drive it. In a show, createShow() builds the stage from its world and worlds options and returns it as show.stage.

Before you call it

Register your worlds, then await stage.activate(name) once; until a world is active, frame() returns null and does nothing. Then call stage.frame(dt, baseState) every frame (a show's loop does).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
containerHTMLElementThe element the worlds draw into. It becomes position: relative if it was static. The stage adds its own layer inside it, so overlays you put in the container (hints, start buttons) are not wiped when a world is switched. optional
paramsParamsThe Params the worlds' schemas are absorbed into, and that frame() resolves. optional
signalsSignalsThe Signals registry handed to every world, so it can subscribe to events. optional
ioObjectExtra output handles for the worlds' update(dt, state, io), such as { midi, osc }. signals is always there. optional default {}

Members

NameDescription
register(world)methodRegister a world by its name and add its params to the shared Params (a key that already exists keeps its first declaration). Returns the stage.
activate(name)methodSwitch to the world with this name. Async: it disposes the previous world (an error in its dispose() is logged, not thrown), empties the stage layer, then awaits the new world's init({ container, signals, params }). Does nothing if that world is already active; rejects with "unknown world" for a name that was never registered.
frame(dt, baseState)methodPer frame: frame(dt, baseState) resolves params.resolve(baseState) (override, else the base, else def), calls the active world's update(dt, state, io) and then render(), and returns the resolved state, or null with no active world. An exception in either call is caught and logged as [stage] update: or [stage] render:; the show keeps running.

Notes

  • Check the name before you activate: activate('nope') disposes the current world first and only then rejects, and the stage keeps pointing at the disposed world (active and activeName do not change), so the next frame() still calls its update() and render().
  • Fields to read: active (the active world object), activeName, worlds (a Map of name → world), container, layer (the element worlds are placed in) and io ({ signals, ...io }, what update receives; add handles later with stage.io.osc = osc).
  • An exception in init() is not caught: activate() rejects. Exceptions in update() and render() are caught. A world must release what it takes (GPU objects, DOM, subscriptions) in dispose(), because worlds get switched live.

webtoeWorld()#

function@openav/world-webtoe
webtoeWorld({ name = 'webtoe', app = 'https://webtoe.openaudiovisual.com/', project = null, params = [], extra = null, } = {})

Turns a WebToe node patch into a world: the patch runs in an iframe and every changed param is posted into it.

WebToe is the sister project: a web-native, node-based dataflow engine that speaks TouchDesigner. webtoeWorld() embeds its app in an iframe that fills the stage (with allow="camera; microphone"), and each frame it posts the resolved params into the iframe as { type: 'webtoe:ext', values }. Inside the patch, any parameter written as ext('name', fallback) follows the value called name, and uses fallback until one arrives.

The contract stays pure: the world reads params and never inputs. Which knob, hand or timeline drives speed is the mapper's business, as for any world. To send less, the world posts only when at least one value differs from the last post.

Before you call it

The page must be able to load the WebToe app in an iframe (the network, by default https://webtoe.openaudiovisual.com/), and the patch file must be reachable by the app. The world does its work when it is activated, so use it with createShow({ world }), or stage.register() and stage.activate().

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
nameStringThe world's name: what Stage registers it under and what you pass to stage.activate(). Give each patch its own. optional default 'webtoe'
appStringThe WebToe app to embed in the iframe. Change it to run your own copy of the app. optional default 'https://webtoe.openaudiovisual.com/'
projectString | nullThe address of a .webtoe.json patch file. It is handed to the app as ?project=<address>, and the app fetches it, so the file's server must allow the app's origin (CORS). Make the address absolute, for example new URL('./garden.webtoe.json', location.href).href. optional default null
paramsArrayThe param schema of the world: [{ key, min, max, def }, …]. The keys are the names the patch reads with ext('name', fallback). optional default []
extraFunction | nullextra(state, out), called every frame: add derived values to out (a copy of the state) that the patch can read too, such as out.hueRad = state.hue * Math.PI / 180. optional default null

Returns

Object A world { name, params, init, update, render, dispose } to pass to createShow({ world }) or stage.register().

Notes

  • The message goes to the iframe with the target origin *, so any page the iframe happens to be showing receives the values. If you point app at a site you do not trust, it can read your params.

Because a value is only posted when it changed, a patch that finishes loading after the first frame may not receive values that never move again until one of them changes; whether that happens with the live app was not checked.

aliasOf()#

function@openav/relay
aliasOf(name, alias = 'any')

The "latest phone" name of a phone signal: aliasOf('phone/ab12/tilt/x') is 'phone/any/tilt/x'. null for anything else.

A route written in a World file cannot know the id of a stranger's phone. The alias fixes that: every phone signal is also filed under phone/any/…, which always holds the value from whichever phone sent last, so { source: 'phone/any/tilt/x', target: 'hue' } can be written before anyone has joined. bindSignals() and localSensors() both file the alias for you.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
nameStringA signal name. Only phone/<id>/… has an alias.
aliasStringThe word that replaces the id. Leave it out for any. optional default 'any'

Returns

String | null The alias name, or null when name is not a phone signal or already uses the alias.

  • localSensors() For a show page that runs on the phone itself: the phone's own sensors go straight into a Signals as phone/local/…, with a phone/any/… copy.

attachRelay()#

function@openav/relay
attachRelay(server, { path = '/relay', log = () => {}, heartbeatMs = 20000 } = {})

Attaches the room relay to a Node http.Server: WebSocket clients that connect to path are put in rooms and routed by role. Returns { hub, close() }.

This is the server half, in Node, with no dependencies (the WebSocket codec is in the package). node serve.js already does it for you at /relay. To use it in your own server: attachRelay(server) before or after server.listen(). Clients connect to ws://host/relay?role=controller|runner|monitor&room=<name>&id=<device>: a bad role becomes controller, a bad room name becomes default, and the id is cut to 64 characters.

Who may talk to whom: a controller's signal and batch go to the runner and the monitors; a runner's go to the monitors only; a runner's feedback and config go to the controllers and monitors; a monitor says nothing. A config is kept per key and replayed to controllers that join later, and the room forgets it when its runner leaves. Rooms never hear each other. A message over 256 KB is ignored and a frame over 1 MB closes the connection.

There is no authentication: anyone who can reach the server and knows a room name can join as a controller. Use a closed network, or a room name nobody will guess.

Before you call it

A Node program, imported from @openav/relay/server (a different entry point from @openav/relay, which is the browser side). Standalone: node packages/relay/server.js [port] (default 7458; /health answers with the room names; RELAY_HOST=127.0.0.1 binds to localhost behind a reverse proxy).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
serverhttp.ServerA Node http.Server (or anything with the same upgrade event, such as an https server). The relay listens for its upgrade events.
pathStringThe URL path clients connect to. Any other path is refused. optional default '/relay'
logFunction(line) => {}, called with a line such as + controller ab12 @main when a client joins and - controller ab12 @main when it leaves. The default says nothing. optional default () => {}
heartbeatMsNumberHow often to ping every client, in milliseconds. A client that has not answered by the next ping is dropped, so a dead phone goes within one to two periods. optional default 20000

Returns

{ hub, close } hub is the RoomHub (hub.rooms is a Map of the rooms; hub.counts(room) gives { controllers, runners, monitors }). close() drops every connected client; it does not close your server.

Examples

Connects a runner's RelayClient to a Signals registry: every signal a phone sends is filed there, plus a phone/any/… copy. Returns an undo function.

Call it once on the show page, after making the runner's client: bindSignals(show, signals). It sets client.onSignal so that each signal that arrives goes through fileSignal(), and a phone signal is filed twice, under its own name (phone/ab12/tilt/x) and under the alias (phone/any/tilt/x). Routes written at author time use the alias.

A callback that was already in client.onSignal keeps running after the filing, so you can still watch the raw messages.

fileSignal()#

Files one incoming signal into a Signals registry: declares the name the first time, fills in the velocity, then sets it or pulses it.

This is the receiving half of the wire format, and every receiver files a message the same way through it: bindSignals() for a show that has a relay, localSensors() for a show on a phone, and a host that runs its own socket. In order: if the registry has never heard the name, declare it with what signalMeta() says (a pulse is never mistaken for a knob, and meters get their range); fill in the missing velocity spelling with normalizeValue(); then signals.pulse(name, value) for a pulse or signals.set(name, value) for the rest.

sourceStringA label stored in the declared metadata (signals.meta.get(name).source), such as 'relay' or 'local'. optional default ''

Returns

Boolean true when it was filed, false for a bad name.

normalizeValue()#

function@openav/relay
normalizeValue(name, value)

Fills in the missing velocity spelling of a note message: vel (0..1) or velocity (1..127). Every other message passes through unchanged.

@openav/midi publishes vel as 0..1, a hardware keyboard talks in velocity 1..127, and senders (an old phone page, a TouchOSC bridge, a sequencer) give one or the other. A sketch is written against one spelling, so the receiving end fills in the other: velocity becomes vel = velocity / 127, and vel becomes velocity = Math.round(vel * 127).

You rarely call it yourself: fileSignal() does it for every message it files.

Returns

any The payload with both vel and velocity. If both were there already, the same object comes back untouched.
