RelayClient#

class@openav/relay
new RelayClient({ role = 'controller', room = 'default', id = deviceId(), url = null, batchHz = 30, resendMs = 1000, onStatus, onSignal, onFeedback, onConfig } = {})

The browser end of the room relay: sends signals to the other pages in a room and receives theirs, as a phone (controller), the show (runner) or a backstage monitor.

Make one client per page, give it a role and a room, and call connect(). A phone calls phone.set('phone/me/tilt/x', 0.3) for values that change continuously and phone.send('midi/note/on', { note: 60 }, true) for events. The show passes its client to bindSignals(), and every phone signal lands in its Signals. The relay itself is attachRelay() on a Node server.

Continuous values are cheap on purpose: set() only stores the value (and does nothing if it is the same as the last), then every 1 / batchHz seconds the changed ones leave in one batch, and every resendMs all of them leave again. Events are the opposite: send() leaves at once and is never batched or repeated, because a note-on delivered twice is a bug.

It looks after the connection itself. When the socket closes it reconnects after 0.5 s, then 1 s, 2 s, 4 s and every 5 s, until you call close(). A ping goes out every 2 s and the answer becomes latency in milliseconds. status is 'connecting', 'open' or 'closed', and peers is how many controllers, runners and monitors the room has.

Before you call it

A relay server for it to reach, such as node serve.js (it hosts one at /relay) or node packages/relay/server.js. Until the socket is open, set() keeps the latest values and sends them when it opens, but send(), feedback() and config() messages are dropped, not queued.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
role'controller' | 'runner' | 'monitor'Who this page is. A controller (a phone) sends signals to the runner and the monitors. A runner (the show) hears the controllers, and can send feedback and config back. A monitor only listens. The server treats any other word as controller. optional default 'controller'
roomStringThe room name. Pages in different rooms never hear each other. 1 to 32 characters of A–Z a–z 0–9 _ -; the server turns anything else into default. optional default 'default'
idStringThis device's id, the <id> in phone/<id>/…. The default is deviceId(), which is kept in localStorage. The server keeps its first 64 characters. optional default deviceId()
urlStringThe full WebSocket address, with the query already on it: wss://host/relay?role=controller&room=main&id=ab12. Nothing is added to it. Leave it out and the client uses ?relay=ws://… from the page's address, or else the page's own /relay (wss: on an https page), and adds role, room and id itself. optional default null
batchHzNumberHow many times a second the values you set() are flushed to the relay, as one batch message. optional default 30
resendMsNumberEvery this many milliseconds, send every stored value again, not only the changed ones. This is what lets a phone that joins late, or a show page that reloads, catch up. optional default 1000
onStatusFunction(client) => {}, called when the connection opens or closes, when a pong gives a new latency, and when the peer counts change. Read client.status, client.latency and client.peers inside it. optional
onSignalFunction(name, value, msg) => {}, for every signal that arrives (a runner or monitor hears the controllers; a monitor also hears the runner). A batch calls it once per item. msg.pulse is true for a pulse. bindSignals() fills this in for you. optional
onFeedbackFunction(name, value) => {}, on a controller: a value the runner sent with feedback(), to show in a meter or to move a fader. optional
onConfigFunction(key, data) => {}, on a controller: a standing config the runner sent with config(), such as the surface layout. A phone that joins late gets the stored ones right away. optional

signalMeta()#

What the relay knows about a signal name: its range and unit, or that it is a pulse. Returns null for names it does not know.

A Signals registry needs to know a name's range before a meter can scale it or a mapping can tell a knob from an event. fileSignal() calls this the first time it hears a name. What it knows: phone/<id>/tilt/* is −1..1, accel/* is −20..20 m/s², rot/* is −360..360 °/s, orient/* is 0..360 °, touch/count is 0..10, knock is a pulse, and every other phone/… name (touch, light) is 0..1. surface/… names are 0..1 (…/raw and …/delta are unscaled, {}). midi/note/on, midi/note/off, midi/virtual and the hit, on, off, last names of a controller are pulses, and midi/cc/* is 0..1.

attachTouchPad()#

function@openav/remote

Makes an element a multi-touch pad: each finger publishes touch/x, touch/y and touch/down (0..1 inside the element), and touch/count says how many are down.

The first finger down is slot 0 and publishes touch/x, touch/y, touch/down; the second is slot 1 and publishes touch/1/x, touch/1/y, touch/1/down, and so on. A slot is given back when its finger lifts, so the lowest free number is used next. x runs 0 at the left edge to 1 at the right, y runs 0 at the top to 1 at the bottom, both held inside the element and rounded to 4 decimals. touch/down is 1 or 0, and touch/count is the number of fingers down.

It publishes touch/down 0 and touch/count 0 at once, so a receiver knows the pad is there before anyone touches it. It uses pointer events, so a mouse works too (one finger).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
padHTMLElementThe element to listen on. Give it touch-action: none in CSS, or the browser may take a drag for a scroll and cancel the touch.
io{ set(name, value) }Where the values go, as for PhoneSensors: only set is used, and the names have no phone/<id>/ in front.
onMoveFunction(slot, x, y, down) => {}, when a finger touches and each time it moves. x and y are 0..1 and down is true. Use it to draw the finger. optional
onEndFunction(slot) => {}, when a finger lifts or the touch is cancelled. optional

Notes

  • The sense tab uses this on its touch pad, with io writing to a RelayClient under phone/<id>/.

localSensors()#

function@openav/remote
localSensors(signals, { prefix = 'phone/local/', alias = 'any', source = 'local', hooks = {} } = {})

For a show page that runs on the phone itself: the phone's own sensors go straight into a Signals as phone/local/…, with a phone/any/… copy.

A remote phone reaches the show through a relay. When the show page is open on the phone itself, there is no one to relay to, so this reads the sensors in place. The names and thresholds are the same as a remote phone's (phone/local/tilt/x is −1..1, phone/local/knock is a pulse), declared the same way by fileSignal(), and mirrored to phone/any/…, so a route written for "the latest phone", phone/any/tilt/x, works whether the phone is in your hand as a controller or is the show.

Before you call it

Call .start() on the result from a tap (iOS asks for permission only inside a gesture, and only on https pages). Until then nothing is published. See PhoneSensors.

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsThe registry to fill (from @openav/core).
prefixStringWhat goes in front of each sensor name. optional default 'phone/local/'
aliasString | nullThe word for the copy, phone/<alias>/…. null turns the copy off. optional default 'any'
sourceStringStored as the signals' source in signals.meta. optional default 'local'
hooksObjectThe hooks of PhoneSensors: onKnock, onSample, notify. optional default {}

Returns

PhoneSensors Nothing is listening yet: call .start() from a tap.

mountJoinCard()#

function@openav/remote
mountJoinCard(parent, host)

Puts a small card on the show page with a QR code and the URL a phone should open, and a line that says whether the relay is reachable and how many phones are in.

The URL is the phone page (packages/remote/ next to this file) with ?room=<room> on it, and with ?relay=… as well when the show uses the public relay or a relay of your own, so the phone ends up in the same room on the same relay. On localhost it asks node serve.js for this machine's LAN address at /__info and puts that in the URL, because a phone cannot open localhost. The QR code is drawn from the URL; if the URL is too long for the encoder, the code is left out and the URL stays.

The status line reads relay ok · 2 phones · room demo when the connection is open (and adds · public relay on the public one), relay offline — is it node serve.js? when a local relay cannot be reached, and can't reach the relay (…) — retrying for a shared one. On a phone held upright the card starts folded, because the stage is small; tap it to open or fold it.

parentHTMLElementThe element to add the card to. The card is position: absolute at its top left, so the parent should be positioned (position: relative) and big enough to show it.
hostObjectThe host from mountRemoteHost(). The card reads host.room, host.relayMode and host.relayUrl, and takes over host.onStatus to write the status line.

Returns

HTMLElement The card's element, already in parent. Remove it with .remove().

Notes

mountRemote()#

function@openav/remote
mountRemote(root, opts = {})

The whole phone app in one call: a status bar and the tabs sense, keys, control and MIDI, talking to the relay as a controller. /packages/remote/ is exactly this.

It is what a phone opens: lockViewport() so nothing scrolls or zooms, keepAwake() so the screen stays on, one RelayClient as a controller that every tab shares, and the tabs. Sense is a tilt ball, readouts, a multi-touch pad (attachTouchPad()) and the sensors (PhoneSensors) behind a start button. Keys is a piano that is one row in landscape and two stacked rows in portrait. Control is a Surface. MIDI is a virtual controller.

The control tab's layout comes from, in order: surfaceUrl or ?surface=, metaUrl or ?meta=, whatever layout the show publishes over the relay (the config surface), and finally a small generic panel so the page is never blank. The signals are phone/<id>/… (sense), midi/note/on|off and midi/cc/64 (keys), and surface/<page>/<id> (control). The app opens on ?tab=, else the tab used last in this browser, else sense.

Before you call it

A page of its own (it takes over the whole screen) and a relay to reach: the same origin's /relay unless relayUrl or ?relay= says otherwise. Without a show in the room the header says it is waiting for the work to open.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
rootHTMLElementWhere to put the app. It fills the whole page (position: fixed), so pass document.body.
optsObject{ room, relayUrl, surfaceUrl, metaUrl }, each optional. room is the relay room (else ?room= in the address, else window.__REMOTE__.room, else default). relayUrl is a ws:// or wss:// relay (else ?relay=; only those two schemes are accepted, so a link cannot point the phone anywhere else). surfaceUrl is a layout JSON for the control tab and metaUrl a JSON with a params array, which the control tab turns into autoSurface(). The address can also say ?tab=sense|keys|control|midi. optional default {}

Returns

Object { relay, show(tab), surface, dispose() }: the RelayClient, a function that switches tab, the control tab's Surface (a getter, null until that tab has been opened), and dispose(), which closes the relay, unlocks the viewport, lets go of the wake lock and removes the app.

Notes

  • The words on the app's tabs and header are in Chinese.

mountRemoteHost()#

function@openav/remote
mountRemoteHost({ signals, params, mapper, world = null, room = 'default', auto = {}, surface = null, feedbackHz = 10, url = null, mode = null, controllers = null } = {})

The show side of the phone remote: joins the relay as the runner, files phone signals, builds the control panel from the params and echoes values back.

createShow({ modules: { remote: true } }) calls this for you, so the world never has to know about phones. Calling it yourself does five things: it makes a RelayClient as the room's runner; files every phone signal into signals with bindSignals() (so phone/any/… always holds the latest phone); builds the layout from surface, world.surface or autoSurface() of the params; adds the surface/… → param routes to the mapper; and, when you call host.frame(dt, state) every frame, sends the resolved param values back about feedbackHz times a second so the phones' faders follow the timeline.

Making the host does not connect it: call host.connect() when you want the socket. On every (re)connection it publishes the layout as relay config surface, so a phone that joins later gets the right panel. host.layout, host.routes and host.bindings are there to look at straight away, and host.dispose() closes the socket.

Before you call it

A relay for connect() to reach: node serve.js hosts one at /relay, a static site uses the public relay (see pickRelay()), or pass url. Building the host needs none of that.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
signalsSignalsThe registry that phone signals are filed in. optional
paramsParamsThe world's params. Its schema is what the control surface is built from. optional
mapperMapperThe mapper that gets the surface/… → param routes (a route it already has is not added twice). optional
worldObjectThe world: its params are used when params.schema is empty, its name becomes the layout's title, and its surface (a hand-written layout) is used instead of a generated one. optional default null
roomStringThe relay room to join. optional default 'default'
autoObjectOptions for autoSurface(): pairs, meters, style, perPage, smooth, title. optional default {}
surfaceObjectAn explicit layout. It wins over world.surface. optional default null
feedbackHzNumberHow many times a second host.frame() sends the param values back to the phones. optional default 10
urlStringA relay to use instead of this page's own /relay, such as wss://host/relay. role, room and id are added to it for you. The runner id is then show- plus four random characters, so two tabs of one show do not collide; without url it is show. optional default null
mode'local' | 'public' | 'custom'What pickRelay() decided. Only the words of the join card depend on it; the host reports it as host.relayMode. optional default null
controllersMidiControllersThe on-screen MIDI controllers of @openav/midi: the phone's MIDI tab then shows the same device, and what is played on either screen shows on the other. optional default null

Returns

Object { relay, layout, routes, bindings, publish, room, relayUrl, relayMode, onStatus, frame(dt, state), connect(), dispose() }. connect() returns the host again.

PhoneSensors#

class@openav/remote
new PhoneSensors(io, hooks = {})

Turns a phone's tilt, acceleration, rotation, knocks and front-camera light into named signals, in screen axes, and hands them to the io you give it.

This is the phone half of the sense tab, with no page in it: make one with an io, call start() from a tap, and signals flow. From the phone's own events it produces tilt/x and tilt/y (−1..1, which is ±45° from the resting pose, x to the right and y toward you, in screen axes, so a phone turned sideways still reports "tilt right is +x"), orient/alpha|beta|gamma (degrees), accel/x|y|z (m/s², gravity included), rot/alpha|beta|gamma (degrees per second), knock (a pulse { strength, delta, t }) and, if you turn the camera on, light (0..1).

A knock is a jolt: when the acceleration vector changes by more than threshold (10 m/s² by default) between two motion samples, and at least 130 ms after the last knock, io.send('knock', { strength, delta, t }, true) fires. delta is the size of the change, and strength runs from 0.15 just over the threshold up to 1. The phone also vibrates for 10 ms where it can. Hold the phone how you want to play it and call calibrate() to make that pose the zero of the tilt.

For the show page itself running on a phone, localSensors() wraps this class and files straight into a Signals.

Before you call it

Call start() from a tap or click, not on page load. iOS asks for motion permission only inside a user gesture, and it only gives motion sensors to pages on https://; touch and keys work over plain http://. start() always resolves true: look at denied for a refusal. If no sensor data arrives within 2.5 s, hooks.notify says so (a desktop, or an iPhone page on http). setCamera(true) also needs a gesture and HTTPS on iOS.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
io{ set(name, value), send(name, value, pulse?) }Where the signals go. set gets the continuous ones, send the knocks (with pulse true). The names have no phone/<id>/ in front: tilt/x, accel/z. A RelayClient with a prefix, or a Signals registry, can sit behind it.
hooks{ onKnock?, onSample?, notify? }Optional callbacks. onKnock(strength) after each knock, onSample(name, value) for every continuous sample (to draw a readout), notify(message) with a one-line problem report such as a refused permission. The messages are written in Chinese. optional default {}

Members

NameDescription
start()methodstart(): async. Ask for the motion permission where the browser requires it, then listen to deviceorientation and devicemotion. Resolves true even when the answer was no (then denied is true and the listeners are attached anyway). Calling it again does nothing.
stop()methodstop(): stop listening and turn the camera off.
calibrate()methodcalibrate(): take the current tilt as the resting pose. Tilt reads 0 here, until the phone moves.
cycleThreshold()methodcycleThreshold(): make the knock threshold 2 m/s² higher and return it; past 24 it wraps to 4. For a "knock sensitivity" button.
setCamera(on)methodsetCamera(on): async. true opens the front camera and publishes light (the mean brightness of a 32 × 24 picture, 0..1) ten times a second; false stops it. Resolves true when done, false if the camera is not available (then hooks.notify says why).
screenTilt(beta, gamma, angle = 0)static methodPhoneSensors.screenTilt(beta, gamma, angle?): static. Turn the two raw tilt angles into screen axes for a screen angle of 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees. Returns { x, y } in degrees.

Notes

  • Public fields: io, hooks, started, gotSensor (true once any sensor data has arrived), denied (iOS said no; it stays no until the Settings app is changed), rest and deg (tilt in degrees), threshold (the knock threshold, 10) and COOLDOWN (130 ms).

autoArrange()#

function@openav/surface
autoArrange(items, cols, fixed = [])

Packs widgets into a grid first-fit, row by row, and never overlaps; fixed placements are kept and block their cells. Returns the placements and the rows used.

Each item takes the first free spot found by scanning left to right, then top to bottom: what a person does laying out a controller. The grid grows downward as far as it must, so rows is a result, not a limit. resolvePage() uses it for widgets without a position and for the automatic reflow.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
items{ id, w, h }[]What to place, in order. Every item needs a numeric w and h in cells, at least 1. A w wider than the grid is cut to cols.
colsNumberHow many columns the grid has.
fixed{ id, x, y, w, h }[]Placements that are already decided. They come first in the result and the other items go around them. optional default []

Returns

{ placements, rows } placements is a list of { id, x, y, w, h } (the fixed ones first), rows is how many rows they fill.

Notes

  • An item with no w (or a w that is not a number) never finds a spot and the function never returns. Give every item a w and an h; DEFAULT_SIZE has the natural size of each widget type.

Examples

Related

  • resolvePage() Works out where every widget of one page goes for one orientation: the grid and a cell for each widget, and which rule produced it.
  • stretchRows() Stretches a last row that stops short to the edge of the grid: five faders in four columns leave one lonely fader, and this makes it four columns wide.
  • DEFAULT_SIZE The natural size of each widget type, in grid cells, as { w, h }: a layout only has to give x, y, w, h when it cares.

autoSurface()#

function@openav/surface
autoSurface(params = [], { perPage = 8, style = 'auto', pairs = [], meters = [], smooth = 0.04, title = '' } = {})

Turns a world's params into a control panel: a layout, the routes that drive the params, and the bindings for echoing values back.

This is how a world that declares what it can be performed with gets a phone panel for free: const { layout, routes, bindings } = autoSurface(world.params), then routes.forEach((r) => mapper.addRoute(r)) and new Surface(el, { layout, sink }). Each param becomes the widget widgetTypeFor() picks. Each group of params gets its own page (a param without a group goes on main), long groups continue on main2, main3 …, and a pair from pairs becomes one XY pad with two routes, …/x and …/y.

Widget ids are the param keys (anything outside A–Z a–z 0–9 _ - becomes _), colours go round cyan, amber, magenta, lime, violet, coral, and a radio's options come from the param or are the numbers. A pulse param gets no binding, since there is no value to show. The routes already scale the normalized signal to the param's min and max. A world that comes with its own layout uses routesFromLayout() instead.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
paramsObject[]The param declarations: { key, label?, min, max, def, step?, pulse?, group?, options?, surface? }. surface: { type, color, label } on a param overrides the choice. optional default []
perPageNumberHow much fits on a page, counted in weights: a fader or a meter weighs 1, an XY pad 4, anything else 2. The default 8 is eight faders, four knobs or two XY pads. A page that scrolls is a page that fails, so a full page starts the next. optional default 8
style'auto' | 'fader' | 'knob'Faders or knobs for the continuous params. 'auto' picks faders up to six, knobs beyond. optional default 'auto'
pairsstring[][]Pairs of param keys to drive with one XY pad: [['cx', 'cy']]. The first key is x and the second is y. optional default []
metersstring[]Param keys to also show as read-only meters, on a page called Meters. optional default []
smoothNumberSeconds of smoothing on the continuous routes, to hide the steps of a 30 Hz network (zipper noise). Pulses, toggles and radios are never smoothed. optional default 0.04
titleStringThe layout's title. optional default ''

Returns

{ layout, routes, bindings } layout is a layout JSON for Surface. routes is a list of mapper routes { source, target, inMin, inMax, curve, smooth, outMin, outMax }, from surface/<page>/<id> to each param. bindings is { param, name, page, widget, min, max, readonly? } for feedbackFor().

True when the page can ask for fullscreen: the browser has requestFullscreen (or the WebKit one). The code treats iPhone Safari as not having it.

Use it to decide whether to show a fullscreen button: if (canFullscreen()) button.hidden = false. It only checks that the function exists; whether a request succeeds is up to the browser, which wants it to come from a tap (toggleFullscreen()).

DEFAULT_SIZE#

The natural size of each widget type, in grid cells, as { w, h }: a layout only has to give x, y, w, h when it cares.

A widget without a w or h takes the size of its type, held to the number of columns of the grid. autoArrange() and resolvePage() use it, and so does autoSurface() when it counts how many widgets fit on a page. A type it does not know counts as 2×2.

feedbackFor()#

function@openav/surface
feedbackFor(state, bindings)

Turns the resolved param state into the normalized values the phone's widgets should show right now: [{ name, value }].

It is pure and cheap, so the show calls it about ten times a second and sends each result to the phones with relay.feedback(name, value); host.frame() of mountRemoteHost() does exactly that. On the phone, Surface's feedback() moves the widget, so a fader follows the timeline and other controllers.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
stateObjectThe resolved param values, such as params.resolve(…): { hue: 90, size: 5.5 }.
bindingsObject[]The bindings that autoSurface() returned.

Returns

{ name, value }[] One entry per binding that has a number in state: name is the widget's signal, value is the param scaled to 0..1 and held in range. A param that is missing, not a number, or with min equal to max is skipped.

Vibrates the phone for ms milliseconds where the browser can (Android Chrome); silent everywhere else, and enabled false turns it off.

keepAwake()#

function@openav/surface
keepAwake()

Asks the browser to keep the screen on (a screen wake lock) and asks again when the tab comes back. Returns { release() }.

A phone that is a controller dims and locks within a minute unless something holds the screen on. keepAwake() requests navigator.wakeLock.request('screen') right away if the page is visible. The operating system drops the lock whenever the page is hidden, so it asks again each time the page becomes visible. It is best effort and silent: a browser with no wake lock, or one that says no, just means the screen may still dim, and it never throws.

Before you call it

A page that is visible, on https or localhost (the wake lock only exists on secure pages). mountRemote() calls it for you.

Returns

{ release } release() stops asking and lets go of the lock.

lockViewport()#

function@openav/surface
lockViewport()

Makes a page behave like an instrument panel instead of a web page: no scrolling, no pinch zoom, no rubber-banding. Returns a function that undoes most of it.

It sets <meta name="viewport"> to width=device-width,initial-scale=1,maximum-scale=1,user-scalable=no,viewport-fit=cover (making the tag if there is none) and adds a style that gives html and body no margin, the full height, overflow: hidden, overscroll-behavior: none and touch-action: none. iOS ignores user-scalable=no, so it also cancels gesturestart and gesturechange (pinch zoom) and the default of every touchmove, except one that starts in an input or textarea, so a text box still works.

This is for a page that is a control panel, such as mountRemote(), which calls it. Do not call it on a page that has to scroll. Without a document (in Node) it returns a function that does nothing.

Returns

Function Call it to remove the stylesheet and the listeners. The viewport <meta> stays as it was set.

planKeyboard()#

function@openav/surface
planKeyboard({ width, height, base = 48, minKeyPx = 38, maxWhites = 22, stackBelow = 2.2, forceRows = 0 })

Decides how many piano keys, in how many rows, fit a box: one wide row, or two stacked rows when the box is tall, so keys stay a playable size.

A piano is two and a half metres wide and a phone held upright is six centimetres, so shrinking the keys makes a toy. Instead the keyboard changes shape with its box. A wide box gets one row with as many octaves as fit at minKeyPx or wider. A tall box gets two rows, the upper one continuing the pitch range where the lower stops, within reach of a thumb. The rows end on E or B and the next one starts on the next white key, so no black key is left alone at the seam. Notes stop at 127. The keyboard widget of Surface calls this every time its box changes size.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
widthNumberThe width of the box, in pixels. optional
heightNumberThe height of the box, in pixels. optional
baseNumberThe MIDI note of the lowest key. 48 is C3 (C4 is 60). optional default 48
minKeyPxNumberThe narrowest a white key may be, in pixels. At least 3 white keys are kept. optional default 38
maxWhitesNumberThe most white keys in a row. Two stacked rows are limited to 14 each. optional default 22
stackBelowNumberStack into two rows when width ÷ height is below this. optional default 2.2
forceRows1 | 21 or 2 to decide yourself; 0 lets the shape of the box decide. optional default 0

Returns

{ stacked, whites, keyPx, rows } stacked is true for two rows, whites the white keys in a row, keyPx the width of a white key. rows is a list of { base, semitones, whites }, the top row first (the higher notes), the way two keyboards are read: base is the MIDI note of the first key and semitones how many notes the row spans.

resolvePage()#

function@openav/surface
resolvePage(page, orientation)

Works out where every widget of one page goes for one orientation: the grid and a cell for each widget, and which rule produced it.

A phone gets turned, so a layout has to survive it. The rules, in order: 1. If the page has a portrait or landscape entry for this orientation, use its grid and its place ({ widgetId: { x, y, w, h } }); widgets it does not mention keep their own position, or are packed into free cells (source is 'explicit'). 2. Else, if the base grid has the right shape (more columns than rows is landscape) and every widget has an x and a y, use the base ('base'). 3. Else reflow: the same widgets in reading order, packed again into half the columns (portrait, at least 2) or twice as many (landscape, up to 16), with a lone last row stretched to the edge by stretchRows() ('reflow').

Rows are a count, not pixels, so the result always fills the screen and nothing scrolls. A widget without w and h takes the size of its type from DEFAULT_SIZE. Surface calls this for every page each time the orientation changes.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
pageObjectOne page of a layout: { grid, widgets, portrait?, landscape? }.
orientation'portrait' | 'landscape'Which way the screen is held.

Returns

{ grid, placements, source } grid is { cols, rows }, placements a list of { id, x, y, w, h }, source is 'explicit', 'base' or 'reflow'.

Examples

signalSink(signals)

Makes a sink for a Surface that writes straight into a Signals registry: for a panel on the same page as the show, with no phone and no relay.

A name it has not met is declared first: { kind: 'pulse' } when info.pulse is set, otherwise { min: 0, max: 1 }. Then a pulse fires with signals.pulse() and anything else is signals.set(). So a route in the mapper, { source: 'surface/main/hue', target: 'hue' }, works whether the finger is on this page or on a phone.

stretchRows()#

function@openav/surface
stretchRows(placements, cols)

Stretches a last row that stops short to the edge of the grid: five faders in four columns leave one lonely fader, and this makes it four columns wide.

A row is stretched only when it is safe: its widgets are all the same height, side by side with no gaps from the left edge, and nothing else sits to their right. The extra columns are dealt out one at a time from left to right, so a short row of three in four columns gives the first widget two columns. A row that does not qualify is left alone, and nothing ever overlaps. resolvePage() calls it at the end of a reflow.

Surface#

class@openav/surface
new Surface(container, { layout, sink, haptics = true, tabs = true, orientation = null, onPage = null } = {})

A TouchOSC-style control panel: draws the pages and widgets of a layout in a container, and sends each touch out as a named signal.

Pass new Surface(container, { layout, sink }) and a panel appears: faders, knobs, an XY pad, pads, a keyboard, whatever the layout names, each with its live number. Widgets are dumb on purpose. Fingers go in, named normalized signals come out of sink, and the surface never knows what the work is. Run it on the show page with signalSink(), or on a phone with a sink that sends to the relay: the same layout works for both. A world's params can grow the whole layout by themselves with autoSurface().

The grid always fills the container and nothing scrolls. When the container is turned, the page is laid out again for the new orientation by resolvePage(): a portrait or landscape variant in the layout if there is one, else the base grid, else the same widgets packed again into half or double the columns. Touching a widget outlines it in its colour, and a double-tap on a fader or knob returns it to its default.

Runner to widget goes the other way: feedback(name, value) moves a fader to follow the timeline, or fills a meter. A widget under a finger ignores feedback while it is touched and for about half a second after, so it does not fight the hand (a button only while it is held).

Before you call it

A browser page (it builds DOM) and a container with a size. The panel injects its look once with injectTheme(). Nothing else to start: it works on the first touch. On a phone page, lockViewport() stops the page from scrolling and zooming under the fingers.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
containerHTMLElementWhere the panel goes. The panel is position: absolute and fills it, so the container needs a position (position: relative) and a size, or the panel has none.
layoutObjectThe layout JSON (see validateLayout()): pages, a grid, widgets. A bad layout throws an error that lists every problem. optional
sinkFunction(name, value, info) => {}, called for every signal a touch makes. name is like surface/main/hue, value is normalized 0..1 (an event is info.pulse, a string for a text box). When a widget's range is not 0..1, info.raw holds the unscaled value, and a second call follows with the name …/raw. signalSink() writes into a Signals; a phone passes one that calls relay.set. optional
hapticsBooleanBuzz the phone briefly on a button, a toggle, a radio choice or a double-tap reset, where the browser can (Android Chrome). false turns it off. optional default true
tabsBooleanShow a tab strip when the layout has more than one page. false hides it, and you switch with setPage(). optional default true
orientation'portrait' | 'landscape'Force the orientation. Left out, it follows the container's shape (wider than tall is landscape) and changes when the container does. optional default null
onPageFunction(pageId) => {}, when the page changes, and once at the start with the first page. optional default null

THEME_VARS#

constant@openav/surface

The look of every control as 15 CSS custom properties on :root (--oav-bg, --oav-accent …): override them to re-skin the whole surface.

The design is a set of rules rather than decoration, because a controller is used in the dark, fast and half-looking: dark cards on near-black, the only saturated thing on screen is a value, every touch target at least 44 px (--oav-touch-min), the number you are changing always visible, and a pressed widget outlines itself in its colour. Everything is a CSS variable, so a work re-skins the surface by overriding a few of them, never by editing widget code.

injectTheme() writes these values into the page once. Override after that, on document.documentElement or in your own stylesheet, with a rule that comes later on :root.

Object

Property name to its default value: --oav-bg #0a0c11, --oav-surface #141922, --oav-surface-2 #1b2230, --oav-line #283044, --oav-text #e8ecf5, --oav-dim #8691a8, --oav-accent #7ea6ff, --oav-ok #3ddc84, --oav-warn #f5a524, --oav-bad #e5484d, --oav-radius 14px, --oav-gap 8px, --oav-touch-min 44px, --oav-font (the system font) and --oav-mono (a monospace font).

The widget classes, one per type, that Surface builds from a layout: WIDGET_CLASSES.fader, .knob, .xy and so on (advanced).

Most pages never touch it: Surface looks each spec.type up here. It is exported for code that wants a single widget without a whole panel. spec is the widget's entry of the layout ({ id, type, label, min, max, … }) and ctx is { page, out(name, value, info), haptic(ms) }, where out is where the widget's signals go and page is the page id used in their names. A widget's element is .el; put it in the page yourself.

Adding your own key here does not make a new layout type: validateLayout() only accepts the names in WIDGET_TYPES.

Object

An object with the same 14 keys as WIDGET_TYPES, each a class: new WIDGET_CLASSES[type](spec, ctx).

WIDGET_TYPES#

constant@openav/surface
WIDGET_TYPES = array, 14 items

The names of the 14 widget types a layout may use: fader, knob, encoder, button, toggle, xy, bank, radio, pads, keyboard, number, text, label, meter.

Each widget publishes under surface/<page>/<id>, normalized 0..1; when its range is not 0..1 the unscaled value also goes out as …/raw. What each type sends:

text
fader, knob, number   <id>
button                 <id>  1 while held, 0 on release
toggle                 <id>  1 or 0
encoder                <id> (phase 0..1, wraps) and <id>/delta (turns)
xy                     <id>/x  <id>/y  <id>/down
bank                   <id>/1 … <id>/N        (count, default 8)
radio                  <id> = index / (n - 1), raw = index
pads                   <id>/hit {pad,row,col,vel}  and  <id>/<n> while held
keyboard               midi/note/on  midi/note/off  midi/cc/64
text                   <id>  a string, as a pulse
label, meter           nothing: they only receive feedback

Fields every widget accepts: id, type, label, min, max, def, step, unit, color (one of COLOR_NAMES) and, for hand-written layouts, target, the param key that routesFromLayout() turns into a route. Others by type: orient (v, h or auto) on a fader, spring: true on an XY pad, count and labels on a bank, options on a radio, rows, cols and labels on pads, pulse on a button.

Type
string[]

The keys of DEFAULT_SIZE, in that order. validateLayout() rejects any type that is not in it.

widgetTypeFor()#

Picks the widget type for one param declaration: a button for a pulse, a toggle, a radio, a fader or a knob.

The rules, first match wins: a surface: { type } hint on the param; pulse is a button; step: 1 over a range of 1 (two values) is a toggle; step: 1 over a range of 2 to 6 (three to seven values) is a radio; style 'knob' or 'fader' as asked; otherwise a fader, or a knob when continuousCount is above 6. Console and monitor#

The director's console and the backstage monitor feed. 4

@openav/console

mountConsole()#

function@openav/console
mountConsole(root, app, opts = {})

Mounts the director's desk into an element: transport and scrubber, layers overview, inputs, mapping, param sliders, signal meters and a fullscreen performance mode.

The desk reads the same objects the loop runs and owns nothing. From top to bottom it has the transport (play, previous and next scene, reset, the clock) and a scrubber with a block for every scene (with a tick for every cue, and a dashed end for a hold, when the scenes have them); with a score, the Director panel; the Layers overview (L1 input, L2 mapping, L3 world, L4 output); L1 · Input (MIDI devices, 🎤 mic, 🖐 hands, 🕺 body, leap); L2 · Mapping (the routes with a mute box and ✕, 🎛 map knobs in order, ⬇ export, ⬆ import, clear); L3 · Params (a slider per param with ✕ to clear the override and a learn chip; a yellow label means overridden); L4 · sound when there is a sound engine; and the Signals meters with the MIDI log. Every panel header collapses its section.

Keyboard, on the whole window: Space play and pause (at a hold: release it), → and ← next and previous scene (→ at a hold releases it), R back to the start, T performance mode (a fullscreen teleprompter for the performer: scene title, note and acts, the clock, the next scene, a HOLD banner), F fullscreen, Esc stops the mapping wizard or leaves keyboard-piano capture. Typing in an input field, a held key and any combination with ⌘, Ctrl or Alt are ignored. While the on-screen piano captures the keyboard the letters (R, T, F) belong to the piano; Space, the arrows and Esc always work.

Before you call it

Call desk.render(state) every frame after stage.frame() (a show's loop does): the desk only redraws when you tell it to. state is the resolved params, params.resolve(timeline.state()).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
rootHTMLElementThe element to build the desk in. It gets the class oav-console, and the desk's styles are added once to the head.
appObjectThe objects the desk reads: { timeline, params, mapper, signals, stage } are needed, and midi, controllers, keys, sound, audio, hands, pose, leap, chord, remote, drums, loop, osc, score, director are optional. A missing part hides its section. createShow() passes show.app.
optsObject{ layers: false } and { signals: false } leave out the Layers and Signals panels; { learnOrder: ['hue', 'size'] } sets the order of the 🎛 map knobs in order wizard (default: the params as declared, skipping hidden ones and any with wizard: false). optional default {}

Returns

Object { render(state), perf, director, wizard, dispose() }: render redraws the desk, perf is the performance mode (toggle(), active, render()), director the Director panel (or null), wizard the knob-mapping wizard, and dispose() removes the keyboard handler and empties the element.

Notes

  • The keyboard handler is on window, so two desks on one page both answer the keys. dispose() removes it. The performance mode's teleprompter is appended to document.body, not to root.
  • Touch a slider (or a mapped control) and that param leaves the timeline's hands until you press its ✕: the score gives way when a person grabs a control.

Where the backstage relay is unless told otherwise: the page's own host on port 7457 as a ws:// address, and null on an https page or where there is no page.

It is the default url of MonitorFeed. Not on an https page: the browser blocks ws:// there (mixed content, logged as an error), and a page published over https (openaudiovisual.com, a tunnel) has no relay beside it. A show that runs one behind TLS passes { url: 'wss://…' } explicitly.

MonitorFeed#

class@openav/monitor
new MonitorFeed({ url = defaultMonitorUrl(), hz = 15 } = {})

Streams snapshots of the running show to the backstage relay over a WebSocket, at most hz times a second, and quietly keeps trying when there is no relay.

A show without a backstage is a rehearsal. Run the relay on the machine that serves the show (node packages/monitor/server.js, port 7457, which also serves the backstage page at / and GET /health), and a stage manager's phone or laptop on the same network opens http://<that machine>:7457/ to see the clock, the scene, the world, the frame rate, the overrides and every signal and param live, with a red "stage feed lost" banner when the stage stops sending for 4 seconds. The show page joins as ?role=stage; every other socket is a monitor. createShow() already creates and connects one, so you only build a MonitorFeed for a show you assembled by hand.

It is made to cost nothing when left on: with no relay it reconnects with a growing delay (about 5 seconds, growing by 1.6 each time up to 30), though the browser logs each refused connection, and that message is expected. frame() throttles itself, so call it every frame with a snapshot (see snapshotOf()).

Before you call it

Call connect() once (a show does), then frame(snapshot) every frame. frame() does nothing while connected is false. The relay must be reachable from the page: on an https page the browser blocks ws:// (mixed content), so give a wss:// address explicitly.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
urlString | nullThe relay address, such as 'ws://192.168.1.20:7457' (?role=stage is added for you). The default comes from defaultMonitorUrl(): the page's own host on port 7457, and null on an https page. With null, connect() does nothing. optional default defaultMonitorUrl()
hzNumberThe most snapshots sent per second. optional default 15

Members

NameDescription
connect()methodOpen the socket. Does nothing without a url. If the connection drops or cannot be made, it tries again after a growing delay. The onStatus(ok) hook is called when it connects and when it drops.
frame(snapshot)methodSend a snapshot (anything that survives JSON.stringify; snapshotOf() builds the usual one). The message is { at: Date.now(), ...snapshot }. Throttled to hz: calls closer together than that are dropped, and nothing is sent while disconnected.

Notes

  • Fields to read and set: url (with ?role=stage appended, or null), hz, connected, ws, and the hook onStatus = (ok) => {}.
  • On a public https page a hand-assembled show that connects to ws://127.0.0.1:7457 meets Chrome's Local Network Access prompt (from Chrome 147 for WebSockets, per the package README): press Allow, or open the page from http://localhost.

checkMesh()#

function@openav/fab
checkMesh(input, opts = {})

Measures a triangle mesh for 3D printing: closed or not, volume, mass, overhang, thinnest wall, fit on the bed, with a plain warning for each problem.

Pure and synchronous, with no DOM. Duplicate vertices are merged first (within 1e-6 of the bounding-box diagonal), because without that every un-indexed mesh (three.js toNonIndexed(), an STL, any triangle soup) reads as open. In the report: triangles (after merging; a face that collapses is dropped), bbox as { min, max, size } in mm, volume in mm³ (always positive; a mesh wound inside out is measured the right way round), watertight (every edge used by exactly two faces, in opposite directions) with the counts openEdges, nonManifoldEdges and inconsistentEdges behind it, and grams: { PETG, PLA }, the weight of the volume as solid plastic (1.27 and 1.24 g/cm³).

overhang is { angle, area, ratio }: the area (mm²) of faces that look down steeper than angle allows, and its share of the whole surface. Faces that rest on the lowest 0.2 mm (the bed) do not count. minWall is { value, min, median, samples } or null: rays are shot into the part from sampled faces, and value is the 5th percentile of the thicknesses found, which is how thin most of the wall is. min is the single thinnest sample, which on a part with holes drilled at an angle is a knife edge and says little about the wall, so it has its own milder note.

warnings is a list of one sentence each, in Chinese: not watertight (with the three counts), overhang above overhangWarn, a wall thinner than minWall, a knife edge thinner than half of it, and a size beyond bed. An empty list means nothing to report. fab.check(x) is checkMesh(meshOf(x), opts).

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
inputTriMeshA mesh { vertices, triangles, units? }: vertices a Float32Array or Float64Array of x, y, z, x, y, z …, triangles a Uint32Array with three vertex numbers per face, counter-clockwise seen from outside, Z up, in millimetres. Use meshOf() to get one from something else.
optsObjectangle (45): the overhang angle in degrees. minWall (1.2): the thinnest wall allowed, in mm. bed ([320, 320, 325]): the size of the print bed in mm. wallSamples (2000): how many faces to measure the wall from; fewer is faster. overhangWarn (0.15): the share of overhanging area that earns a warning. weld (true): merge duplicate vertices first; false skips it. optional default {}

Returns

Object { units, triangles, bbox, volume, watertight, openEdges, nonManifoldEdges, inconsistentEdges, overhang, minWall, grams, warnings }. See the description.

Notes

  • grams is the weight of a solid part: it does not know about infill or wall count, so a sliced print weighs less.

Examples

Exports a shape as STL, OBJ, GLB, STEP or DXF and resolves to { bytes, mime, ext, report }: the same as fab.export(), without the Fab class.

Fab#

class@openav/fab
new Fab(opts = {})

Checks a shape for 3D printing and exports it as STL, OBJ, GLB, STEP or DXF; takes a mesh, a three.js object or a smlibwasm solid.

Make one Fab and hand it whatever you made: fab.check(x) returns a manufacturability report (is it closed, how much material, how much overhang, how thin is the thinnest wall, how many grams), and await fab.export(x, 'stl') returns the file as bytes. x can be a plain triangle mesh { vertices, triangles }, a three.js Mesh, Object3D or BufferGeometry (recognised by its shape, three.js is never imported), or a smlibwasm Part or Shape. meshOf() says exactly what is accepted.

Formats: stl, obj and glb work for any input; step only for a smlibwasm Part, and dxf only for a smlibwasm Shape or Sketch, because a mesh has no curved-surface information. The CAD kernels are not bundled: the first time one is needed, fab.smlib() or fab.manifold() imports it from a URL (unpkg by default) and remembers it.

fab.save() writes the file through fab.saver if you set one (the lab's dev server does), and otherwise as a browser download. Zero runtime dependencies: nothing is fetched until you ask for a kernel.

Before you call it

Nothing for meshes and three.js objects. A smlibwasm Part has to be tessellated by the kernel: call await fab.smlib() once before the synchronous check(), or use checkAsync(), meshOfAsync() and export(), which load it for you. Loading needs a network, or urls / window.__LAB__.vendor pointing somewhere that has the kernel.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
optsObject{ scale, urls, importer, download, context }, all optional. scale is millimetres per unit for a three.js object (10 means one three.js unit is 10 mm). urls is { smlib, manifold }, a URL or a list of them, to load the CAD kernels from. importer(url) replaces the dynamic import() that loads a kernel. download(bytes, info) replaces the browser download that save() falls back to. context() returns { id, params } for save() to put in info. optional default {}

Members

NameDescription
smlib()methodsmlib(): a promise of the smlibwasm module, imported on the first call and remembered (the same promise comes back). A failed load is forgotten, so the next call tries again.
manifold()methodmanifold(): the same for manifold-3d. The WebAssembly is initialised for you (setup() is called), and the result is the ready-to-use module.
meshOf(x, opts = {})methodmeshOf(x, opts?): the same as meshOf(), with this Fab's scale and, once smlib() has loaded, the kernel's tessellator.
meshOfAsync(x, opts = {})methodmeshOfAsync(x, opts?): the same as meshOfAsync(), and it loads the smlib kernel when it needs it.

checkAsync(x, opts = {})methodcheckAsync(x, opts?): the same through meshOfAsync, so a smlibwasm Part works without loading the kernel first. Returns a promise of the report.

fromMeshLike()#

function@openav/fab
fromMeshLike(m, scale = 1)

Turns a mesh-like object (positions and indices under any of the usual names) into a triangle mesh, multiplying the positions by scale.

This is what meshOf() uses for a kernel's tessellation result, whichever way the kernel spells it. It throws an Error (in Chinese) when m is empty or has no positions. It does not check that the faces point outward or that the mesh is closed: that is checkMesh().

fromStlBytes()#

function@openav/fab
fromStlBytes(bytes)

Reads a binary STL file back into a triangle mesh: every face has its own three vertices, in 32-bit floats.

It reads what toStlBytes() writes, or any binary STL: the normals and the two attribute bytes are skipped, and the result is a triangle soup. Give it to checkMesh(), which merges the vertices itself, or to weldMesh(). The text (ASCII) form of STL, which starts with solid, is not supported and would read as garbage.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
bytesUint8ArrayThe contents of a binary STL file. The face count is read from the header; the file's length is not checked against it.

Returns

TriMesh { vertices: Float32Array (9 per face), triangles: Uint32Array (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 …), units: 'mm' }.

loadKernel()#

function@openav/fab
async loadKernel(kind, opts = {})

Imports a CAD kernel (smlibwasm or manifold-3d) from the first URL that works, and resolves to the ready module.

The kernels are not bundled, because open-audiovisual has no dependencies and no build step: the first time a page needs one, it is imported from a URL. The order is candidateUrls(): opts.urls[kind], then window.__LAB__.vendor[kind], then unpkg (DEFAULT_URLS). If every URL fails it rejects with an Error (in Chinese) that names each URL and why it failed. It does not remember anything: fab.smlib() and fab.manifold() keep the promise for you, so call those unless you want to manage it yourself.

Before you call it

A network, or urls pointing at a place that serves the kernel (the lab uses window.__LAB__.vendor), or an importer that returns one.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
kind'smlib' | 'manifold'Which kernel: 'smlib' for smlibwasm (solid modelling, STEP and DXF) or 'manifold' for manifold-3d (fast mesh booleans).
optsObjecturls: { smlib, manifold }, a URL or a list of URLs for each kernel. importer: async (url) => module, to use instead of the dynamic import(). optional default {}

Returns

Promise<Object> The smlibwasm module as it came, or the manifold-3d module with its WebAssembly started (setup() called).

Examples

meshOf()#

function@openav/fab
meshOf(x, opts = {})

Turns whatever you made into a triangle mesh { vertices, triangles, units }: a mesh, a three.js object, a mesh-like object or a smlibwasm shape.

Everything is recognised by its shape and nothing is imported, so three.js and smlibwasm are never loaded for you. A three.js object has its matrixWorld applied (a mirrored object keeps its faces facing outward), indexed or not, and Y up is turned into Z up as (x, y, z) → (x, −z, y), then everything is multiplied by scale. A missing input, or something it cannot read, throws an Error whose message (in Chinese) says what to do.

It is synchronous, so it cannot wait for a kernel: a smlibwasm solid without opts.tessellator throws a message that tells you to load the kernel first, and a tessellate() that returns a promise throws too. Use meshOfAsync() for those.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
xObjectThe thing to convert. Accepted, tried in this order: a mesh { vertices, triangles } (returned as it is); a three.js Mesh, Object3D (every visible mesh below it) or BufferGeometry; anything with a tessellate() method; an object with positions / vertices / points and, optionally, indices / triangles / faces / index; a smlibwasm solid or shape (given opts.tessellator).
optsObjectscale: millimetres per unit for a three.js or mesh-like input (default 1). A mesh { vertices, triangles } is never scaled. tessellator(shape): a function that turns a smlibwasm shape into a mesh (the Fab class passes the kernel's once it is loaded). tessellate: an argument passed on to the shape's own tessellate(). optional default {}

Returns

TriMesh { vertices, triangles, units }: counter-clockwise faces seen from outside, Z up, millimetres.

Examples

meshOfAsync()#

function@openav/fab

Like meshOf(), but it waits for a tessellate() that returns a promise, and can load the smlibwasm kernel to tessellate a solid.

Use it where the conversion may have to wait: a shape whose tessellate() is asynchronous, or a smlibwasm Part when the kernel is not loaded yet. With opts.kernel.smlib it awaits the module and uses its tessellate(part); an error says so if the module has none. Everything else is passed on to meshOf(). fab.meshOfAsync() fills in kernel for you.

toGlbBytes()#

function@openav/fab
toGlbBytes(mesh)

Writes a triangle mesh as a minimal binary glTF (.glb): one mesh with welded positions and indices, in millimetres.

Vertices are welded first with weldMesh(). The file has POSITION and indices only: no normals, no materials, no colours, so a viewer shades it flat or works the normals out itself. The positions stay in millimetres and Z up, and asset.extras says { units: 'mm', up: 'Z' }. glTF itself assumes Y up, so a viewer that does not read the extras shows the part lying on its side.

await fab.export(part, 'glb') of a smlibwasm Part uses the kernel's own toGlb when it has one, and this function otherwise.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
meshTriMeshA mesh { vertices, triangles }, in millimetres.

Returns

Uint8Array A glTF 2.0 binary: the glTF header, one JSON chunk, one binary chunk with 32-bit float positions and 32-bit indices. The length is a multiple of 4.

toStlBytes()#

function@openav/fab
toStlBytes(mesh)

Writes a triangle mesh as a binary STL file: 84 + 50 bytes per face, with a normal worked out for every face.

Every face becomes its own 50 bytes: STL has no shared vertices. The normal comes from the order of the corners (right-hand rule), so counter-clockwise faces seen from outside give outward normals. Positions are written as they are, as float32: nothing is converted to millimetres, so give it a mesh that is already in mm. await fab.export(x, 'stl') is the same thing with the conversions and the check done for you.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
meshTriMeshA mesh { vertices, triangles }, in millimetres.

Returns

Uint8Array The file: an 80-byte header (the text open-audiovisual fab STL (mm)), the face count as a little-endian 32-bit integer, then per face the normal and three corners as 32-bit floats and two zero bytes.

Examples

weldMesh()#

function@openav/fab
weldMesh(mesh, tolerance)

Merges vertices that sit closer together than a tolerance and drops the faces that collapse; returns a new mesh with shared vertices.

A triangle soup, where every face has three vertices of its own (what an STL file or three.js toNonIndexed() gives), has no neighbours as far as topology goes: every edge looks open. Welding gives the faces shared vertices, so checkMesh() can see that they join. checkMesh(), toObjText() and toGlbBytes() call it themselves; toStlBytes() does not need it.

Parameters

NameTypeDescription
meshTriMeshA mesh { vertices, triangles }. It is not changed.
toleranceNumberVertices closer than this (in each of x, y and z) become one, in the mesh's units. Left out: 1e-6 times the diagonal of the bounding box. optional

Returns

TriMesh { vertices: Float64Array, triangles: Uint32Array, units } with each position once, and no face that has two corners on the same vertex.

list_controllers#

tool@openav/mcp
list_controllers

Lists every MIDI controller profile that ships with the framework: id, name, maker, kind, control mix, how many controls are unverified, and its page URL.

No input: send "arguments": {}. It reads the profiles in packages/midi/profiles/, the same ones the controller pages and <oav-controller> use. Use it to find the id for read_profile, or to check that a controller is already covered before writing a new profile with scaffold_profile.

Returns

Object { count, controllers } as JSON text. Each controller is { id, short, name, maker, kind, controls, unverified, url }: id such as arturia-minilab3, short the signal namespace (midi/<short>/…), kind 'device' or 'generic', controls the mix as { knob: 8, pad: 8, keys: 25 } (a keyboard counts one per key), unverified how many of those controls still carry "verified": false, url like https://openaudiovisual.com/controllers/<id>/.

read_doc

Returns the text of one framework document: the agent briefing, a handbook chapter or the README, chosen by name.

Most names are docs/<name>.md. Two are not, and they are easy to mix up: agents is AGENTS.md at the root of the repository (the briefing), agents-guide is docs/agents.md (the handbook chapter), and readme is README.md.

read_profile

Reads one controller profile in full, plus a readable MIDI map: for each control its type, the exact message, the signal name and whether the number is verified.

Input: id (required), a profile id or its short, for example arturia-minilab3 or minilab3. Where a control says verified: false, its number is a placeholder or a guess that no source has confirmed yet. An unknown id is an error that lists every id it knows. list_controllers shows what is there.

tool@openav/mcp
run_checks

Runs the framework's whole test suite (node --test on every file in tests/), the same gate CI uses, and says whether it passed.

No input: send "arguments": {}. An agent calls it after every change to know whether the repository is still green. It runs node --test over every tests/*.test.js of the checkout the server lives in, waits for it to finish and gives up after 60 seconds.

Returns

Object When the run finishes cleanly: { pass, fail, ok } (numbers from the report, and ok true only when fail is 0), as JSON text. Otherwise { ok: false, output }, where output holds the lines of the report that say not ok or give the totals.

Notes

  • At the time of writing, in the checkout this was written from, the whole suite takes about 50 seconds and prints about 3.6 MB of report, while the tool reads at most 1 MiB of it. Past that the child process is stopped, and the tool answers { ok: false, output } with only the failing lines found in that first megabyte, even if every test passes. Until that changes, do not read ok: false with an empty output as a failing test: run node --test tests/*.test.js in a terminal.

scaffold_profile#

tool@openav/mcp
scaffold_profile

Generates a valid skeleton profile for a new controller from maker, model and control counts. Every number is an unverified placeholder; nothing is written.

Input, all required: maker (such as Arturia), model (such as MiniLab 3) and controls, a list of { type, count, from? } that describes the faceplate, for example [{"type":"knob","count":8},{"type":"pad","count":8},{"type":"keys","count":25,"from":48}]. type is one of knob, encoder, fader, pad, button, keys, wheel, strip; count is a whole number from 1 to 128; from is the lowest note of a keys section (default 48).

The skeleton passes validateProfile() and it is deliberately honest: every control has "verified": false, the source list holds one TODO entry, and the numbers are placeholders. Knobs, faders and strips get consecutive CC numbers from 20, pads get notes from 36 (skipping a keys range), buttons get momentary CCs, encoders get relative CCs, the first wheel is a pitch bend and any further wheel falls back to a CC. The id comes from maker and model (acme-pad-pro-16), short is the model without hyphens, and match.ports is a pattern made of the model's words.

Wrong input is an error with the reason: no maker or model, controls empty or not a list, an unknown type, a count outside 1..128, keys outside notes 0..127, or more controls than there are CC numbers (about 108) or pad notes. After that the agent sources every number from the maker's MIDI chart, runs validate_profile, and saves the file in packages/midi/profiles/; next_steps lists these.

Returns

Object { profile, problems, unverified, next_steps } as JSON text, plus warnings when the id or short name collides with a shipped profile. profile is the skeleton, problems is what validateProfile() says about it (empty), unverified is how many controls are placeholders (all of them), next_steps is what to do to turn it into a real profile.

scaffold_world#

tool@openav/mcp
scaffold_world

Creates a new numbered example by copying a donor example's files; then the agent edits the World in main.js. This tool writes to disk.

Input: slug (required), a kebab-case name made of lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, such as jellyfish-bloom; and donor (optional, default 01-hello-particles), the name of a folder in examples/ to copy. Good donors: 01-hello-particles (a minimal canvas), 02-chord-garden (driven by chords), 03-pose-field (the camera), 05-prebiotic-flake (p5 and sound). The new folder is examples/<number>-<slug>, where the number is the highest one already in examples/ plus 1, with two digits (28).

It copies every file of the donor folder (the donors have no sub-folders, and a sub-folder would stop the copy with an error), so the new example starts as a working copy. A slug with anything else in it, or an unknown donor, or a folder that already exists is an error (slug must be kebab-case, unknown donor: …, already exists: …).

Returns

Object { created, next_steps } as JSON text: created is the new folder (examples/28-jellyfish-bloom), next_steps is three lines: edit the World in main.js, edit the <title> and hint in index.html, then open it with node serve.js.

Notes

  • Send slug every time. It is marked required in the input schema, but the tool does not check that it is there: without it the folder is created with the name examples/<number>-undefined.
  • donor is used as a folder name without further checks, so give it a plain name from examples/.

tool@openav/mcp
validate_profile

Checks a controller profile with validateProfile() and against the shipped ones: same id, same short name, or port patterns that claim the same device.

Input: profile (required), the profile as an object or as a JSON string. A string that is not valid JSON does not raise an error: the answer is { ok: false, problems: ['not valid JSON: …'], conflicts: [] }. The checks cover the id and short name (lower-case, and short must not be one of the reserved generic names), a name and a kind (device or generic), a source for every device profile, the port regular expressions, the faceplate size, every control (a known type and message, cc or note in 0..127, two controls never on the same message, an encoder's relative mode) and that every control is shown on the faceplate.

The conflicts are what the validator cannot see by itself: id and short are taken by a shipped profile (the short becomes the signal namespace midi/<short>/…), and port means a regular expression in match.ports is identical to a shipped one or matches its name, so the framework could not tell the two devices apart when one is plugged in. A profile for a new device passes when ok is true; a clone of a shipped one comes back with all three kinds.

Returns

Object { ok, problems, conflicts } as JSON text. problems is a list of sentences from validateProfile() (controls[0] (a): cc must be 0..127). conflicts is a list of { with, kind, detail }: with is the shipped profile, kind is 'id', 'short' or 'port'. ok is true only when both are empty.

Examples

Related

  • scaffold_profile Generates a valid skeleton profile for a new controller from maker, model and control counts. Every number is an unverified placeholder; nothing is written.
  • read_profile Reads one controller profile in full, plus a readable MIDI map: for each control its type, the exact message, the signal name and whether the number is verified.
  • list_controllers Lists every MIDI controller profile that ships with the framework: id, name, maker, kind, control mix, how many controls are unverified, and its page URL.
